input.title: Land Office Returns from Calder County, Nebraska, 1863-1873

sources.title: Homestead Entries and Railroad Land Sales, Calder County, Nebraska, 1863-1873
sources.attribution: Compiled by Elias Varnum, register of the fictional Calder County land office, for an 1874 report to the General Land Office; ALTON-composed illustrative data, not real statistics (ALTON-composed, in the style of a nineteenth-century federal land office return)
sources.body: The table shows the number of homestead entries filed at a fictional Nebraska land office and the acres of railroad grant land sold to settlers in the same county in selected years from 1863 to 1873.

columns: Railroad grant land sold to settlers (acres)

items.stem: The Homestead Act of 1862 encouraged filings like those recorded in the table chiefly by

options.text: offering 160 acres of public land to settlers who lived on and improved it for five years
options.label: key
options.why: The Homestead Act granted up to 160 acres of public land to settlers who resided on and cultivated it for five years, which drove the rising entries at land offices like the one in the table.

options.text: granting each state federal land whose sale would fund colleges of agriculture and the mechanic arts
options.label: misattributed
options.why: This describes the Morrill Land-Grant College Act of 1862, a different law passed the same year, not the Homestead Act.

options.text: promising freedpeople forty acres of confiscated plantation land through a federal land redistribution law
options.label: unrelated_development
options.why: Congress never passed a law redistributing confiscated plantations to freedpeople. The forty-acre promise came from a wartime military order that was later reversed, and it had nothing to do with Nebraska homesteads.

options.text: banning slavery in the Nebraska Territory so that free white farmers could settle there without competition
options.label: reversal
options.why: The Kansas-Nebraska Act of 1854 did the opposite of a ban. It repealed the Missouri Compromise line and left slavery to popular sovereignty. The Homestead Act also said nothing about slavery.

facts: The Homestead Act of 1862 offered up to 160 acres of public land to settlers who lived on and improved it for five years.
The Morrill Act of 1862 granted federal land to states to fund agricultural and mechanical colleges.

items.stem: Which of the following claims is best supported by the data in the table?

options.text: Homestead filings and railroad land sales rose together in the years after 1865
options.label: key
options.why: Homestead entries went from 95 in 1865 to 880 in 1871. Railroad land sales went from zero to 41,000 acres over the same years, so the two rose together.

options.text: Homestead filings fell off once the railroad began selling its grant lands to incoming settlers at market prices
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: Homestead filings kept rising from 1867 to 1871 while railroad sales grew, so railroad sales did not push homesteading down.

options.text: The economic downturn of 1873 brought railroad land sales and homestead filings in the county to a complete halt
options.label: overstated
options.why: Both numbers dropped in 1873 but stayed well above zero (540 entries and 22,000 acres), so nothing came to a complete halt.

options.text: Most farmland in the county passed to settlers through purchase of land-grant college scrip rather than homesteading
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: The table has no data on college land scrip, so it cannot support any claim about how much land passed through scrip.

facts: The Pacific Railway Act of 1862 gave railroad companies land grants along their routes, which the companies sold to settlers.
The Union Pacific began building west from Omaha, Nebraska, in the mid-1860s.

derived.desc: Change in railroad acres sold, 1865 to 1871

items.stem: Congress passed the 1862 laws that encouraged the settlement shown in the table in the context of

options.text: the departure of Southern members of Congress who had blocked federal aid to western development
options.label: key
options.why: Southern lawmakers had blocked homestead and northern-route railroad bills because they feared free-soil expansion. After secession, the Republican majority passed the Homestead, Morrill, and Pacific Railway Acts in 1862.

options.text: the Compromise of 1850, which admitted California as a free state and organized the Utah and New Mexico territories
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The Compromise of 1850 came more than a decade earlier and dealt with lands taken from Mexico, not with homestead or railroad legislation.

options.text: Populist Party demands that the federal government nationalize railroads and expand credit for farmers
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The Populist Party formed in the early 1890s, three decades after these laws were passed.

options.text: peace treaties that followed the Battle of the Little Bighorn and opened the northern Plains to settlers
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The Battle of the Little Bighorn took place in 1876, long after the 1862 laws were passed.

facts: Congress passed the Homestead, Morrill, and Pacific Railway Acts in 1862, after the secession of Southern states removed much of the opposition.
The Battle of the Little Bighorn took place in 1876.

items.stem: The decline in both homestead filings and railroad land sales between 1871 and 1873 shown in the table was most likely connected to

options.text: a financial panic set off by the failure of a major bank heavily invested in railroad bonds
options.label: key
options.why: The Panic of 1873 started when a major banking house that had overextended itself on railroad bonds collapsed. The depression that followed cut into railroad expansion and western land sales.

options.text: the Dawes Act's allotment of reservation lands, which flooded western markets with acreage for sale
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The Dawes Act passed in 1887, more than a decade after the 1873 decline.

options.text: the withdrawal of federal troops from Southern statehouses as part of the bargain that settled the election of 1876
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The Compromise of 1877 came after the decline and dealt with Southern Reconstruction, not Plains land sales.

options.text: drought and falling crop prices that led Plains farmers to organize the Farmers' Alliances in the late 1880s
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The Farmers' Alliances grew in the 1880s and cannot explain a drop that happened in 1873.

facts: The Panic of 1873 began with the failure of a major banking house heavily invested in railroad financing.
The Dawes Severalty Act was passed in 1887.

derived.desc: Percent change in homestead entries, 1871 to 1873
Percent change in railroad acres sold, 1871 to 1873

input.title: Removal of Japanese Americans from the Pacific Coast, 1942

sources.title: A historian on the local roots of Japanese American removal
sources.attribution: Harriet Selwyn, historian, Fields and Fences: Farming, Race, and Removal in the Arroyo Verde Valley, 1900-1945, a study of a fictional California farming district, published 2011 (ALTON-composed, in the style of a regional social history)
sources.body: When Army notices went up on telephone poles in the Arroyo Verde Valley in April 1942, ordering every person of Japanese ancestry to report for removal, the official reason was military necessity. Yet the orders landed in a district where Japanese farmers had been resented for thirty years. Issei growers there raised much of the valley's lettuce and strawberries, often on poor land they had made productive. California's Alien Land Law of 1913 had barred immigrants who could not become citizens from owning farmland, so many families held their acres in the names of their American-born children. In early 1942 a white growers' association from the valley sent a delegate to Washington to urge removal. A local editor wrote that the war gave the valley a chance to settle the Japanese question for good. Seen from Arroyo Verde, removal did not begin with Pearl Harbor. It finished a campaign that rival growers and nativist groups had waged for decades.

items.stem: Which of the following, if added to the excerpt, would most strengthen the author's argument about the causes of Japanese American removal?

options.text: Few people of Japanese ancestry in Hawaii, where they were a large share of the population, were sent to camps.
options.label: key
options.why: Selwyn argues that local hostility, not military necessity, drove removal. Hawaii was closer to the war and had a much larger Japanese American population, yet it saw no mass removal. That weakens the military-necessity explanation and supports her argument.

options.text: Military planners feared that Japan's navy, after its December 1941 attack on Pearl Harbor, could next strike the Pacific Coast.
options.label: reversal
options.why: Fear of an attack on the coast backs the official military-necessity reason, which is the explanation the author questions. It weakens her argument instead of strengthening it.

options.text: The War Relocation Authority later permitted thousands of camp residents to leave for jobs and college enrollment in the Midwest and East.
options.label: true_but_not_responsive
options.why: This is true, but it describes how the camps were run after removal. It says nothing about why removal happened in the first place.

options.text: Wartime farm labor shortages led the United States to begin recruiting Mexican agricultural workers through the Bracero Program in 1942.
options.label: unrelated_development
options.why: The Bracero Program was a real wartime labor measure, but it has nothing to do with the motives behind removing Japanese Americans.

facts: Executive Order 9066, signed in February 1942, authorized the removal of about 120,000 people of Japanese ancestry from the West Coast.
Despite a large Japanese American population in Hawaii, no mass removal took place there during World War II.

items.stem: Which of the following would most directly modify the author's argument about why the removal of Japanese Americans occurred?

options.text: Federal military commanders, citing espionage fears after Pearl Harbor, recommended and administered the removal.
options.label: key
options.why: The excerpt stresses local growers and nativists. Evidence that federal military authorities, acting on national security fears, drove the decision would push the argument toward national wartime causes and away from purely local pressure.

options.text: Many Japanese American families were forced to sell farms, equipment, and crops to neighbors at a fraction of their value.
options.label: reversal
options.why: Neighbors buying up farms at forced-sale prices fits the author's claim that economic rivals gained from removal. It supports her argument instead of modifying it.

options.text: Congress passed the Civil Liberties Act of 1988, formally apologizing and paying 20,000 dollars to each surviving internee.
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: This law came more than four decades later and dealt with redress. It cannot show what caused removal in 1942.

options.text: Some Nisei men volunteered from the camps to serve in the 442nd Regimental Combat Team, which fought with distinction in Europe.
options.label: true_but_not_responsive
options.why: The 442nd's service is true and shows Nisei loyalty, but it does not speak to whether local or national forces caused the removal.

facts: Military authorities, including the Army's Western Defense Command, recommended and carried out the 1942 exclusion of Japanese Americans from the West Coast.
The Civil Liberties Act of 1988 apologized and provided 20,000 dollars in compensation to surviving internees.

items.stem: The policy described in the excerpt is best understood in the context of which broader pattern in United States history?

options.text: Laws targeting Asian immigrants, such as the near-total ban on Japanese immigration in 1924
options.label: key
options.why: Removal followed decades of anti-Asian measures, including Chinese exclusion, the Gentlemen's Agreement, and the Immigration Act of 1924, which ended Japanese immigration. That is the racial and nativist background the author describes.

options.text: The federal campaign against suspected radicals during the Red Scare, including the Palmer Raids and deportations of 1919 and 1920
options.label: unrelated_development
options.why: The Red Scare went after people for their political beliefs, not their race or national ancestry. It does not fit the anti-Asian pattern behind removal.

options.text: Federal policy pressing Native Americans to assimilate by dividing reservation land into individual allotments under the Dawes Act
options.label: misattributed
options.why: Dawes Act allotment was about forcing Native Americans to assimilate. It is a different policy aimed at different people and was not part of the hostility toward Asian immigrant farmers.

options.text: World War I prosecutions of antiwar speakers under the Espionage and Sedition Acts, upheld by the Supreme Court in Schenck
options.label: true_but_not_responsive
options.why: These wartime limits on civil liberties were real, but they punished dissenting speech. They do not explain a policy aimed at a whole group by ancestry.

facts: The Immigration Act of 1924 effectively barred immigration from Japan.
California's Alien Land Law of 1913 barred immigrants ineligible for citizenship, chiefly Japanese, from owning agricultural land.

items.stem: Which of the following best explains how the Supreme Court responded during the Second World War to a legal challenge to the exclusion orders described in the excerpt?

options.text: It upheld the exclusion in Korematsu v. United States, deferring to claims of wartime military necessity.
options.label: key
options.why: In Korematsu v. United States (1944), the Court upheld the exclusion orders and accepted the government's claim that wartime military necessity justified them.

options.text: It struck down Executive Order 9066 in Korematsu v. United States as an unconstitutional classification based on race.
options.label: reversal
options.why: The Court did the opposite and upheld the exclusion. Korematsu's conviction was set aside only in 1983, by a lower federal court.

options.text: It applied the clear and present danger test from Schenck v. United States to overturn convictions of Nisei who resisted removal.
options.label: misattributed
options.why: Schenck (1919) was a World War I free speech case. Its test was not used to overturn the convictions of Japanese Americans who resisted removal.

options.text: It ruled that the Fourteenth Amendment barred any wartime restriction on citizens, forcing the Army to close every camp in 1942.
options.label: overstated
options.why: No such ruling happened. The camps stayed open through most of the war, and the Court did not issue a sweeping ban on wartime restrictions.

facts: In Korematsu v. United States (1944), the Supreme Court upheld the constitutionality of the exclusion of Japanese Americans from the West Coast.
Fred Korematsu's conviction was vacated by a federal district court in 1983.

input.title: Ledgers and Rifles: Economic Containment, 1947-1950

sources.title: Economic Aid and Early Containment
sources.attribution: Corinne Albrecht, Ledgers and Rifles: American Aid and the Remaking of Western Europe, 1947-1952, a university press monograph, 2009 (ALTON-composed, in the style of a diplomatic history monograph)
sources.body: Historians who picture the early Cold War as a contest of tanks and bombers miss how the Truman administration first chose to fight it. When the president asked Congress in March 1947 for aid to Greece and Turkey, he described the struggle as a choice between two ways of life. Even so, he asked for dollars and advisers, not American combat troops. The European Recovery Program, approved the following year, carried that logic further. State Department planners reasoned that hungry, unemployed voters in France and Italy, where communist parties polled strongly, were the Kremlin's best allies. Grain, coal, and machine tools, they believed, would do more than divisions of soldiers to keep western Europe out of Soviet hands. The aid also came with conditions. Recipients had to coordinate their recovery plans and lower barriers to trade, which tied them to one another and to the United States. Until 1950, containment was a wager that ledgers could accomplish what rifles could not.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes the author's main argument in the excerpt?

options.text: United States officials initially relied on economic aid to make western Europe less receptive to communism.
options.label: key
options.why: The author argues that planners expected grain, coal, and machine tools to undercut communist appeal, so containment before 1950 rested mainly on economic tools.

options.text: United States officials sought mainly to roll back Soviet control in eastern Europe by applying direct military pressure on the Kremlin.
options.label: reversal
options.why: The excerpt stresses economic means and the absence of combat troops. Rollback by military pressure is the opposite of what the author describes.

options.text: United States officials designed postwar aid chiefly to open European markets to American goods, with anticommunism serving only as a public excuse.
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: The author mentions lower trade barriers but presents anticommunism as the real goal of the planners, not a cover story for commercial motives.

options.text: United States officials regarded the Truman Doctrine as a mistake and replaced its ideological language with a purely humanitarian relief program.
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: The author says the recovery program carried the Truman Doctrine's logic further. It did not reject that doctrine, and it was not purely humanitarian.

facts: In 1948 Congress approved the European Recovery Program (Marshall Plan), which sent billions of dollars in aid to western European nations.
Communist parties drew strong support in France and Italy in the late 1940s.

items.stem: Which of the following developments would most directly challenge the author's argument that containment before 1950 relied on economic rather than military means?

options.text: The United States joined a peacetime military alliance with western European nations in 1949.
options.label: key
options.why: The United States joined NATO in 1949, a peacetime military commitment to defend western Europe made before 1950. This shows military tools were part of containment earlier than the author suggests.

options.text: The United States flew food and fuel into West Berlin for nearly a year after the Soviet Union blocked land access to the city in 1948.
options.label: true_but_not_responsive
options.why: The Berlin Airlift resisted Soviet pressure without combat, so it fits the author's argument instead of challenging it.

options.text: The United States sent hundreds of thousands of troops to Vietnam after Congress passed the Gulf of Tonkin Resolution in 1964.
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The large troop buildup in Vietnam came long after 1950. It cannot challenge a claim about containment before 1950.

options.text: The Truman administration created a loyalty review program in 1947 to screen federal employees for possible communist sympathies.
options.label: unrelated_development
options.why: The loyalty program was a domestic anticommunist measure. It says nothing about whether containment abroad used military or economic tools.

facts: The United States joined the North Atlantic Treaty Organization (NATO) in 1949.
The Berlin Airlift supplied West Berlin from 1948 to 1949 during the Soviet blockade.

items.stem: The aid programs described in the excerpt developed most directly in the context of

options.text: Soviet efforts to install communist-dominated governments in eastern Europe after the Second World War
options.label: key
options.why: After 1945 the Soviet Union backed communist-dominated governments across eastern Europe. That alarmed American leaders and led to the Truman Doctrine and the Marshall Plan.

options.text: a strong isolationist movement that sought to keep the United States out of European political and economic affairs
options.label: reversal
options.why: These aid programs marked a break from isolationism, which had lost much of its support after Pearl Harbor. They did not grow out of it.

options.text: the economic collapse of the early 1930s, which led European governments to default on their First World War debts to the United States
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The debt defaults belong to the Depression era. The excerpt deals with postwar devastation and the Soviet threat after 1945.

options.text: the outbreak of the Korean War, which persuaded American leaders that communist powers would use force to expand across Asia
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The Korean War began in June 1950, after the Truman Doctrine (1947) and the Marshall Plan (1948) were already in place.

facts: After World War II the Soviet Union backed communist-dominated governments in eastern European nations such as Poland.
President Truman announced the Truman Doctrine in March 1947, asking Congress for aid to Greece and Turkey.

items.stem: Which of the following was most likely a result of the European Recovery Program described in the excerpt?

options.text: It deepened the division of Europe, since the Soviet Union refused aid and kept eastern European states from taking part.
options.label: key
options.why: The Soviet Union turned down Marshall Plan aid and kept its eastern European satellites out of it. This hardened the split between western and Soviet-controlled Europe.

options.text: It persuaded the Soviet Union to permit free elections in Poland and other eastern European nations in return for American loans.
options.label: reversal
options.why: The Soviet Union rejected the program and tightened its control over eastern Europe. It did not allow free elections.

options.text: It allowed the United States to withdraw nearly all of its military forces from western Europe by the early 1950s.
options.label: reversal
options.why: Through NATO, the United States kept and expanded its military presence in western Europe in the early 1950s.

options.text: It caused a prolonged recession in the United States because the cost of the program forced Congress to raise income taxes sharply after 1948.
options.label: overstated
options.why: The American economy grew strongly in the postwar years. The aid program did not cause a long recession.

facts: The Soviet Union rejected participation in the Marshall Plan in 1947 and kept eastern European states from joining it.
The United States experienced sustained economic growth in the years after World War II.

input.title: A Georgia Farm Wife Petitions Her Governor, 1863

sources.title: Letter to the Governor of Georgia from Sweetwater Creek
sources.attribution: Letter from Martha Pruitt, wife of a conscripted soldier, Sweetwater Creek settlement, upcountry Georgia, to the governor of Georgia, November 1863 (ALTON-composed, in the style of petitions sent by Confederate soldiers' wives to state governors)
sources.body: Sir, I write for myself and for eleven other women of our settlement whose husbands and sons are with the army in Virginia. My husband was taken under the conscript law last spring before our corn was planted. Since then the tithe agent has carried off a tenth of our wheat and bacon, and an impressing officer took our only mule at a price the government fixed, paid in notes that will not buy a sack of salt. Salt has gone past thirty dollars the sack in town. Meanwhile Mr. Haskell down the river, who works some thirty slaves, keeps his grown son at home as overseer under the law that spares one white man on every place of twenty slaves, and his fields still stand in cotton. We do not ask to quit the cause. We ask that the burden be shared, or that our men be furloughed home before our children go hungry this winter.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes the purpose of the letter?

options.text: To persuade state officials to distribute wartime burdens more fairly among poorer white families
options.label: key
options.why: Pruitt contrasts her family's losses with a planter's exemption and asks that 'the burden be shared' or soldiers be furloughed, an appeal to the governor for relief.

options.text: To urge state leaders to open peace negotiations with the Union and to restore Georgia's place in the federal Union
options.label: overstated
options.why: The author explicitly says 'We do not ask to quit the cause'; she seeks relief, not reunion.

options.text: To protest the destruction of crops and livestock by Union troops marching from Atlanta to the coast
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: Sherman's March to the Sea took place in late 1864; the letter's losses come from Confederate tithe agents and impressment officers in 1863.

options.text: To argue that enslaved men should be armed and enlisted in the Confederate army in return for their freedom
options.label: unrelated_development
options.why: The Confederacy debated arming enslaved men late in the war, but the letter says nothing about it.

facts: The Confederacy enacted the first national conscription law in American history in April 1862.
Many Confederate soldiers' wives wrote to state governors in 1862-1864 seeking relief and furloughs for their husbands.

items.stem: Which of the following claims does the author make in the excerpt?

options.text: Confederate policies demanded heavier sacrifices from nonslaveholding families than from large planters
options.label: key
options.why: The letter sets the draft, tithe, and impressment burdens on her family against the planter Haskell, whose son is exempt and whose fields stay in cotton.

options.text: Confederate paper currency held its value well enough that farm families could pay their taxes in cash
options.label: reversal
options.why: The author says government notes 'will not buy a sack of salt,' which points to severe inflation.

options.text: The national conscription law violated the rights of the states and should be nullified by the Georgia state legislature
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: Some Georgia leaders did make states' rights objections to conscription, but the letter makes a complaint about fairness, not a constitutional argument.

options.text: Large slaveholders had refused to pay any of the taxes and tithes imposed by the government in Richmond
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: The letter criticizes the overseer exemption and the planting of cotton, not any refusal by planters to pay taxes.

facts: In October 1862 the Confederate Congress exempted from the draft one white man on each plantation with twenty or more enslaved people, the so-called Twenty Negro Law.
In 1863 the Confederacy adopted a tax-in-kind (tithe) of one-tenth of farm produce and authorized impressment of supplies.

items.stem: The economic conditions described in the excerpt were most directly shaped by which of the following?

options.text: The Union naval blockade and the Confederacy's heavy printing of paper money
options.label: key
options.why: The blockade cut imports and created shortages, and the Confederacy financed the war mainly with paper money, which caused runaway inflation, as seen in the price of salt and the worthless notes.

options.text: The Homestead Act of 1862, which drew many Southern farm families to claim free land in western territories
options.label: unrelated_development
options.why: The Homestead Act was a Union measure passed after Southern members left Congress; it did not shape conditions in Confederate Georgia.

options.text: The Emancipation Proclamation, which immediately freed all enslaved people working on Georgia plantations in 1863
options.label: overstated
options.why: The Proclamation could not be enforced in Confederate-held areas, and the letter describes a planter still working his enslaved laborers.

options.text: The Panic of 1857, which caused a long collapse in world cotton prices and ruined small Southern farmers
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: Cotton prices recovered quickly after 1857, and the wartime shortages in the letter came from the war itself.

facts: The Union blockade of Southern ports, part of the Anaconda Plan, was proclaimed in 1861 and caused widespread shortages in the Confederacy.
The Confederacy financed its war effort largely by printing paper money, producing severe inflation by 1863.

items.stem: The grievances expressed in the excerpt were most similar to which of the following developments in the North during the Civil War?

options.text: Anger at draft rules letting wealthier men avoid service by paying a fee or hiring a substitute
options.label: key
options.why: The 1863 Enrollment Act's 300-dollar commutation fee and substitution provisions caused resentment that a poor man fights a rich man's war, which fed the New York City draft riots. This parallels Pruitt's complaint about the planter exemption.

options.text: Abolitionist criticism of President Lincoln for delaying emancipation until the second year of the war
options.label: true_but_not_responsive
options.why: Abolitionists did press Lincoln to act on emancipation, but that was not a complaint about class inequality in wartime burdens.

options.text: Opposition among Western farmers to the Pacific Railway Act's large federal land grants to railroad companies
options.label: unrelated_development
options.why: Farmer anger at railroads grew mainly after the war, in the Granger era, and it was not about unequal military service.

options.text: Free-soil protests against the Kansas-Nebraska Act's repeal of the Missouri Compromise line in the territories
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: Those protests took place in 1854, before the war, and concerned slavery's expansion, not wartime burdens.

facts: The Union Enrollment Act of March 1863 allowed drafted men to hire a substitute or pay a 300-dollar commutation fee.
Resentment of the draft helped spark the New York City draft riots in July 1863.

input.title: A Planter Writes from the Tombigbee, 1834

sources.title: Letter from a planter newly settled in the Southwest
sources.attribution: Letter from Josiah Marlow, a slaveholding cotton planter who moved from Edgefield District, South Carolina, to the Tombigbee River country, to his brother in Virginia, 1834 (ALTON-composed, in the style of private letters of planters who migrated to the Deep South)
sources.body: Dear Brother, I write from the new purchase on the Tombigbee, where we arrived after six weeks upon the road with the wagons and the hands. The land here is black and deep, nothing like our worn hills in Edgefield, which at the last would not yield three hundred pounds of cotton to the acre. My neighbors here gather near a thousand. Since the treaty with the Choctaws the country fills with movers every week, and the price of land climbs by the month. Men talk of nothing but bales and the price at Mobile, and a gin house goes up before a dwelling house. I tell you plainly that your tobacco acres will never pay as this soil pays, and that hands who would fetch a modest sum in Richmond bring near double from the traders at Natchez. Sell what you cannot work and come out before the best lands are taken. The English mills will want all we can raise.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes the purpose of the letter in the excerpt?

options.text: To persuade a relative to move his labor force from a declining region to new cotton lands
options.label: key
options.why: Marlow contrasts worn Edgefield and Virginia tobacco land with rich Tombigbee soil and urges his brother to sell what he cannot work and come west, reflecting the planter migration into the Deep South in the 1830s.

options.text: To urge the federal government to adopt protective tariffs that would raise the price paid for Southern cotton at Mobile
options.label: reversal
options.why: The letter is private and addressed to a brother, not to the government; also, cotton planters generally opposed protective tariffs, as the nullification crisis showed.

options.text: To argue that falling tobacco profits in Virginia made the gradual emancipation of enslaved workers a practical choice
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: Marlow points to the high prices enslaved people bring in the Natchez market, suggesting sale or relocation, not emancipation.

options.text: To warn eastern planters that Native resistance in the Southwest required more federal troops
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: The letter mentions the Choctaw treaty only as having opened land; it says nothing of resistance or a need for troops.

facts: Planters from the seaboard South migrated in large numbers to Alabama and Mississippi in the 1820s and 1830s in search of fresh cotton land.
In the Treaty of Dancing Rabbit Creek (1830), the Choctaw ceded their remaining lands in Mississippi.

items.stem: Which of the following pieces of evidence would best support the excerpt's suggestion that the cotton economy was drawing enslaved people westward?

options.text: Records showing that the domestic slave trade moved large numbers of enslaved people from the Upper South to the Deep South
options.label: key
options.why: Marlow notes that enslaved people sell for far more at Natchez than in Richmond. Between 1790 and 1860 about one million enslaved people were forcibly moved from the Upper South to the Deep South by sale and planter migration, which directly supports this.

options.text: Census figures showing that the Missouri Compromise barred slavery from Louisiana Purchase lands north of latitude 36 degrees 30 minutes
options.label: true_but_not_responsive
options.why: The 1820 compromise did limit slavery north of that line, but this says nothing about enslaved people being moved into the Deep South cotton region.

options.text: Payroll accounts showing that textile mills in Lowell, Massachusetts, hired thousands of young New England farm women as wage workers
options.label: unrelated_development
options.why: The Lowell mills did employ young women, but this is evidence about Northern industrial labor, not about enslaved people being moved to the Southwest.

options.text: Church records showing that free Black communities in Philadelphia and other Northern cities founded independent congregations
options.label: unrelated_development
options.why: Free Black communities did found churches such as the AME Church, but this has nothing to do with the forced movement of enslaved people to cotton lands.

facts: An estimated one million enslaved people were relocated from the Upper South to the Deep South between 1790 and 1860, many through the domestic slave trade.
Natchez, Mississippi, and New Orleans were major markets of the interstate slave trade in the antebellum period.

items.stem: The economic expectations expressed in the excerpt are best understood in the context of which broader development of the early nineteenth century?

options.text: Growing British and New England textile manufacturing, which made raw cotton the nation's leading export
options.label: key
options.why: Marlow's line about English mills wanting all he can raise reflects the industrial demand that made cotton the leading United States export by the 1830s and tied Southern slavery to Atlantic markets.

options.text: The Embargo Act of 1807, which sharply restricted American shipments to Europe and encouraged planters to seek new domestic buyers
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The embargo did cut exports, but it was repealed in 1809. The letter expects strong export demand from English mills, not a closed market.

options.text: The Panic of 1837, which drove down cotton prices and land values and pushed indebted Southwestern planters to seek cheaper acreage
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The panic came after this 1834 letter and caused falling prices, while the letter describes rising land prices and boom conditions.

options.text: The expansion of commercial wheat farming along the Erie Canal, which linked Northern farmers to Atlantic markets
options.label: true_but_not_responsive
options.why: The Erie Canal (1825) did commercialize Northern agriculture, but it does not explain the expectations of a Deep South cotton planter.

facts: By the 1830s cotton was the leading United States export, much of it shipped to textile mills in Britain.
The Embargo Act of 1807 was repealed in 1809, and the Panic of 1837 began a sharp economic downturn.

items.stem: The invention of the cotton gin in 1793 contributed to the conditions described in the excerpt in which of the following ways?

options.text: It made short-staple cotton profitable to process, spreading cultivation inland and raising demand for enslaved labor
options.label: key
options.why: The gin quickly removed seeds from short-staple cotton, which grew across the interior South. This made upland cotton profitable and pushed planters, and the enslaved people they held, onto lands like the Tombigbee country.

options.text: It mechanized the picking of cotton, which reduced the number of enslaved workers needed on large plantations in the Deep South
options.label: reversal
options.why: The gin cleaned cotton but did not pick it. Picking stayed hand labor, so as cultivation grew, the demand for enslaved workers increased rather than fell.

options.text: It encouraged Southern planters to build large textile factories that soon rivaled the mills of New England in output
options.label: overstated
options.why: The South stayed overwhelmingly agricultural and sent its raw cotton to Northern and British mills. Southern textile output never rivaled New England's in this period.

options.text: It led Congress to prohibit the importation of enslaved Africans in 1808 because domestic cotton production now required fewer workers
options.label: misattributed
options.why: The 1808 ban came after the constitutional twenty-year protection of the trade ran out, and it was not caused by a falling need for labor. Cotton actually raised the demand for enslaved labor.

facts: Eli Whitney's cotton gin (1793) made it practical to remove seeds from short-staple cotton.
Congress prohibited the importation of enslaved people beginning in 1808, the earliest date the Constitution allowed.

input.title: Neutrality, the Jay Treaty, and the Price of Peace

sources.title: A historian reassesses the Jay Treaty
sources.attribution: Clement Arvidson-Pryor, a fictional historian, in The Price of Quiet: Neutrality and Party in the Federalist Decade, a published lecture first delivered to the fictional Tidewater Historical Society, 2011 (ALTON-composed, in the style of a modern diplomatic historian)
sources.body: Crowds in 1795 burned John Jay in effigy, and it is tempting to read the treaty that bears his name as a surrender. That reading misses what the Washington administration was trying to buy. The president had already declared in 1793 that the United States would take no side in the war between Britain and France. When Jay sailed for London the next year, he carried little leverage. The nation had no navy worth the name, and most federal revenue came from import duties, the bulk of them collected on British goods. Measured against those weaknesses, the bargain looks rational. Britain promised to give up the forts it still held in the Northwest, and war with the strongest sea power was avoided. Yet Jay won nothing on the seizure of American sailors, and the price at home was steep. Protest meetings spread from Boston to Charleston, and the ratification fight turned a loose quarrel over policy into rival party organizations. Neutrality kept the republic out of Europe's war; it did not keep Europe's war out of American politics.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes the author's main argument in the excerpt?
facts: The Jay Treaty was negotiated in 1794 and approved by the Senate in 1795 amid widespread public protest.
Under the Jay Treaty, Britain agreed to evacuate its posts in the Northwest Territory, which it did in 1796.
The Jay Treaty did not end British impressment of American sailors.

options.text: A treaty that disappointed many Americans was a reasonable bargain for a weak nation, but it intensified partisan conflict.
options.label: key
options.why: The author rejects the surrender reading, calls the bargain rational given American weakness, and says the ratification fight hardened rival party organizations.

options.text: The treaty was a humiliating capitulation to British demands that gained the United States nothing it had sought in negotiations.
options.label: reversal
options.why: The author mentions this view only to reject it, pointing to the promised evacuation of the Northwest forts and the avoidance of war.

options.text: Washington's neutrality policy successfully kept disputes over the European war from shaping American domestic politics in the 1790s.
options.label: reversal
options.why: The closing sentence says the opposite: neutrality did not keep Europe's war out of American politics.

options.text: Jay's mission succeeded chiefly because he persuaded British officials to stop seizing American sailors and forcing them into Royal Navy service.
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: The author states that Jay won nothing on impressment, and historically the treaty left impressment unresolved.

items.stem: Which of the following developments would best support the author's claim that the Jay Treaty was a rational bargain that improved the United States' position?
facts: Pinckney's Treaty (Treaty of San Lorenzo) of 1795 gave Americans navigation of the Mississippi River and the right of deposit at New Orleans.
Spanish concern about closer Anglo-American relations after the Jay Treaty helped lead Spain to agree to Pinckney's Treaty in 1795.

options.text: Spain, fearing closer Anglo-American ties, granted Americans use of the Mississippi and New Orleans in 1795.
options.label: key
options.why: Pinckney's Treaty followed partly from Spanish worry over the Anglo-American agreement, so it shows the Jay Treaty strengthening the American position, as the author argues.

options.text: The XYZ Affair of 1797-1798, in which French agents demanded bribes from American diplomats before negotiations could begin.
options.label: true_but_not_responsive
options.why: The XYZ Affair came out of French anger at American policy and points to the treaty's costs, so it does not support the claim that the bargain improved the nation's position.

options.text: The continued British impressment of American sailors in the 1800s, which became a leading grievance behind the War of 1812.
options.label: reversal
options.why: Continued impressment points to the treaty's limits and would weaken the claim that it improved the nation's position.

options.text: The Washington administration's use of militia to suppress the Whiskey Rebellion in western Pennsylvania in 1794.
options.label: unrelated_development
options.why: The Whiskey Rebellion was about federal excise taxes and federal authority at home, not the results of diplomacy with Britain.

items.stem: Which of the following provides the most direct context for the 1793 neutrality policy mentioned in the excerpt?
facts: France declared war on Great Britain in February 1793 during the French Revolutionary Wars.
Washington issued the Neutrality Proclamation in April 1793.
The United States and France signed a Treaty of Alliance in 1778.

options.text: War between Britain and revolutionary France, which raised questions about the 1778 alliance with France
options.label: key
options.why: The 1793 war between Britain and France, along with the existing 1778 alliance, pushed Washington to declare that the United States would take no side.

options.text: Napoleon's Continental System and the British Orders in Council, which together restricted neutral American shipping
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: These measures date from 1806-1807 and form the context for Jefferson's Embargo Act, not the 1793 proclamation.

options.text: Spain's closing of the lower Mississippi River to American traders in 1784, which angered western settlers
options.label: true_but_not_responsive
options.why: This happened, but it relates to Spanish-American relations and Pinckney's Treaty, not to the decision to stay out of the Anglo-French war.

options.text: Shays' Rebellion in Massachusetts, which convinced many leaders that the Articles of Confederation were too weak
options.label: unrelated_development
options.why: Shays' Rebellion (1786-1787) shaped the move toward the Constitution, not foreign policy toward the European war.

items.stem: The approach to foreign affairs that the excerpt attributes to the Washington administration was most consistent with which later development?
facts: The Monroe Doctrine, announced in 1823, stated that the United States would not interfere in European wars or affairs and warned against new European colonization in the Americas.
The United States declared war on Great Britain in 1812.

options.text: The Monroe Doctrine's 1823 pledge that the United States would stay out of European wars
options.label: key
options.why: Like Washington's neutrality, the Monroe Doctrine kept the United States out of European conflicts, which continues the pattern of avoiding entanglement.

options.text: The declaration of war against Britain in 1812 after War Hawks demanded action over impressment and frontier raids
options.label: reversal
options.why: Going to war with Britain broke from the policy of avoiding war with the strongest sea power that the excerpt describes.

options.text: The Alien and Sedition Acts of 1798, which restricted immigrants and criticism of the government during the Quasi-War
options.label: unrelated_development
options.why: These were domestic security laws about dissent and immigration, not a continuation of a nonentanglement foreign policy.

options.text: The Treaty of Alliance of 1778, which bound the United States and France together in a military partnership against Britain
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The 1778 alliance came before the neutrality policy, not after it, and it was an entangling alliance, the opposite of neutrality.

input.title: From Inclusion to Self-Determination: Chicano and American Indian Activism

sources.title: A historian on postwar Mexican American and Native activism
sources.attribution: Marisol Etcheverry, historian, from Claiming the Ground: Mexican American and Native Activism in the Postwar West, a book based on her lectures at a university in Albuquerque, 2011 (ALTON-composed, in the style of a modern historical monograph)
sources.body: Between the late 1940s and the early 1970s, Mexican American and American Indian activists moved away from a politics that asked for inclusion on the majority's terms and toward one that demanded control over their own communities. Earlier organizations such as the American GI Forum, founded by Mexican American veterans in 1948, had stressed citizenship, patriotism, and legal equality. By 1968, students walking out of East Los Angeles high schools were demanding bilingual instruction and teachers who knew their history, while the American Indian Movement was organizing in Minneapolis. The nineteen-month occupation of Alcatraz Island that began in 1969 cast Native claims in the language of treaty rights and nationhood rather than integration. What linked these campaigns was less a shared program than a shared conviction that cultural identity was a source of political power, not an obstacle to be shed.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes the main argument of the excerpt?
facts: The American GI Forum was founded by Mexican American veterans in 1948.
Mexican American students staged walkouts from East Los Angeles high schools in 1968.
American Indian activists occupied Alcatraz Island from November 1969 to June 1971.

options.text: Activists moved from seeking acceptance through assimilation toward using cultural identity to claim community control.
options.label: key
options.why: The author contrasts the GI Forum's emphasis on citizenship and equality with later demands for bilingual schooling and treaty-based nationhood, concluding that identity became a source of political power.

options.text: Activists abandoned legal and political methods in favor of armed resistance to federal and state authorities across the West.
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: The excerpt describes walkouts, organizing, and an occupation, not armed resistance; it makes no claim that legal methods were abandoned.

options.text: Activists built a single coalition with a shared program of economic demands borrowed directly from the African American labor movement.
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: The author explicitly says the campaigns were linked by a shared conviction rather than a shared program, and does not discuss economic demands.

options.text: Activists achieved their goals mainly through federal antipoverty funding provided by Great Society programs of the late 1960s.
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: The excerpt does not mention Great Society funding or attribute the movements' success to federal programs.

items.stem: Which of the following developments would most directly support the author's argument about the direction of Mexican American activism?
facts: La Raza Unida Party was founded in Texas in 1970 to elect Mexican American candidates.
In Hernandez v. Texas (1954), the Supreme Court held that excluding Mexican Americans from juries violated the Fourteenth Amendment.

options.text: Mexican American activists in Texas founded La Raza Unida Party in 1970 to win local power for their communities.
options.label: key
options.why: An independent ethnic party seeking community political control fits the author's claim that activists shifted toward self-determination grounded in cultural identity.

options.text: A 1954 federal deportation campaign removed many thousands of Mexican immigrants, and some United States citizens, from the Southwest.
options.label: true_but_not_responsive
options.why: The 1954 deportation campaign was real, but it was a federal action, not evidence about how activists changed their goals or methods.

options.text: In Hernandez v. Texas (1954), the Supreme Court held that excluding Mexican Americans from juries violated the Fourteenth Amendment.
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: This case reflects the earlier legal-equality strategy the author describes, not the later turn toward community control.

options.text: Some Mexican American civic groups in the 1970s continued to stress patriotism, English fluency, and gradual integration over cultural pride.
options.label: reversal
options.why: Continued emphasis on integration in the 1970s would complicate or modify the author's argument rather than support it.

items.stem: The shift in activism described in the excerpt took place most directly in the context of which of the following?
facts: Black Power emerged as a prominent slogan and movement in the African American freedom struggle in the mid-to-late 1960s.
The Indian Reorganization Act was passed in 1934.

options.text: The growth of the Black Power movement and other calls for racial pride in the late 1960s
options.label: key
options.why: Chicano and Native activists of the late 1960s drew on the example of Black Power, which emphasized racial pride, cultural identity, and community control.

options.text: The Indian Reorganization Act of 1934, which ended allotment and encouraged tribes to adopt written constitutions
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: This New Deal measure came decades before the activism of the late 1960s and does not explain its turn toward cultural nationalism.

options.text: The rise of a conservative coalition in the 1980s that sought to reduce federal spending on social programs
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The rise of conservatism under Reagan came after the activism the excerpt describes, which peaked in the late 1960s and early 1970s.

options.text: Economic decline in the industrial Northeast caused by deindustrialization and the 1973 oil embargo
options.label: unrelated_development
options.why: Deindustrialization in the Northeast was a real 1970s trend, but it does not explain why activism in the West turned toward identity and self-determination.

items.stem: The Native American activism described in the excerpt was most directly a reaction against which federal policy of the 1950s?
facts: In the 1950s Congress pursued termination of federal recognition of certain tribes and the government sponsored relocation of Native Americans to cities.
The Indian Self-Determination and Education Assistance Act was passed in 1975.
The Dawes Act was passed in 1887 and allotment was ended by the Indian Reorganization Act in 1934.

options.text: Efforts to end federal recognition of tribes and relocate Native Americans from reservations to cities
options.label: key
options.why: Termination and relocation policies of the 1950s threatened tribal existence and brought many Native people to cities such as Minneapolis and San Francisco, producing the urban activism and treaty-rights claims the excerpt describes.

options.text: The Dawes Act's division of reservation land into individual farm plots, a policy Congress first adopted in 1887
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: Allotment began in 1887 and ended in 1934; it was not a policy of the 1950s and was not the most direct target of the 1960s protests.

options.text: The Indian Citizenship Act of 1924, which granted United States citizenship to all Native Americans born in the country
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The citizenship act came in the 1920s, not the 1950s, and it was not the federal policy that prompted the demands of the late 1960s.

options.text: The Indian Self-Determination and Education Assistance Act, which expanded tribal control over federally funded programs
options.label: reversal
options.why: This 1975 law came after the activism and was partly a federal response to it, so it was an effect rather than a cause.

input.title: A Vietnam Veteran Weighs the Gulf War, 1991

sources.title: Remarks at a Community Forum on the War in the Persian Gulf
sources.attribution: Remarks by Walter Brannigan, a Vietnam veteran and member of the Corbin County school board, at a community forum held in the Millersport High School gymnasium, Millersport, Missouri, February 1991 (ALTON-composed, in the style of a local public speech)
sources.body: I stood in this gymnasium in 1968 and argued with my own father about a war neither of us understood. Tonight I want to tell you why this one feels different to me. When Iraq's army rolled into Kuwait last August, the President did not act alone. The United Nations set a deadline, and nations from Britain to Egypt to Saudi Arabia sent forces. Congress debated and voted before the bombing began, which is more than it did in my war. Even the Soviets, who once would have blocked anything we proposed, stood aside. I am not naive. Oil is part of this, and so is pride. Some of our generals want to bury the memory of Saigon for good. But our sons and daughters over there have a mission they can name: push Iraq out of Kuwait and come home. So tie your yellow ribbons, and keep your questions sharp.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes Brannigan's point of view in the excerpt?
facts: Iraq invaded Kuwait on August 2, 1990.
The UN Security Council authorized force against Iraq if it did not leave Kuwait by January 15, 1991, and Congress voted to authorize force in January 1991.

options.text: He backs the war mainly because it has international and congressional support that Vietnam lacked.
options.label: key
options.why: Brannigan contrasts the UN deadline, the multinational coalition, and the congressional vote with his own war in Vietnam, which was never formally declared or debated in the same way.

options.text: He opposes the war because he believes it is being fought chiefly to protect American access to Persian Gulf oil.
options.label: reversal
options.why: He admits oil is a factor but asks listeners to support the troops; he does not oppose the war.

options.text: He supports the war as a necessary step toward overthrowing the Iraqi government and occupying Baghdad indefinitely.
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: He describes the mission as expelling Iraq from Kuwait and coming home, not regime change or occupation.

options.text: He favors the war as a continuation of the containment policy aimed at checking Soviet influence in the Middle East.
options.label: misattributed
options.why: He notes that the Soviets stood aside; he does not present the war as a fight against Soviet influence.

items.stem: Which of the following developments would best support Brannigan's claim that American forces had a limited mission they "can name"?
facts: The coalition ground offensive in Operation Desert Storm lasted about one hundred hours, and a ceasefire took effect at the end of February 1991 after Iraqi forces were expelled from Kuwait.
Saddam Hussein remained in power after the 1991 war.

options.text: Coalition forces ended the ground campaign once Iraqi troops had been driven out of Kuwait.
options.label: key
options.why: The ceasefire after Kuwait was liberated, without a march on Baghdad, matches the limited goal Brannigan describes.

options.text: In 2003 American forces invaded Iraq, removed Saddam Hussein from power, and began a lengthy occupation of the country.
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The 2003 Iraq War was a separate, later conflict and points to a broader commitment, not the limited 1991 mission.

options.text: Retreating Iraqi troops set hundreds of Kuwaiti oil wells on fire, creating a severe environmental disaster in the region.
options.label: true_but_not_responsive
options.why: The oil well fires did happen, but they say nothing about whether the American mission stayed limited.

options.text: American aircraft patrolled no-fly zones over northern and southern Iraq for more than a decade after the fighting.
options.label: reversal
options.why: The long-running no-fly zones show an ongoing commitment, which would weaken his claim that troops would simply come home.

items.stem: Brannigan's remark that the Soviets "stood aside" is best understood in the context of which of the following?
facts: Mikhail Gorbachev's reforms of glasnost and perestroika began in the mid-1980s.
Communist governments in Eastern Europe fell in 1989, and the Soviet Union dissolved in December 1991.

options.text: Gorbachev's reforms and the 1989 fall of Eastern European communist regimes had eased superpower rivalry.
options.label: key
options.why: As the Cold War wound down, the Soviet Union did not use its Security Council veto against action on Iraq, which made the coalition possible.

options.text: Nixon's policy of détente had produced arms limitation treaties and expanded trade between the superpowers in the 1970s.
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: Détente in the 1970s gave way to renewed tension around 1980 and does not explain Soviet behavior in 1990 and 1991.

options.text: The Soviet Union had already dissolved into independent republics, leaving Russia too weak to oppose American policy.
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The Soviet Union dissolved in December 1991, after the Gulf War had ended.

options.text: The Soviet withdrawal from Afghanistan had freed Soviet troops to join the coalition forces assembling in Saudi Arabia.
options.label: overstated
options.why: The Soviets did leave Afghanistan by 1989, but they did not send troops to fight with the coalition.

items.stem: Brannigan's comment that some generals wanted to "bury the memory of Saigon" relates most directly to which effect of the Persian Gulf War?
facts: The Persian Gulf War ended in a quick coalition victory in February 1991 with relatively few American casualties.
The War Powers Resolution was passed in 1973, during the final years of the Vietnam War.

options.text: Quick victory revived confidence in American military power and eased post-Vietnam reluctance to intervene.
options.label: key
options.why: The fast, low-casualty victory raised public trust in the military and made Americans less wary of using force abroad, a wariness that dated to defeat in Vietnam.

options.text: Congress responded by passing the War Powers Resolution, requiring presidents to consult lawmakers before sending troops into combat.
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The War Powers Resolution was passed in 1973 as a reaction to Vietnam, not to the Gulf War.

options.text: The war's outcome led the United States to withdraw its forces from the Persian Gulf and sharply reduce its reliance on imported oil.
options.label: reversal
options.why: After the war the United States kept a larger military presence in the Gulf, and oil imports remained high.

options.text: Public anger over high casualties produced a large antiwar movement that forced Congress to cut the defense budget.
options.label: reversal
options.why: American casualties were low and the war was popular. Later defense cuts came from the end of the Cold War, not from an antiwar movement.

input.title: Interest and Principle in Philadelphia: Compromises of 1787

sources.title: Truces Between Rival Interests
sources.attribution: Historian Marian Tollefsen, The Bargained Republic: Interest and Principle in Philadelphia, a study prepared for a seminar series at the fictional Harrow Valley Historical Society, 2009 (ALTON-composed, in the style of a modern historical monograph)
sources.body: Delegates who arrived in Philadelphia in May 1787 agreed that the Articles of Confederation had failed, but they agreed on little else. The bargains that followed are often remembered as triumphs of statesmanship, yet they are better understood as truces between rival interests. The Connecticut plan, which gave each state an equal vote in the Senate and apportioned the House by population, ended weeks of deadlock only after small-state delegates made clear they would reject any plan that denied them equal standing. Southern delegates secured the counting of three-fifths of enslaved people for representation and direct taxes, along with a clause barring Congress from ending the Atlantic slave trade before 1808. In return, New England delegates won a simple majority for laws regulating commerce rather than the two-thirds vote southerners had sought. Each settlement protected a particular constituency, and each postponed rather than resolved the questions of power that divided the states.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes the author's main argument in the excerpt?

options.text: The Convention's major settlements were deals among competing interests that deferred conflicts over power.
options.label: key
options.why: The author calls the bargains 'truces between rival interests' that 'postponed rather than resolved' questions of power, citing the Senate, three-fifths, slave trade, and commerce deals.

options.text: The delegates reached agreement mainly because they shared a common commitment to republican principles over local interests.
options.label: reversal
options.why: The author explicitly rejects the statesmanship view and stresses particular constituencies over shared principle.

options.text: The Convention's bargains permanently resolved disputes between large and small states and between slave and free states.
options.label: overstated
options.why: The author argues the opposite: the settlements postponed rather than resolved divisions.

options.text: The delegates chose to preserve the Articles of Confederation by adding modest amendments instead of drafting a new framework.
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: The excerpt says delegates agreed the Articles had failed and describes the structure of a new government, not amendments to the Articles.

facts: The Constitutional Convention met in Philadelphia beginning in May 1787.
The Great (Connecticut) Compromise of 1787 created a Senate with equal state representation and a House apportioned by population.

items.stem: Which of the following developments would most strongly support the author's argument that the Convention's bargains postponed rather than resolved divisions among the states?

options.text: The Missouri crisis of 1819-1820, in which Congress fought over keeping the Senate balanced between slave and free states
options.label: key
options.why: The Missouri crisis showed that the sectional conflict over slavery and Senate representation, built into the 1787 bargains, resurfaced and had to be settled again by the Missouri Compromise.

options.text: The ratification of the Bill of Rights in 1791, which answered Antifederalist demands for written protections of individual liberties
options.label: true_but_not_responsive
options.why: The Bill of Rights addressed ratification debates over individual liberties, not the sectional and state-power bargains the author discusses.

options.text: The Supreme Court's ruling in Marbury v. Madison in 1803, which established the courts' power to review the constitutionality of federal laws
options.label: unrelated_development
options.why: Judicial review concerned the power of the courts, not the divisions between large and small or slave and free states.

options.text: The unanimous selection of George Washington by the Electoral College in 1789, reflecting broad agreement across the new nation's sections
options.label: reversal
options.why: Cross-sectional unity behind Washington would suggest harmony, which tends to challenge rather than support the claim of deferred conflict.

facts: The Missouri Compromise of 1820 admitted Missouri as a slave state and Maine as a free state, preserving the sectional balance in the Senate.
The dispute over Missouri statehood began in Congress in 1819.

items.stem: The compromises described in the excerpt were most directly a response to which of the following?

options.text: Fears that the Articles of Confederation left the central government unable to tax or regulate trade
options.label: key
options.why: The Articles gave Congress no power to tax or regulate interstate and foreign commerce; these weaknesses, highlighted by Shays' Rebellion in 1786-1787, led to the Convention.

options.text: Alarm among American leaders at the radical turn of the French Revolution and the execution of King Louis XVI in 1793
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The French Revolution began in 1789 and the king was executed in 1793, after the Convention had finished its work in 1787.

options.text: Anger over the Proclamation of 1763, which barred colonial settlement west of the Appalachian Mountains
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The Proclamation was a British policy that fed the imperial crisis of the 1760s, not the concerns behind the 1787 Convention.

options.text: Federal efforts to suppress the Whiskey Rebellion among western Pennsylvania farmers protesting an excise tax
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The Whiskey Rebellion occurred in 1794 under the new Constitution, years after the Convention.

facts: Under the Articles of Confederation (ratified 1781), Congress lacked the power to levy taxes or regulate commerce.
Shays' Rebellion in Massachusetts (1786-1787) heightened calls for a stronger national government.

items.stem: The three-fifths clause described in the excerpt most directly affected national politics in the early 1800s in which of the following ways?

options.text: It enlarged the South's share of House seats and electoral votes, adding to slaveholding states' national influence
options.label: key
options.why: Counting three-fifths of enslaved people increased southern representation in the House and therefore in the Electoral College, strengthening slaveholding states in early national politics.

options.text: It prompted the Confederation Congress to ban slavery north of the Ohio River through the Northwest Ordinance of 1787
options.label: misattributed
options.why: The Northwest Ordinance was passed by the Confederation Congress in July 1787 independently of the Convention's three-fifths clause.

options.text: It drove New England Federalists at the Hartford Convention of 1814 to demand the immediate abolition of slavery throughout the South
options.label: overstated
options.why: The Hartford Convention proposed ending the three-fifths clause for representation, but it did not demand abolition of slavery in the South.

options.text: It granted free and enslaved African American men in southern states the right to vote in elections for the House
options.label: reversal
options.why: The clause counted enslaved people for apportionment without giving them any political rights; voting rules were left to the states.

facts: The three-fifths clause of the Constitution (1787) counted three-fifths of enslaved people for apportionment of House seats and direct taxes.
Because each state's electoral votes equal its House seats plus its two Senate seats, the three-fifths clause also increased southern electoral votes.
The Hartford Convention (1814-1815) proposed constitutional amendments including ending the three-fifths clause for representation.

input.title: A Machinist's Testimony for the Equal Rights Amendment, 1973

sources.title: Testimony at a state ratification hearing on the Equal Rights Amendment
sources.attribution: Testimony of Ruth Ellen Dvorak, a drill press operator at a valve plant and member of a machinists' union local, before a ratification hearing of a Midwestern state legislature, 1973 (ALTON-composed, in the style of public hearing testimony on the Equal Rights Amendment)
sources.body: I have run a drill press at the Hollis Valve plant in Marlow County for eleven years. Last spring the company posted an opening for a setup man, paying forty cents more an hour. I was told I could not bid on it, because the law of this state says a woman may not lift more than twenty-five pounds or work more than nine hours in a day. They call these laws protection. I call them a fence. The men on my line lift what I lift, and they get the overtime and the promotions. The Congress sent you this amendment last year by a wide margin, and all it says is that equality of rights under the law shall not be denied on account of sex. Some ladies have come before you to warn that it will draft our daughters and end a wife's claim to support. I am a wife and a mother myself, and I ask you this: what support is there in a paycheck made smaller because of who I am?

items.stem: Which of the following best describes the speaker's purpose in the excerpt?

options.text: To persuade state legislators to ratify the amendment by showing how sex-based laws held down women's earnings
options.label: key
options.why: The speaker addresses a state ratification hearing, describes being barred from a better-paying job by state weight and hour limits, and asks lawmakers to approve the amendment Congress sent to the states in 1972.

options.text: To urge members of Congress to approve the amendment by a wide margin so that it could finally be sent to the states
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: The speaker says Congress already sent the amendment to the states the year before. Her audience is a state legislature, not Congress.

options.text: To defend state limits on women's working hours and lifting loads as necessary safeguards for the health of wives and mothers
options.label: reversal
options.why: The speaker calls these protective laws a fence that keeps women out of better jobs. Defending them was the position of some opponents, not hers.

options.text: To call on fellow members of her union local to strike until the company opened its setup positions to women
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: She speaks to legislators about a constitutional amendment. She does not call for a strike or speak to her union.

facts: Congress approved the Equal Rights Amendment and sent it to the states for ratification in 1972.
Ratification of a constitutional amendment requires approval by three-fourths of the states.

items.stem: Which of the following pieces of evidence would most directly support the speaker's argument about how sex-based laws and practices affected women's paychecks?

options.text: Data showing that women working full time in the 1970s earned about 60 percent of what men earned
options.label: key
options.why: A large wage gap between full-time women and men workers in the 1970s supports her claim that women's pay was held down because of their sex.

options.text: Reports that the Supreme Court in Roe v. Wade (1973) had recognized a constitutional right of women to choose abortion
options.label: true_but_not_responsive
options.why: Roe v. Wade was a major development of the 1970s women's movement, but it says nothing about wages or labor laws.

options.text: Writings by conservative activists warning that the amendment would end a wife's legal claim to financial support from her husband
options.label: reversal
options.why: These were arguments made by ERA opponents. The speaker is answering them, so they would challenge her case rather than support it.

options.text: Records showing that postwar GI Bill benefits and federal mortgage loans helped millions of veterans' families buy suburban homes
options.label: unrelated_development
options.why: Postwar suburban growth is a real development, but it has no bearing on whether sex-based laws reduced women's pay.

facts: In the 1970s, women who worked full time earned roughly 59 to 60 cents for every dollar earned by men.
Roe v. Wade was decided by the Supreme Court in 1973.

items.stem: The speaker's situation as described in the excerpt most directly reflects which broader context of the decades after 1945?

options.text: The growing share of married women and mothers who held paid jobs outside the home
options.label: key
options.why: The speaker is a wife and mother with eleven years in a factory. That fits the steady rise after 1945 in married women and mothers working for wages, which helped drive feminist demands for workplace equality.

options.text: The mass recruitment of women into shipyards and aircraft plants to meet the production demands of the Second World War
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: Women's wartime industrial work took place from 1941 to 1945. The testimony comes from 1973 and is about postwar laws and job rules.

options.text: The loss of manufacturing jobs as factories in the Northeast and Midwest closed or relocated to the Sun Belt and overseas in the 1980s
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: Deindustrialization sped up mainly after this testimony. Also, the speaker's complaint is about being excluded from a job, not about losing one.

options.text: The expansion of federal health coverage for older and poor Americans through the creation of Medicare and Medicaid
options.label: unrelated_development
options.why: Medicare and Medicaid (1965) were Great Society programs that had nothing to do with women's job opportunities or protective labor laws.

facts: The share of married women in the paid labor force rose steadily from the late 1940s through the 1970s.
Medicare and Medicaid were created in 1965 as part of the Great Society.

items.stem: Which of the following best explains why the amendment discussed in the excerpt had not been added to the Constitution by the early 1980s?

options.text: A conservative grassroots campaign persuaded enough state legislatures to reject or stall ratification
options.label: key
options.why: Opponents organized by conservative activists such as Phyllis Schlafly's STOP ERA argued that the amendment threatened homemakers and traditional gender roles. Ratification stalled, and the amendment fell three states short when the deadline passed in 1982.

options.text: Congress responded to the economic troubles of the late 1970s by withdrawing its approval and ending the ratification process
options.label: reversal
options.why: Congress did not withdraw the amendment. In 1978 it extended the ratification deadline to 1982.

options.text: The AFL-CIO and other major labor organizations campaigned against the amendment throughout the 1970s to preserve protective laws
options.label: reversal
options.why: Some unions opposed the ERA earlier, but the AFL-CIO endorsed it in 1973. Organized labor was not the main force that defeated it.

options.text: Most supporters concluded that the Equal Pay Act and Title VII had already secured women full legal equality in every area
options.label: overstated
options.why: These laws banned some kinds of job discrimination, but supporters kept pushing for the amendment until the deadline because they believed those laws were not enough.

facts: Conservative activist Phyllis Schlafly led the STOP ERA campaign against ratification beginning in 1972.
Congress extended the ERA ratification deadline to 1982, and the amendment expired three states short of the 38 needed.
The AFL-CIO endorsed the Equal Rights Amendment in 1973.

input.title: A Roadside Diner Owner Confronts the 1973-1974 Oil Embargo

sources.title: Statement to a county board of commissioners, central Pennsylvania, January 1974
sources.attribution: Statement of Delia Marchetti, owner of the Crossroads Grill on Route 22, to a county board of commissioners' hearing on local economic conditions, January 1974 (ALTON-composed, in the style of public testimony at a local hearing during the 1973-1974 oil embargo)
sources.body: I have run the Crossroads Grill on Route 22 for nineteen years, and I have never seen a winter like this one. Since the Arab oil countries cut off shipments in October, the truckers who were my bread and butter sit in gas lines in Harrisburg instead of at my counter. The new 55-mile limit and the Sunday station closings keep the tourists at home. Meanwhile everything I buy costs more: coffee, beef, the heating oil for the dining room. I have raised the price of a hamburger twice since summer and still lost money in December. My cook's husband was laid off at the steel fabricating plant, so she asked for a raise I cannot give her. They tell us on television that prices climb when business is booming and fall when business is slow. Then somebody in Washington should explain why we have both troubles at once. I ask this board to press our congressman for fuel allocation rules that remember small businesses, not only the big oil companies.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes Marchetti's point of view in the excerpt?

options.text: A small business owner seeking federal fuel policies that protect independent firms like hers
options.label: key
options.why: Marchetti describes her own diner's losses and closes by asking the board to press for fuel allocation rules that remember small businesses, not only big oil companies.
