options.text: An oil company spokesperson arguing that higher fuel prices were needed to encourage new domestic drilling and exploration
options.label: reversal
options.why: Marchetti contrasts small businesses with the big oil companies and complains about rising costs; she does not defend higher prices.

options.text: A union organizer demanding that employers raise wages for workers to keep pace with the rising cost of living
options.label: misattributed
options.why: She is an employer who says she cannot give her cook a raise; the wage request comes from her employee, not from her.

options.text: An environmental activist praising the speed limit and station closings as needed steps toward reducing air pollution
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: She mentions the 55-mile limit and Sunday closings only as reasons tourists stay home, not as environmental gains.

facts: Arab members of OPEC imposed an oil embargo on the United States in October 1973.
In late 1973 President Nixon asked gasoline stations to close voluntarily on Sundays to conserve fuel.

items.stem: Marchetti supports her claim that the economy had 'both troubles at once' mainly by pointing to which of the following?

options.text: Rising prices for her supplies alongside a local layoff and fewer customers
options.label: key
options.why: She pairs higher costs for coffee, beef, and heating oil with lost trucker and tourist business and her cook's husband's layoff, showing rising prices during a slowdown.

options.text: Soaring profits reported by the major oil companies during the months after the embargo began
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: She mentions big oil companies only in her policy request and cites no profit figures.

options.text: Her decision to grant her cook a raise to keep pace with the rising cost of food and fuel
options.label: reversal
options.why: She says the cook asked for a raise that she cannot give.

options.text: Tourists trading in large automobiles for smaller and more fuel-efficient imported cars
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: The shift toward smaller imported cars was real in the 1970s, but the excerpt says only that tourists stay home.

facts: In the 1970s the United States had high inflation together with slow growth and rising unemployment, which economists called stagflation.
The national 55-mile-per-hour speed limit was enacted in early 1974 to save fuel.

items.stem: The economic hardships Marchetti describes are best understood in the context of which of the following?

options.text: Growing U.S. reliance on imported oil, exposed when Arab OPEC states imposed an embargo in 1973
options.label: key
options.why: By the early 1970s the United States imported a large share of its oil. The embargo, imposed in response to U.S. support for Israel in the 1973 Arab-Israeli War, caused the shortages and price increases she describes.

options.text: The 1979 Iranian Revolution, which disrupted Middle Eastern oil exports and produced a second round of gasoline shortages
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The excerpt is dated January 1974 and refers to the cutoff that began in October 1973, years before the 1979 crisis.

options.text: Federal deregulation of the trucking and airline industries, which lowered freight rates and pressured small roadside firms
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: Airline and trucking deregulation came in 1978 and 1980, after this testimony, and it is not what she blames.

options.text: The postwar Marshall Plan, which shifted American petroleum supplies toward the rebuilding of Western European industry
options.label: unrelated_development
options.why: The Marshall Plan (1948-1952) was economic aid to postwar Europe and has nothing to do with the fuel shortages of 1973-1974.

facts: The 1973 Arab oil embargo was a response to U.S. support for Israel during the October 1973 Arab-Israeli (Yom Kippur) War.
By the early 1970s the United States depended heavily on imported oil.

items.stem: The combination of economic problems Marchetti describes is best identified as which of the following developments of the 1970s?

options.text: Stagflation, in which high inflation coincided with slow growth and rising unemployment
options.label: key
options.why: She describes prices climbing while business slows and workers lose jobs. That pairing defined stagflation in the 1970s and undercut the usual assumption that inflation and unemployment move in opposite directions.

options.text: Deflation, in which falling prices and wages squeezed debtors much as they had in the early 1930s
options.label: reversal
options.why: She describes rising prices, not falling ones. Deflation marked the Great Depression, not the 1970s.

options.text: An economic boom driven by consumer credit, suburban home building, and federal highway spending
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: This describes postwar prosperity in the 1950s and 1960s, not the slump in the excerpt.

options.text: Supply-side recovery, in which tax cuts spurred investment and business expansion across the country
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: Supply-side policies are tied to the Reagan administration in the 1980s, which came after and partly in response to stagflation.

facts: Stagflation, inflation combined with economic stagnation and high unemployment, marked the U.S. economy in the 1970s.
Supply-side tax cuts were a centerpiece of Reagan administration policy beginning in 1981.

input.title: An Empire of Access: The Open Door Policy and China

sources.title: A historian on the Open Door notes
sources.attribution: Eleanor Strand Whitcomb, An Empire of Access: Americans and the China Market, 1895-1925, from a lecture series published by the fictional Harlow College Press, 2009 (ALTON-composed, in the style of a diplomatic historian's interpretive survey)
sources.body: When Secretary of State John Hay sent out his Open Door notes in 1899, he was not rejecting empire so much as redefining it. American manufacturers, especially the cotton mills of the Carolinas and New England, pictured China's four hundred million people as buyers of American cloth and kerosene. Yet the United States held no sphere of its own on the Chinese coast, and few in Congress wanted to pay for one. Hay's answer was an empire of access: equal tariffs and harbor rights for every foreign trader, protected not by garrisons but by the mutual suspicion of the great powers. The policy was cheap, and that was its appeal. It was also fragile. For two decades Washington defended the principle chiefly with notes, conferences, and treaties, trusting that rival powers would honor in China a restraint they would never have accepted at home.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes the author's main argument about the Open Door policy?

options.text: It sought commercial access to China without the costs of holding colonies there.
options.label: key
options.why: The author calls the policy an 'empire of access' that gave equal trade rights without garrisons or a U.S. sphere, which Congress did not want to pay for.

options.text: It marked an American turn toward seizing Chinese ports to match the spheres that European powers held.
options.label: reversal
options.why: The author stresses that the United States held no sphere and chose access over territorial control, the opposite of seizing ports.

options.text: It grew mainly out of Protestant missionary demands that Washington protect converts and mission schools in the Chinese interior.
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: Missionaries were active in China, but the excerpt traces the policy to manufacturers' hopes for markets, not missionary pressure.

options.text: It successfully abolished the foreign spheres of influence in China and restored full Chinese control over tariffs.
options.label: overstated
options.why: The author calls the policy fragile and dependent on rivals' restraint; the spheres of influence were not abolished.

facts: Secretary of State John Hay circulated the Open Door notes in 1899 asking the powers to give equal trading access in their spheres of influence in China.
The United States did not hold its own sphere of influence in China.

items.stem: Which of the following developments would most directly modify the author's claim about how the United States defended the Open Door?

options.text: American troops joined a multinational force that entered Beijing during the Boxer Rebellion in 1900.
options.label: key
options.why: The author says Washington defended the principle chiefly with notes and treaties; sending troops to Beijing in 1900 shows a willingness to use force, qualifying that claim.

options.text: The Nine-Power Treaty of 1922 committed the major powers at the Washington Conference to respect the Open Door in China.
options.label: reversal
options.why: A treaty-based pledge supports, rather than modifies, the author's claim that the policy rested on paper agreements.

options.text: Congress extended the ban on Chinese immigration in 1902, restricting entry by Chinese laborers under the exclusion law of 1882.
options.label: true_but_not_responsive
options.why: Chinese exclusion was real, but it concerns immigration policy, not the means by which the United States defended trade access.

options.text: The Roosevelt administration acquired rights to build a canal across Panama in 1903 after backing a revolt against Colombia.
options.label: unrelated_development
options.why: The Panama episode involved force in the Western Hemisphere, not the defense of the Open Door in China.

facts: In 1900 the United States sent troops to join an international expedition that relieved the foreign legations in Beijing during the Boxer Rebellion.
Hay's second Open Door note in 1900 called for preserving China's territorial and administrative integrity.
The Nine-Power Treaty of 1922 affirmed the Open Door in China.

items.stem: The policy described in the excerpt is best understood in the context of which broader development of the 1890s?

options.text: A drive by business and political leaders to find overseas markets after the depression of 1893
options.label: key
options.why: The severe depression that began in 1893 sharpened arguments that American industry needed foreign markets, a key motive for overseas expansion and the Open Door.

options.text: A Wilsonian effort to promote national self-determination and collective security through a league of nations
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: Wilson's Fourteen Points and the League of Nations came after World War I, two decades after the Open Door notes.

options.text: A Populist campaign for free coinage of silver to relieve indebted farmers in the South and on the Great Plains
options.label: unrelated_development
options.why: The free silver campaign was a real 1890s movement but concerned domestic monetary policy, not trade access in China.

options.text: A broad revival of the anti-imperialist movement that blocked the annexation of overseas territories after 1898
options.label: reversal
options.why: Anti-imperialists organized after 1898 but failed; the United States annexed Hawaii, the Philippines, Guam, and Puerto Rico.

facts: A severe economic depression began with the Panic of 1893.
The United States annexed Hawaii in 1898 and acquired the Philippines, Guam, and Puerto Rico under the 1898 treaty ending the Spanish-American War.

items.stem: The commitment to the Open Door described in the excerpt contributed most directly to which development in the period from 1931 to 1941?

options.text: Growing conflict with Japan, which led to American economic sanctions as Japan expanded in China
options.label: key
options.why: Japan's seizure of Manchuria in 1931 and its invasion of China in 1937 violated the Open Door; U.S. opposition led to sanctions, including the 1941 oil embargo, before Pearl Harbor.

options.text: Passage of the Neutrality Acts, which barred loans and arms sales to nations at war in order to keep the country out of conflict
options.label: true_but_not_responsive
options.why: The Neutrality Acts came from disillusionment with World War I and fears about Europe, not from the commitment to trade access in China.

options.text: Adoption of the Good Neighbor policy, which renounced armed intervention in the internal affairs of Latin American nations
options.label: unrelated_development
options.why: The Good Neighbor policy concerned Latin America and did not grow out of the Open Door in China.

options.text: The Senate's rejection of the Treaty of Versailles because of objections to the League of Nations covenant
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The Senate rejected the treaty in 1919 and 1920, before the 1931 to 1941 period, and the vote turned on the League, not China trade.

facts: Japan seized Manchuria in 1931 and began a full-scale war against China in 1937.
The United States froze Japanese assets and cut off oil exports to Japan in 1941, before the attack on Pearl Harbor in December 1941.

input.title: The French Alliance and the Peace of 1783: Two Interpretations

sources.title: Excerpt A: Corinne Valcourt on French aid
sources.attribution: Corinne Valcourt, fictional historian, Bourbon Coin, Republican Victory, 2011 (ALTON-composed, in the style of a diplomatic and military history of the Revolution)
sources.body: Without the alliance signed in February 1778, the American cause would probably have stalled into an exhausting stalemate. French loans and gifts kept the Continental Army clothed and armed after Congress's paper money had nearly collapsed. More decisively, French sea power changed the geography of the war. In the autumn of 1781, a French fleet held the mouth of the Chesapeake while French and American troops tightened the siege at Yorktown, leaving the British army there with no escape by water. The surrender that followed persuaded Parliament to give up offensive war in America. Independence was won on American soil, but a Bourbon king's treasury and navy made it possible.

sources.title: Excerpt B: Desmond Hallorann on the peace negotiations
sources.attribution: Desmond Hallorann, fictional historian, The Commissioners' Gamble: Americans at the Paris Peace, 2004 (ALTON-composed, in the style of a history of early American diplomacy)
sources.body: Historians who credit France with American independence tend to end the story at Yorktown. Yet a military victory did not settle the shape of the peace. The French court had its own aims, including obligations to its Spanish ally, and it showed little interest in an American republic stretching to the Mississippi. Congress had instructed its commissioners in Paris to act only with French knowledge and advice. In 1782 they quietly set those instructions aside and bargained directly with British envoys. The result was a treaty in 1783 that granted not only independence but a western boundary at the Mississippi River and access to the Newfoundland fisheries, terms more generous than France would have pressed for.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes a difference between the arguments in Excerpt A and Excerpt B?

options.text: A credits French military and financial aid for victory, while B credits American diplomats for the favorable peace terms.
options.label: key
options.why: Valcourt stresses French loans and the fleet at the Chesapeake as making victory possible; Hallorann argues that the commissioners' separate bargaining with Britain in 1782 produced the generous terms of 1783.

options.text: A argues that American diplomats outmaneuvered France at the peace talks, while B argues that the French fleet at the Chesapeake decided the war's outcome.
options.label: reversal
options.why: This swaps the two arguments. The fleet is A's evidence, and the diplomacy is B's.

options.text: Both argue that France entered the war mainly out of sympathy for republican ideals and wanted to spread American-style self-government across Europe.
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: Neither excerpt says France acted from republican sympathy. B actually points to France's own aims and its ties to Spain.

options.text: B denies that the French alliance contributed anything to the military campaign, while A contends that the Continental Army fought no significant battles on its own.
options.label: overstated
options.why: B does not deny French military help. It argues that victory did not settle the peace. A says independence was won on American soil and never claims Americans fought no battles alone.

facts: France and the United States signed a treaty of alliance in February 1778.
American commissioners negotiated preliminary peace articles with Britain in 1782 without first consulting France, despite instructions from Congress.
The Treaty of Paris (1783) recognized American independence, set the western boundary at the Mississippi River, and granted fishing rights off Newfoundland.

items.stem: Which of the following, if true, would most directly support Excerpt A's claim about the importance of French aid to the American war effort?

options.text: By 1780 Continental paper money had lost nearly all its value, leaving Congress dependent on foreign loans.
options.label: key
options.why: The collapse of Continental currency shows how much Congress needed outside money, which supports A's claim that French loans kept the army supplied.

options.text: Continental and militia forces defeated a British army at Saratoga in 1777, before any French troops or warships had arrived in America.
options.label: reversal
options.why: This points to American success before French help arrived, so it would weaken A's claim rather than support it.

options.text: The treaty of 1783 set the western boundary of the United States at the Mississippi River and recognized American fishing rights.
options.label: true_but_not_responsive
options.why: This is accurate, but it backs B's point about the peace terms. It says nothing about French aid during the war.

options.text: Spain entered the war in 1779 as a formal treaty ally of the United States, sending troops to join Washington's army in the north.
options.label: misattributed
options.why: Spain joined the war in 1779 as France's ally, not as a treaty ally of the United States. It fought Britain mainly in the Gulf region.

facts: Continental currency lost most of its value by 1780, when Congress revalued it at about 40 to 1.
Spain entered the war against Britain in 1779 as an ally of France but never signed an alliance treaty with the United States.
The American victory at Saratoga in 1777 came before the French alliance of 1778.

items.stem: France's decision to ally with the United States in 1778, described in Excerpt A, is best understood in the context of

options.text: a French desire to reverse losses suffered at British hands in the Seven Years' War
options.label: key
options.why: France lost Canada and its other North American lands in 1763. Weakening Britain by supporting its rebellious colonies gave France a chance at revenge.

options.text: the spread of revolutionary ideals in France that had already toppled the monarchy before the alliance was signed
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The French Revolution began in 1789, and the monarchy fell in 1792. The alliance was made by Louis XVI's government in 1778.

options.text: a long-standing French policy of supporting colonial self-government, dating back to the founding of New France
options.label: reversal
options.why: New France was governed by royal officials with little self-government, so the alliance did not come from any such tradition.

options.text: French efforts to defend the Louisiana Territory, which France then held, against American settlers moving westward
options.label: misattributed
options.why: France gave Louisiana to Spain in 1762. Spain held it in 1778, and France did not get it back until 1800.

facts: The Treaty of Paris of 1763 ended the Seven Years' War and removed France as a colonial power on the North American mainland.
France transferred Louisiana to Spain in 1762.
The French Revolution began in 1789.

items.stem: The alliance described in both excerpts was most directly connected to which of the following later developments in the 1790s?

options.text: Debate over U.S. obligations to France after France went to war with Britain in 1793
options.label: key
options.why: When France went to war with Britain in 1793, Americans argued over whether the 1778 treaty bound them to help France. Washington answered with the Neutrality Proclamation.

options.text: Spain's agreement in Pinckney's Treaty of 1795 to open the Mississippi River and the port of New Orleans to American trade
options.label: unrelated_development
options.why: Pinckney's Treaty was an agreement with Spain about navigation. It did not come out of the French alliance.

options.text: The Treaty of Greenville of 1795, in which Ohio Valley Indian nations ceded land after their defeat at the Battle of Fallen Timbers
options.label: unrelated_development
options.why: This treaty came from frontier warfare with American Indian nations, not from the alliance with France.

options.text: The Louisiana Purchase, by which the United States bought from France the vast territory west of the Mississippi River
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The Louisiana Purchase took place in 1803, not the 1790s. It came from Napoleon's circumstances, not from the obligations of the 1778 alliance.

facts: France declared war on Britain in 1793, raising questions about U.S. obligations under the 1778 treaty.
President Washington issued the Neutrality Proclamation in 1793.
The Louisiana Purchase occurred in 1803.

input.title: The Eastern Atlantic Origins of Iberian Plantation Slavery

sources.title: Excerpt on the origins of African bondage in the Iberian Americas
sources.attribution: Marisol Ekwueme-Barros, historian, from the fictional book Salt, Sugar, and Sail: The Iberian Roots of Atlantic Bondage, published by a university press in Lisbon and Chicago, 2011 (ALTON-composed, in the style of a modern scholarly monograph)
sources.body: The Atlantic slave trade did not begin in the Americas; it was carried there. By the 1480s Portuguese captains at fortified posts along the Gold Coast were buying captives from African rulers and shipping them to sugar estates on Madeira and Sao Tome. Those island plantations served as a rehearsal. They joined European capital, African labor, and a single export crop under harsh discipline. When Spanish settlers on Hispaniola watched the Taino population collapse within a generation of 1492, they turned to this proven model. Royal licenses to import Africans soon followed, and the crown's later efforts to curb abuses of Native laborers only deepened colonists' reliance on African captives. By the end of the sixteenth century, the sugar mills of Portuguese Brazil had become the largest destination for enslaved Africans in the Americas. Bondage in the Iberian colonies, in short, was less an improvisation than the export of a system already tested in the eastern Atlantic.

items.stem: Which of the following does the author use as evidence that bondage in the Iberian colonies was the export of an earlier system?
facts: Portuguese colonists established sugar plantations on Madeira and Sao Tome in the fifteenth century using enslaved African labor.
The Portuguese built the fortified trading post of Elmina on the Gold Coast in 1482.

options.text: Plantations on Madeira and Sao Tome that already combined African captives with sugar production
options.label: key
options.why: The author calls the Atlantic island sugar estates a rehearsal that joined capital, African labor, and an export crop before the model was carried to the Americas, which is the evidence for the export claim.

options.text: The rapid decline of the Taino population on Hispaniola during the first generation after Columbus arrived in 1492
options.label: true_but_not_responsive
options.why: The excerpt mentions the Taino collapse, but as the reason Spanish settlers sought new labor, not as evidence that the system already existed elsewhere.

options.text: A rigid racial caste hierarchy that ranked people of Spanish, Native, African, and mixed ancestry in colonial cities
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: The casta system was real, but the excerpt never discusses it or uses it as evidence.

options.text: Debates among Spanish theologians over whether Native peoples possessed souls and could be lawfully enslaved
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: Debates such as the one at Valladolid happened, but the author does not cite them; the excerpt refers only generally to crown efforts to curb abuses.

items.stem: Which of the following sixteenth-century developments would most directly modify the author's argument about labor in the Iberian colonies?
facts: Beginning in the 1570s, Spanish authorities in Peru used the mita, a system of rotating forced Native labor, to work the silver mines of Potosi.
The Spanish crown issued the New Laws in 1542 to limit Native enslavement and the encomienda system.

options.text: Spanish officials compelled Native communities in the Andes to send laborers to the silver mines of Potosi
options.label: key
options.why: The mita shows that Spanish colonies continued to depend heavily on coerced Native labor, qualifying the claim that colonists simply shifted to an imported African plantation model.

options.text: Portuguese merchants purchased captives from African rulers at fortified trading posts such as Elmina on the Gold Coast
options.label: reversal
options.why: This supports rather than modifies the argument, since the author describes exactly this trade as the origin of the system.

options.text: The Spanish crown's New Laws of 1542 sought to restrict the enslavement of Native peoples and to phase out the encomienda
options.label: reversal
options.why: The New Laws fit the author's claim that crown restrictions on Native labor deepened reliance on African captives, so they support the argument.

options.text: Epidemics of smallpox and other Old World diseases sharply reduced Native populations across the Caribbean and Mexico
options.label: reversal
options.why: Native demographic collapse reinforces the author's explanation for why colonists turned to African labor.

items.stem: The Portuguese trading activity along the West African coast in the 1480s, described in the excerpt, is best understood in the context of
facts: Bartolomeu Dias rounded the Cape of Good Hope in 1488.
Vasco da Gama reached India by sea in 1498.

options.text: Portuguese efforts to reach Asian markets by sea and bypass Mediterranean trade intermediaries
options.label: key
options.why: Portuguese voyages down the African coast were part of a search for a sea route to Asia, which Dias and da Gama completed in 1488 and 1498, and they produced trading posts along the way.

options.text: Competition between Catholic and Protestant states that followed Martin Luther's challenge to the papacy in 1517
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The Reformation began decades after the Portuguese posts of the 1480s and did not motivate them.

options.text: Rivalry with English and Dutch joint-stock companies chartered to control the trade of the Atlantic and Indian Oceans
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: English and Dutch chartered companies emerged around 1600, more than a century after the Portuguese posts.

options.text: The arrival of American food crops such as maize and cassava, which transformed farming in West African societies
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: American crops reached Africa through the Columbian Exchange after 1492, so they could not be the context for trade in the 1480s.

items.stem: The pattern of labor and production described in the excerpt is most similar to which of the following developments in the seventeenth century?
facts: In the mid-1600s English colonists on Barbados developed sugar plantations that relied on enslaved African labor.
The Pueblo Revolt against Spanish rule in New Mexico took place in 1680.

options.text: English planters on Barbados turning to enslaved Africans to grow sugar for export
options.label: key
options.why: The Barbados sugar boom repeated the Iberian model the author describes: a single export crop, European capital, and enslaved African labor under harsh discipline.

options.text: Puritan settlers in New England building towns around family farms, congregations, and local town meetings
options.label: unrelated_development
options.why: New England's family-farm economy did not depend on large plantations worked by enslaved Africans.

options.text: French traders in the Saint Lawrence valley forming fur-trading alliances and marriages with Native peoples
options.label: unrelated_development
options.why: The French fur trade depended on partnership with Native peoples, not on plantation labor by enslaved Africans.

options.text: Spanish missionaries in New Mexico compelling Pueblo peoples to labor and convert, provoking the Pueblo Revolt of 1680
options.label: true_but_not_responsive
options.why: This was real coerced labor, but it relied on Native workers in missions, not on enslaved Africans producing an export crop.

input.title: A Jackson Day Toast in Ohio, 1833: The Bank Veto and the Nullification Crisis

sources.title: Address at a Jackson Day dinner, January 8, 1833
sources.attribution: Ezekiel Thorne, a blacksmith and county Democratic committeeman, speaking at an anniversary dinner for the Battle of New Orleans, Harmony Falls, Ohio, January 8, 1833 (ALTON-composed, in the style of a Jacksonian partisan address)
sources.body: Fellow citizens, we meet on the anniversary of New Orleans to honor the old soldier who has twice this year stood between the people and their enemies. In July he struck down the charter of that great monied monster at Philadelphia, a corporation whose stock is held by foreign lords and eastern brokers, and which would make the farmer's harvest and the mechanic's wages hang upon the pleasure of its directors. In December he told the gentlemen of Charleston that no single state may cancel a law of the Union and still keep its place within it. Some call these acts contradictory, saying he strikes at federal power with one hand and wields it with the other. I say both spring from one principle: that the government belongs to the majority of plain people, and neither a chartered aristocracy nor a convention of planters may set itself above their will. Let us drink, then, to the Union and to equal rights.

items.stem: The speaker's point of view in the excerpt is best described as that of
facts: Andrew Jackson vetoed the bill to recharter the Second Bank of the United States in July 1832.
In December 1832 Jackson issued a proclamation rejecting South Carolina's nullification of the federal tariffs.

options.text: a Jackson supporter who viewed both the Bank veto and the rejection of nullification as defenses of majority rule
options.label: key
options.why: The speaker praises the July veto and the December stand against Charleston and argues both follow from the principle that government belongs to the majority of plain people.

options.text: a National Republican who wanted the Second Bank rechartered as a central part of Henry Clay's American System of economic development
options.label: reversal
options.why: The speaker calls the Bank a monied monster and celebrates the veto; recharter was the position of Jackson's opponents.

options.text: a states' rights advocate who endorsed South Carolina's claim that a state convention could void a federal tariff law within its borders
options.label: reversal
options.why: The speaker explicitly denies that a convention of planters or any single state may cancel a law of the Union.

options.text: an abolitionist who regarded the dispute with South Carolina chiefly as a moral struggle over slavery's spread
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: The excerpt frames the dispute as one of Union and majority rule and says nothing about slavery or its expansion.

items.stem: Which of the following would best support the speaker's argument that Jackson's attack on the Bank defended ordinary citizens against privilege?
facts: Jackson's 1832 veto message criticized the Second Bank's charter as granting exclusive privileges that benefited the wealthy and foreign stockholders.
Jackson issued the Specie Circular in 1836.

options.text: Jackson's 1832 veto message argued that the charter gave exclusive privileges benefiting the wealthy and foreign stockholders
options.label: key
options.why: The veto message made the same case the speaker makes, that the Bank was a privileged monopoly serving the rich and foreign investors at the expense of the people.

options.text: The Second Bank's practice of restraining state banks' note issues helped keep the nation's paper currency relatively stable in the 1820s
options.label: reversal
options.why: Evidence of the Bank's stabilizing role would challenge, not support, the claim that it harmed farmers and mechanics.

options.text: Jackson's Specie Circular of 1836 required that purchases of public land be paid for in gold or silver rather than paper bank notes
options.label: true_but_not_responsive
options.why: This later policy targeted land speculation and paper money; it does not show that the Bank's charter itself favored a privileged few.

options.text: The Compromise Tariff of 1833 lowered tariff rates gradually over a decade, easing tensions between South Carolina and Washington
options.label: true_but_not_responsive
options.why: The Compromise Tariff concerns the nullification crisis, not the speaker's argument about the Bank and privilege.

items.stem: The conflict the speaker associates with the gentlemen of Charleston is best understood in the context of
facts: South Carolina's 1832 Ordinance of Nullification declared the federal tariffs of 1828 and 1832 void within the state.
Jackson vetoed the Maysville Road bill in 1830.
The Missouri Compromise was adopted in 1820.

options.text: Southern fears that protective tariffs hurt cotton exporters and that federal power might later threaten slavery
options.label: key
options.why: South Carolina nullified the 1828 and 1832 tariffs because planters believed protection raised their costs and hurt cotton exports, and many feared a strong federal government could eventually move against slavery.

options.text: Western demands for federal funding of internal improvements, which Jackson rejected in vetoing the Maysville Road bill in 1830
options.label: misattributed
options.why: The Maysville Road veto concerned a Kentucky road project and western interests, not South Carolina's resistance to the tariff.

options.text: New England Federalists' objections to the War of 1812, which led delegates at the Hartford Convention to propose constitutional amendments
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The Hartford Convention met in 1814 to 1815, almost two decades before the nullification crisis, and involved New England, not Charleston.

options.text: Congressional disputes over admitting Missouri as a slave state, settled by drawing a line across the Louisiana Purchase
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The Missouri Compromise of 1820 dealt with slavery's spread into territories, not the tariff dispute of 1832 to 1833.

items.stem: The speaker's claim that the government belongs to the majority of plain people most directly reflects which development of the 1820s and 1830s?
facts: By the 1820s and 1830s most states had dropped property requirements for voting by white men.
Mass political parties such as the Democrats used rallies, partisan newspapers, and celebrations to mobilize ordinary voters in the 1830s.

options.text: Expanded white male suffrage and mass party campaigns that encouraged politicians to claim to speak for common men
options.label: key
options.why: As states removed property qualifications, Democrats used rallies and partisan events like this dinner to present their policies as the will of the common man.

options.text: The Second Great Awakening's emphasis on individual moral choice, which inspired revivalists to organize reform societies across the North
options.label: unrelated_development
options.why: Revivalism shaped reform movements, but the speaker's language about majority rule comes from Jacksonian party politics, not religious revival.

options.text: Henry Clay's American System, which proposed uniting the regions through a national bank, protective tariffs, and internal improvements
options.label: reversal
options.why: The American System backed the national bank that the speaker condemns; it was the program of Jackson's opponents.

options.text: The growth of factory labor in New England textile towns, where young women organized early protests over wage cuts
options.label: true_but_not_responsive
options.why: The Lowell mill protests were real, but they do not explain the speaker's democratic political rhetoric about majority rule.

input.title: The Great Migration in a Great Lakes Industrial City, 1900-1940

sources.title: Population of Calder City, a Great Lakes Industrial City, by Census Year, 1900-1940
sources.attribution: Table prepared by statistician Odessa Pruitt for the Calder City Bureau of Social Statistics, annual report, 1941. ALTON-composed illustrative data, not real statistics; Calder City is fictional (ALTON-composed, in the style of a municipal research bureau report)
sources.body: The table shows Calder City's total population, its African American population, the African American share of all residents, and the percentage of African American residents born in a southern state, for each census year from 1900 to 1940.

columns: African American share of total population (percent)
African American residents born in the South (percent)

items.stem: Which of the following most directly explains the change in Calder City's African American population between 1910 and 1920 shown in the table?
facts: During the First World War (1914-1918), European immigration to the United States fell sharply, creating labor shortages in northern industry.
Northern factories recruited African American workers from the South during the war years, accelerating the Great Migration after about 1915.

options.text: Northern factories' demand for workers during the First World War as European immigration sharply declined
options.label: key
options.why: The table shows the Black population more than quadrupling from 7.5 to 33.0 thousand between 1910 and 1920, with the southern-born share jumping to 78 percent. Wartime industrial demand plus the drop in European immigration after 1914 opened northern jobs to Black southerners.

options.text: Federal relief and public works jobs created by New Deal agencies that hired African Americans in northern cities
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: New Deal agencies dated from 1933 onward and could not explain growth during the 1910s.

options.text: Widespread adoption of mechanical cotton pickers that displaced sharecroppers across the Mississippi Delta and other cotton areas
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: Mechanical cotton harvesting spread mainly in the 1940s and 1950s, so it drove the later Second Great Migration, not the 1910s increase.

options.text: Promotional campaigns by railroad companies urging Black families to claim homesteads on the Great Plains under federal land laws
options.label: unrelated_development
options.why: Homesteading drew rural settlers westward, as with the Exodusters around 1879. It does not explain urban growth in a Great Lakes industrial city.

derived.desc: Increase in African American population, 1910 to 1920 (thousands)

items.stem: Which of the following claims is best supported by the data in the table?
facts: The Great Migration continued at high volume through the 1920s before slowing during the Great Depression of the 1930s.

options.text: The Black population grew by a larger number of people in the 1920s than in the 1910s
options.label: key
options.why: The Black population rose by 45.0 thousand from 1920 to 1930, compared with 25.5 thousand from 1910 to 1920. This matches the migration continuing strongly through the 1920s.

options.text: The proportion of Black residents born in the South increased in every census year from 1900 through 1940
options.label: reversal
options.why: The southern-born share peaked at 78 percent in 1920 and then fell to 74 and 66 percent.

options.text: Black migration into the city ceased entirely during the 1930s as the Depression eliminated industrial jobs
options.label: overstated
options.why: Growth slowed in the 1930s, but the Black population still rose from 78.0 to 92.0 thousand, so migration did not stop.

options.text: Most Black newcomers in the 1910s and 1920s found steady work in the city's steel mills and auto plants
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: The table reports population and birthplace only. It contains no employment data.

derived.desc: Increase in African American population, 1920 to 1930 (thousands)
Increase in African American population, 1910 to 1920 (thousands)
Increase in African American population, 1930 to 1940 (thousands)

items.stem: Which of the following conditions in the South most directly contributed to the migration pattern reflected in the table?
facts: By the early 1900s, southern states had enacted Jim Crow segregation laws and disfranchised most Black voters through poll taxes, literacy tests, and similar measures.
Lynching and other racial violence against African Americans were widespread in the South in the late 1800s and early 1900s.

options.text: Jim Crow segregation laws, disfranchisement, and the threat of racial violence
options.label: key
options.why: Legal segregation, the loss of voting rights, and the danger of lynching were major push factors behind the large rise in southern-born Black residents of northern cities shown in the table.

options.text: Expansion of the Freedmen's Bureau's land redistribution programs across the former Confederacy
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The Freedmen's Bureau was shut down in the early 1870s and never carried out large-scale land redistribution, so it could not shape migration after 1910.

options.text: The rapid growth of unionized textile mill jobs open to Black workers in the Carolina Piedmont
options.label: reversal
options.why: Southern textile mills hired mostly white workers and were largely non-union. They did not offer Black southerners such opportunities.

options.text: Federal crop subsidies under the Agricultural Adjustment Act that rewarded tenant farmers for staying on the land
options.label: reversal
options.why: The AAA dates from 1933, and its payments to landowners often pushed tenants and sharecroppers off the land rather than keeping them there.

items.stem: The pattern of migration shown in the table from 1910 to 1930 most closely resembles which of the following later developments?
facts: During the Second World War (U.S. involvement 1941-1945), defense industry jobs drew large numbers of African Americans from the South to cities in the North and West, including West Coast shipyards and aircraft plants.
In 1941, Executive Order 8802 banned racial discrimination in the defense industry.

options.text: Wartime defense jobs after 1941 drawing Black southerners to cities in the North and on the West Coast
options.label: key
options.why: As in the 1910s and 1920s, wartime industrial labor demand pulled Black southerners into northern and western cities in the Second Great Migration.

options.text: The movement of white middle-class families from central cities to new suburbs financed by federally insured mortgages after 1945
options.label: unrelated_development
options.why: Postwar suburbanization moved people out of cities, and a different population was involved. It does not resemble southern-born migrants moving into industrial cities.

options.text: The Dust Bowl migration of displaced farm families from Oklahoma and nearby states to California's agricultural valleys in the 1930s
options.label: true_but_not_responsive
options.why: The Dust Bowl migration was real, but drought and agricultural collapse drove it, and it moved people mainly into farm labor, not into industrial cities.

options.text: The return of many Black families to the rural South in the 1970s and 1980s as Sun Belt economies expanded
options.label: reversal
options.why: This late-century return migration ran in the opposite direction, from North to South, so it is the reverse of the pattern in the table.

input.title: A Nebraska Farmers' Alliance Petition for Federal Railroad Regulation, 1887

sources.title: Petition to the Nebraska Congressional Delegation
sources.attribution: Elias Brandt, secretary of a Farmers' Alliance chapter in Kearney, Nebraska, petition to the state's members of Congress, January 1887 (ALTON-composed, in the style of a Gilded Age farmers' petition)
sources.body: Gentlemen: The farmers of Buffalo County send their wheat to Omaha at a charge per bushel nearly equal to what the same car pays from Omaha all the way to Chicago, five times the distance. Where one road holds the only track, it names its price; where two roads compete, the rate falls by half. Meanwhile the great elevator companies receive private rebates that no small shipper is ever offered, so the man who hauls two wagons to the depot pays to subsidize his largest rival. Our legislature has tried to correct these wrongs, but since the Supreme Court's decision of last October no state may regulate a rate that crosses its border. The power now rests with Congress alone. We ask that you support the bill before you, forbidding rebates and unjust discrimination and establishing a commission to hear our complaints. The railroads were built with public lands and public credit; they cannot claim to be purely private concerns.

items.stem: Brandt's main purpose in the petition was most likely to
facts: In Wabash, St. Louis and Pacific Railway Co. v. Illinois (1886), the Supreme Court ruled that states could not regulate interstate railroad rates.
Congress passed the Interstate Commerce Act in 1887, banning rebates and rate discrimination and creating the Interstate Commerce Commission.

options.text: persuade federal lawmakers to regulate railroads after a court ruling limited state power
options.label: key
options.why: Brandt says that since the Supreme Court's decision of last October (Wabash, 1886) states cannot regulate interstate rates, so he asks Congress to pass the bill that became the Interstate Commerce Act of 1887.

options.text: urge the Nebraska legislature to pass new Granger laws setting maximum freight and grain storage rates
options.label: reversal
options.why: Brandt says the state legislature's efforts are now powerless and addresses Congress, not the state legislature.

options.text: demand that the federal government purchase and operate the nation's railroads, telegraphs, and telephones as public utilities
options.label: overstated
options.why: Government ownership was a later Populist demand (Omaha Platform, 1892); Brandt asks only for regulation through a commission.

options.text: call on Congress to expand the money supply through the unlimited coinage of silver to relieve indebted farmers
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: Free silver was a real farmer demand, but the petition deals only with freight rates and rebates, not currency.

items.stem: Which of the following pieces of evidence would best support Brandt's claim that railroads treated shippers unequally?
facts: In the 1870s and 1880s Standard Oil obtained rebates from railroads on its shipments, which gave it an advantage over smaller competitors.

options.text: Large firms such as Standard Oil obtained secret rebates on freight charges from railroads
options.label: key
options.why: Rebates to favored large shippers like Standard Oil are direct evidence of the unequal treatment Brandt describes with the elevator companies.

options.text: Railroad companies received millions of acres of federal land grants to build transcontinental lines during the 1860s
options.label: true_but_not_responsive
options.why: Land grants back up Brandt's point about public aid, not his claim that railroads treated shippers unequally.

options.text: Major railroads adopted standardized time zones across the country in 1883 to coordinate their train schedules
options.label: unrelated_development
options.why: Standard time was about scheduling and has nothing to do with rate discrimination among shippers.

options.text: Railroad workers walked off the job across several states during the Great Railroad Strike of 1877 after wage cuts
options.label: true_but_not_responsive
options.why: The 1877 strike shows conflict between railroads and labor, not unequal rates charged to shippers.

items.stem: The petition is best understood in the context of which broader development of the late nineteenth century?
facts: The Grange (founded 1867) and the Farmers' Alliances of the 1870s and 1880s organized farmers to challenge railroad rates and the power of middlemen.
These farmer movements helped form the People's (Populist) Party in 1892.

options.text: Farmers organizing to challenge the power of railroads and other corporations over their livelihoods
options.label: key
options.why: An Alliance secretary protesting freight rates and rebates fits the Grange and Farmers' Alliance movements against railroad and corporate power.

options.text: Former Radical Republicans using federal authority to protect the civil and political rights of freedpeople in the South
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: Federal enforcement during Reconstruction had largely ended by 1877, and it concerned civil rights, not railroad rates.

options.text: Nativist groups lobbying Congress to restrict immigration from Asia, culminating in the Chinese Exclusion Act
options.label: unrelated_development
options.why: Anti-Chinese nativism was real in the period, but the petition does not deal with immigration.

options.text: Social Gospel ministers urging churches to address urban poverty through missions and charity work in industrial cities
options.label: unrelated_development
options.why: The Social Gospel was an urban, religious reform effort; the petition is about rural shippers and freight rates.

items.stem: Which of the following later developments most directly continued the regulatory effort Brandt called for?
facts: The Hepburn Act of 1906 gave the Interstate Commerce Commission the power to set maximum railroad rates.
Court decisions in the 1890s had weakened the Interstate Commerce Commission's ability to enforce rates.

options.text: The Hepburn Act of 1906 allowing the Interstate Commerce Commission to set maximum railroad rates
options.label: key
options.why: The Hepburn Act strengthened the commission created in 1887, carrying forward federal control of railroad rates in the Progressive Era.

options.text: The Adamson Act of 1916 establishing an eight-hour workday for interstate railroad workers to avert a strike
options.label: true_but_not_responsive
options.why: The Adamson Act regulated railroad labor hours, not the rates and discrimination against shippers that Brandt protests.

options.text: The Federal Reserve Act of 1913 creating regional banks to manage the currency and provide credit to member banks
options.label: unrelated_development
options.why: The Federal Reserve Act reformed banking and currency, not railroads.

options.text: The Pacific Railway Acts of the 1860s granting land and loans to companies building a transcontinental line
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: These laws came before the petition and promoted railroad building rather than regulating rates.

input.title: A Reform Club Greets the Pendleton Act, 1883

sources.title: Address to a civil service reform club
sources.attribution: Address by Ephraim T. Haskell, secretary of the Hartwell Civil Service Reform Club, to the club's members, Hartwell, Connecticut, February 1883 (ALTON-composed, in the style of a Gilded Age reform club address)
sources.body: Gentlemen, the bill is law. For the first time since the days of Jackson, a young man may enter the service of the United States by proving his fitness in an open examination rather than by carrying a ward boss's letter. A clerk in our own post office told me he paid two percent of his wages each autumn to the party committee, and he knew his desk would go to another man if he refused. Every change of administration brought a swarm of applicants to Washington, and the President spent his days parceling out offices like the spoils of a conquered town. The tragedy of the summer before last showed the nation where that road ends. Yet let no member mistake this act for a complete victory. The commission it creates reaches only a small portion of the offices; the rest remain the property of whichever party holds power. Our work is to see the classified list extended, office by office, until merit is the rule.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes the purpose of Haskell's address?

options.text: To urge reformers to keep pressing for merit hiring in more federal offices
options.label: key
options.why: Haskell welcomes the new law but warns it is not a complete victory and calls for extending the classified list office by office. That is the goal of Gilded Age civil service reformers after 1883.

options.text: To call for repeal of the new law because it weakens the party organizations that mobilize voters
options.label: reversal
options.why: Haskell praises the law and attacks party patronage. Defending the parties was the position of spoilsmen, not reformers.

options.text: To recruit postal clerks into a national labor union seeking higher wages and an eight-hour day
options.label: unrelated_development
options.why: The post office clerk is mentioned only as an example of party assessments. The address is about how offices are filled, not about labor organizing.

options.text: To ask Congress to regulate railroad rates, since monopolies had captured the state legislatures
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: Railroad regulation was a separate Gilded Age reform cause, and the excerpt never mentions it.

facts: The Pendleton Civil Service Reform Act, signed in January 1883, created a Civil Service Commission and required competitive examinations for classified federal positions.
At first the Pendleton Act covered only a small share of federal jobs (about 10 percent), and later presidents expanded the classified list.

items.stem: Which of the following developments would best support Haskell's argument about how party patronage worked in federal offices before 1883?

options.text: Hayes's 1878 removal of New York Custom House officials accused of running it as a party machine
options.label: key
options.why: Hayes removed Chester Arthur and other officials of the New York Custom House, which was widely seen as a center of patronage and party assessments. This is direct evidence for Haskell's claim that federal offices served as party property.

options.text: The Bland-Allison Act of 1878 requiring the Treasury to buy a limited amount of silver each month for coinage
options.label: unrelated_development
options.why: The Bland-Allison Act dealt with monetary policy and the silver question. It says nothing about how federal jobs were handed out.

options.text: The Supreme Court's 1886 Wabash decision denying states the power to regulate interstate railroad rates
options.label: unrelated_development
options.why: Wabash v. Illinois concerned railroad regulation and federal power over interstate commerce, not patronage. It also came after the address.

options.text: Mugwump Republicans' decision in 1884 to bolt their party and support the Democratic nominee Grover Cleveland
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The Mugwump bolt came after the address and shows how reformers acted in politics. It is not evidence of how patronage worked before 1883.

facts: In 1878 President Rutherford B. Hayes removed Chester A. Arthur as Collector of the Port of New York in a dispute over patronage at the New York Custom House.

items.stem: Which of the following provided the most immediate context for the passage of the law that Haskell celebrates?

options.text: The 1881 assassination of President James Garfield by a disappointed seeker of federal office
options.label: key
options.why: Speaking in early 1883, Haskell calls it 'the tragedy of the summer before last,' which points to Garfield's shooting in July 1881 by Charles Guiteau, a disappointed office seeker. The killing built public support for the Pendleton Act.

options.text: The impeachment of President Andrew Johnson in 1868 after he removed his secretary of war in defiance of the Tenure of Office Act
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: Johnson's impeachment came out of Reconstruction conflicts about fifteen years earlier. It was not the immediate background to civil service reform in 1883.

options.text: The disputed presidential election of 1876 and the bargain that ended federal military support for Reconstruction governments
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The Compromise of 1877 settled the disputed election and ended Reconstruction. It came years before the law and did not set off merit reform.

options.text: The Panic of 1873 and the long wave of railroad bankruptcies and unemployment that followed in its wake
options.label: unrelated_development
options.why: The depression of the 1870s shaped labor and monetary politics. It was not the event that pushed Congress to pass civil service reform.

facts: President James A. Garfield was shot in July 1881 by Charles Guiteau, a disappointed office seeker, and died in September 1881.
Garfield's assassination strengthened public support for the Pendleton Act of 1883.

items.stem: Which of the following was a significant effect of the type of law described in the excerpt on national politics in the decades after 1883?

options.text: Political parties grew more dependent on contributions from wealthy businessmen and corporations
options.label: key
options.why: The law cut back the parties' ability to collect assessments from federal officeholders. As a result, national party organizations turned more and more to business donors for campaign money, as in the large corporate fundraising of 1896.

options.text: Party machines in large cities collapsed as municipal jobs became subject to federal competitive examinations
options.label: misattributed
options.why: The Pendleton Act covered only federal jobs. Urban machines such as Tammany Hall kept local patronage and stayed strong into the Progressive Era.

options.text: Federal employees won the right to bargain collectively and to strike against the national government
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: The law set up merit hiring and protections, not collective bargaining. Federal workers gained no right to strike in this period.

options.text: Voter turnout in national elections fell sharply in the 1880s because patronage no longer drew partisans to the polls
options.label: reversal
options.why: Turnout in presidential elections stayed very high through the 1880s and 1890s. Strong party loyalty remained a defining feature of Gilded Age politics.

facts: The Pendleton Act of 1883 barred the coercion of federal employees into making political contributions, which reduced the parties' reliance on officeholder assessments.
After the Pendleton Act, national parties relied more heavily on contributions from businesses and wealthy donors, as in the 1896 Republican campaign.

input.title: Colonial Assemblies and the Power of the Purse, 1689-1754

sources.title: Assemblies in an Age of Imperial Neglect
sources.attribution: Lydia Fenwright-Osei, historian, The Bargaining Houses: Colonial Legislatures in the British Atlantic, 1689-1754, published 2011 (ALTON-composed, in the style of a scholarly monograph on colonial political history)
sources.body: Historians often call the decades between the Glorious Revolution and the Seven Years' War an era of imperial neglect, but the word hides what colonists were actively doing. Ministers in London, especially during Robert Walpole's long tenure, chose not to press trade regulations too hard. Meanwhile colonial lower houses steadily claimed the power of the purse. From Virginia to Massachusetts, assemblies refused to vote governors permanent salaries and granted them year by year instead. They insisted on naming the treasurers who spent public money. Royal governors arrived with sweeping instructions, yet they could not build a road or raise a militia company without bargaining with local planters and merchants. By 1750 the assemblies regarded these practices not as favors granted by the Crown but as rights rooted in English liberty. That conviction would matter greatly once London changed course.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes the author's main argument in the excerpt?
facts: Between 1689 and 1754 British imperial authorities enforced trade laws loosely, a policy later called salutary neglect.
Colonial assemblies in this period gained power by controlling taxation and appropriations, including governors' salaries.

options.text: Colonial assemblies used a period of loose imperial oversight to expand their control over public finances
options.label: key
options.why: The author argues that while London did not press its regulations, lower houses took the power of the purse by voting governors' salaries yearly and naming treasurers.

options.text: Royal governors armed with detailed instructions from London kept colonial legislatures firmly subordinate to the Crown
options.label: reversal
options.why: The excerpt says governors had sweeping instructions but still had to bargain with assemblies, which is the opposite of keeping them subordinate.

options.text: Colonial lower houses openly sought independence from Britain well before the start of the Seven Years' War in 1754
options.label: overstated
options.why: The author describes assemblies claiming rights as English subjects, not seeking independence, which colonists did not pursue until the 1770s.

options.text: British ministers deliberately transferred authority over taxation and defense to the colonies through formal charters and statutes
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: The excerpt says assemblies took these powers through practice and bargaining, not through any formal grant from London.

items.stem: Which of the following developments would most directly modify the author's argument about the extent of colonial self-government between 1689 and 1754?
facts: Throughout the colonial period, the Privy Council in England reviewed colonial legislation and disallowed some colonial laws.
The Dominion of New England (1686-1689) suspended elected assemblies and collapsed after the Glorious Revolution in 1689.
Colonial merchants widely evaded the Molasses Act of 1733.

options.text: The Privy Council in London continued to review colonial laws and disallowed a number of them
options.label: key
options.why: Continued royal review and disallowance of colonial statutes shows that London kept real limits on the assemblies, which qualifies the picture of near-total self-government.

options.text: Colonial merchants routinely evaded the Navigation Acts and the Molasses Act with little interference from customs officials
options.label: reversal
options.why: Widespread, unpunished smuggling supports the author's picture of loose imperial enforcement rather than modifying it.

options.text: James II's consolidation of northern colonies into the Dominion of New England, which suspended their elected assemblies
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The Dominion lasted from 1686 to 1689 and collapsed with the Glorious Revolution, before the period the author covers.

options.text: Revivals of the Great Awakening challenged the authority of established ministers in many colonial congregations
options.label: unrelated_development
options.why: The Great Awakening concerned religious authority, not the balance of political power between assemblies and the Crown.

items.stem: The colonists' view that their assemblies' powers were rights rooted in English liberty, as described in the excerpt, was most directly shaped by which broader context?
facts: The Glorious Revolution of 1688-1689 and the English Bill of Rights (1689) strengthened Parliament relative to the Crown, including its control of taxation.
Thomas Paine published Common Sense in 1776.

options.text: Parliament's strengthened authority over the Crown, including over taxation, after the Glorious Revolution
options.label: key
options.why: Colonists modeled their assemblies on Parliament, and the settlement after 1688-1689 confirmed that elected representatives, not the monarch, controlled taxes, which made the power of the purse look like an English right.

options.text: Thomas Paine's widely read arguments in Common Sense against hereditary monarchy and in favor of immediate American independence
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: Common Sense appeared in 1776, decades after the assembly practices the author describes for the years before 1750.

options.text: The Spanish practice of governing American colonies through viceroys appointed directly by the Crown in Madrid
options.label: unrelated_development
options.why: Spanish royal government was centralized and gave colonists no model of elected legislatures controlling taxes.

options.text: Mercantilist doctrine holding that colonies existed to supply raw materials and markets for the mother country
options.label: true_but_not_responsive
options.why: Mercantilism shaped imperial trade policy, but it did not give colonists their ideas about representative rights and English liberty.

items.stem: The convictions described in the last two sentences of the excerpt most directly contributed to which development in the 1760s?
facts: Parliament passed the Stamp Act in 1765, and colonists protested that only their own assemblies could tax them.
The Articles of Confederation (ratified 1781) did not give Congress the power to levy taxes.
The Treaty of Paris (1763) gave Britain Canada and Florida.

options.text: Colonial protests against the Stamp Act of 1765 as a tax imposed without colonial representation
options.label: key
options.why: Once London tightened control after 1763, colonists argued that only their own assemblies could tax them, a belief grown out of the power of the purse described in the excerpt.

options.text: The Articles of Confederation's grant to Congress of broad power to levy direct taxes on the states and their citizens
options.label: reversal
options.why: The Articles withheld the taxing power from Congress, and they were drafted in the late 1770s, not the 1760s.

options.text: Britain's acquisition of French Canada and Florida under the Treaty of Paris that ended the Seven Years' War in 1763
options.label: true_but_not_responsive
options.why: The treaty came out of a war between empires, not from colonists' belief that their assemblies held rights as Englishmen.

options.text: Pontiac's alliance of western nations attacking British forts in the Great Lakes region after 1763
options.label: unrelated_development
options.why: Pontiac's War was American Indian resistance to British expansion, not a result of colonial assemblies' views about their authority.

input.title: Direct Democracy in Progressive Oregon

sources.title: The Petition and the Pamphlet
sources.attribution: Thaddeus Reinholt, historian, Ballots Against the Bosses: Direct Democracy in the Pacific Northwest, 1898-1914, published 2019 (ALTON-composed, in the style of a modern political history of the Progressive Era)
sources.body: Oregon reformers after 1902 liked to describe the initiative and referendum as the people taking lawmaking back from a corrupt legislature, and that image has lasted. The record tells a more complicated story. The petitions that put measures on the ballot were circulated mostly by organized groups: the state Grange, a direct-legislation league, prohibitionists, and by 1910 paid canvassers working for business associations. In some elections voters received pamphlets describing more than two dozen measures, and many left the bottom of the ballot blank. Oregon practiced popular choice of senators years before the Seventeenth Amendment, but even that system depended on legislators keeping a pledge to follow the popular vote. Direct democracy did weaken the party machines and railroad lobbies that had dominated the statehouse. It did not abolish organized influence, however. It moved that influence out of the legislative cloakroom and into the petition drive and the campaign pamphlet.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes the main argument of the excerpt?
facts: Oregon adopted the initiative and referendum in 1902.
Progressive reformers promoted direct democracy as a way to reduce the power of party machines and corporate lobbies in state legislatures.

options.text: Direct democracy shifted organized interests' influence over lawmaking into new channels rather than ending it.
options.label: key
options.why: The author concludes that direct democracy moved organized influence from the legislative cloakroom into the petition drive and campaign pamphlet; it did not abolish it.

options.text: Direct democracy let ordinary voters wrest lawmaking from organized interests and permanently end lobbying in the state.
options.label: overstated
options.why: This is the reformers' own image, and the author says the record complicates it. The author explicitly denies that organized influence was abolished.

options.text: Direct democracy strengthened party machines and railroad lobbies by burdening voters with long ballots they could not master.
options.label: reversal
options.why: The author says direct democracy weakened the machines and railroad lobbies. The long ballots are offered as a complication, not as evidence that the old powers grew stronger.

options.text: Direct democracy collapsed in Oregon because legislators refused to honor their pledges on the choice of United States senators.
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: The excerpt notes that the senatorial system depended on legislators keeping a pledge, but it never says the pledges were broken or that direct democracy collapsed.

items.stem: Which of the following, if true, would most directly support the author's argument about direct democracy in the excerpt?
facts: The Seventeenth Amendment, ratified in 1913, provided for the direct popular election of United States senators.
Oregon voters approved woman suffrage through an initiative measure in 1912, before the Nineteenth Amendment was ratified in 1920.

options.text: Most measures adopted by initiative in western states in the 1910s were drafted and funded by labor, business, or temperance groups
options.label: key
options.why: Evidence that organized groups wrote and paid for successful measures would back the author's claim that organized influence moved into the petition process instead of disappearing.

options.text: The Seventeenth Amendment, ratified in 1913, required that voters in every state directly elect their United States senators to six-year terms
options.label: true_but_not_responsive
options.why: This is accurate, but national ratification of direct Senate elections says nothing about whether organized interests controlled the initiative process.

options.text: Most initiative petitions in Oregon were written and circulated by individual farmers acting on their own without help from any organized association
options.label: reversal
options.why: Evidence like this would undercut the author, who argues that organized groups, not unaffiliated individuals, ran the petition drives.

options.text: Oregon voters approved woman suffrage by initiative in 1912, adding thousands of new voters to the state's electorate eight years before the Nineteenth Amendment
options.label: true_but_not_responsive
options.why: This is a real use of the initiative, but a larger electorate does not show who sponsored measures or whether organized influence continued.

items.stem: The reforms discussed in the excerpt are best understood in the context of which broader development?
facts: Progressive Era reformers, roughly 1890 to 1920, pursued the initiative, referendum, recall, direct primary, and direct election of senators to reduce corruption and corporate influence in government.
The Pendleton Civil Service Act was passed in 1883.

options.text: Progressive efforts to curb corruption and corporate power over government by giving citizens a more direct voice
options.label: key
options.why: The initiative, referendum, and popular choice of senators belonged to a wider Progressive campaign against machines and corporate lobbies, carried out by expanding direct citizen participation.

options.text: New Deal programs that expanded federal regulatory power and built a lasting coalition of urban workers, farmers, and African American voters
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The New Deal began in 1933, decades after the Oregon reforms of 1902 to 1914, and it centered on federal economic programs, not state-level direct democracy.

options.text: Gilded Age civil service reform that replaced the spoils system with competitive examinations for many federal jobs after the Pendleton Act
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The Pendleton Act of 1883 was an earlier reform that targeted federal patronage, not the way citizens made state laws or chose senators.

options.text: Southern state laws imposing poll taxes, literacy tests, and white primaries that sharply reduced the number of eligible voters in the region
options.label: reversal
options.why: Disfranchisement laws from the same years narrowed participation, mainly by African Americans. The reforms in the excerpt were meant to widen voters' direct role in lawmaking.

items.stem: The movement for direct election of senators, mentioned in the excerpt, developed primarily because many Americans in the period believed that
facts: Before the Seventeenth Amendment (1913), state legislatures elected United States senators, and the system was criticized for bribery and deadlocked elections.
The Populist Party's Omaha Platform of 1892 endorsed direct election of senators; the Populist-backed candidate William Jennings Bryan lost the 1896 presidential election.
The Supreme Court's one-person, one-vote ruling in Reynolds v. Sims came in 1964.

options.text: state legislatures choosing senators invited bribery and deadlock and let corporate interests buy seats
options.label: key
options.why: Reformers charged that legislative election of senators produced corruption, deadlocks, and a Senate tied to railroads and trusts. That critique drove the push that ended in the Seventeenth Amendment in 1913.

options.text: the Senate had become too responsive to popular majorities and needed insulation from the passing passions of ordinary voters
options.label: reversal
options.why: This turns the reform logic around. Critics thought the Senate was too insulated from voters, and that is why they wanted popular election.

options.text: the Populist Party's victory in the 1896 presidential election had given reformers a national mandate to rewrite the Constitution
options.label: misattributed
options.why: Populists did support direct election of senators, but they lost in 1896 when William McKinley defeated William Jennings Bryan. No such mandate existed.

options.text: Supreme Court rulings requiring legislative districts of equal population had made state legislatures unrepresentative of their voters
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The equal-population rulings, such as Reynolds v. Sims, came in the 1960s, long after the Seventeenth Amendment.

input.title: Watergate as Confirmation: Declining Trust in Government, 1964-1975

sources.title: Watergate and the Decade of Doubt
sources.attribution: Corinne Haldane, historian, from The Broken Covenant: Americans and Their Government, 1964-1980, a lecture series delivered at a public university in Sacramento, California, 2009 (ALTON-composed, in the style of a historian's interpretive study of postwar political culture)
sources.body: It is tempting to treat Watergate as the moment Americans stopped believing their leaders, but the scandal is better understood as a confirmation than a cause. By 1968, the distance between official optimism about Vietnam and the scenes on the evening news had already earned its own label among reporters: the credibility gap. The publication of the Pentagon Papers in 1971 showed that several administrations, Democratic and Republican alike, had misled the public about the war's course and prospects. What Watergate added was proof that deception reached into domestic politics and into the Oval Office itself. The White House tapes, released after the Supreme Court ruled against the president in 1974, turned private suspicion into documented fact. Congressional investigations of the intelligence agencies the following year deepened the damage. Watergate, in short, gave a name and a face to a distrust that had been a decade in the making.

items.stem: Which of the following does the author use as evidence that public distrust of government existed before the Watergate scandal?

options.text: Documents published in 1971 showing that several administrations had misled the public about the war
options.label: key
options.why: The author cites the Pentagon Papers (1971), which revealed that multiple administrations had misrepresented the Vietnam War, to show that deception and distrust predated Watergate.

options.text: White House tape recordings released in 1974 after the Supreme Court ruled against the president's claim
options.label: true_but_not_responsive
options.why: The tapes appear in the excerpt, but as evidence of the Watergate cover-up itself, not of distrust that existed before the scandal.

options.text: Congressional investigations into the conduct of the intelligence agencies held in the year following the tapes
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The author says these 1975 investigations came after Watergate and deepened the damage. They do not show distrust that existed earlier.

options.text: Opinion polls showing that a majority of voters approved of the president's decision to resign from office in 1974
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: The excerpt mentions no opinion polls about the resignation, and such evidence would not show distrust before Watergate anyway.

facts: The Pentagon Papers were published by newspapers in 1971.
The Pentagon Papers revealed that the government had misled the public about U.S. involvement in Vietnam across several administrations.

items.stem: Which of the following, if true, would most directly challenge the author's argument about the origins of public distrust of government?

options.text: Surveys showing public trust in government stayed steady through 1972 and fell only after the hearings
options.label: key
