options.why: The author argues that distrust had been building for a decade before Watergate. Evidence that trust stayed steady until the Watergate hearings would suggest the scandal caused the decline instead of confirming it.

options.text: Records showing the FBI had conducted surveillance of civil rights and antiwar groups through the 1960s
options.label: reversal
options.why: FBI surveillance programs such as COINTELPRO in the 1960s point to government abuses before Watergate, so this evidence would support the author's argument.

options.text: Evidence that many Americans doubted official reports of progress in Vietnam after the Tet Offensive of early 1968
options.label: reversal
options.why: Doubt after Tet in 1968 fits the author's claim that a credibility gap existed before Watergate, so it would support the argument.

options.text: Evidence that President Ford's 1974 pardon of Richard Nixon provoked widespread public anger and protest
options.label: true_but_not_responsive
options.why: Anger over the 1974 pardon shows that distrust continued after Watergate. It says nothing about whether distrust began earlier, which is the author's claim.

facts: The Senate Watergate hearings were televised in 1973.
The Tet Offensive in 1968 led many Americans to doubt official claims of progress in Vietnam.
President Gerald Ford pardoned Richard Nixon in September 1974.

items.stem: The developments described in the excerpt are best understood in the context of which broader trend of the 1970s?

options.text: Congressional efforts to limit presidential power, such as the War Powers Resolution of 1973
options.label: key
options.why: Vietnam and Watergate led Congress to push back against what critics called the imperial presidency. Examples include the War Powers Resolution (1973) and the 1975 intelligence investigations the excerpt mentions.

options.text: Renewed fears of internal communist subversion that led to loyalty investigations of federal employees
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: Loyalty investigations of federal employees belong to the Second Red Scare of the late 1940s and early 1950s, not to the 1970s.

options.text: Expansion of federal antipoverty programs such as Medicare, Medicaid, and the Office of Economic Opportunity
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: These Great Society programs were created in 1964 and 1965 under Lyndon Johnson, before the 1970s developments in the excerpt.

options.text: Supreme Court rulings expanding the rights of accused criminals, such as the requirement of Miranda warnings
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: Miranda v. Arizona (1966) was a Warren Court decision of the 1960s. It is unrelated to the 1970s struggle over executive power.

facts: Congress passed the War Powers Resolution over President Nixon's veto in 1973.
Medicare and Medicaid were created in 1965.
Miranda v. Arizona was decided in 1966.

items.stem: The "credibility gap" mentioned in the excerpt most directly reflected which of the following developments of the late 1960s?

options.text: Events such as the Tet Offensive that contradicted official claims of progress in Vietnam
options.label: key
options.why: The phrase credibility gap described the distance between the Johnson administration's upbeat claims about Vietnam and events like the 1968 Tet Offensive, which showed the war was far from won.

options.text: The government's denial of U-2 spy flights over the Soviet Union before the capture of an American pilot
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The U-2 incident took place in 1960 under Eisenhower. It did involve official deception, but it was not the Vietnam-era credibility gap the excerpt describes.

options.text: Nixon's policy of Vietnamization, which shifted the burden of ground combat to South Vietnamese forces
options.label: unrelated_development
options.why: Vietnamization, begun in 1969, was a policy to withdraw U.S. troops. It was a strategy, not the gap between official optimism and battlefield reality.

options.text: The Kerner Commission's conclusion that the nation was moving toward two separate and unequal societies
options.label: unrelated_development
options.why: The 1968 Kerner Commission report dealt with urban unrest and racial inequality, not with official claims about the Vietnam War.

facts: The Tet Offensive was launched by North Vietnamese and Viet Cong forces in January 1968.
The term credibility gap was widely applied to the Johnson administration's statements about the Vietnam War.
The U-2 incident occurred in 1960.

input.title: Two Interpretations of the Railroads and Western Settlement

sources.title: Text A: The Railroad as a Federal Project
sources.attribution: Margaret Ellison Thorne, historian, Rails Across the Plains: Federal Promotion and the Making of the West, 1998 (ALTON-composed, in the style of a historian of western economic development)
sources.body: The transcontinental lines were less triumphs of private enterprise than creations of Washington. Congress gave the Union Pacific and Central Pacific alternate sections of public land along their routes and lent them federal bonds for every mile of track they finished. Without that support, few investors would have risked capital on rails through country with so few paying customers. The payoff was real. Eager to turn their land grants into cash, railroad companies advertised in Scandinavia, Germany, and the eastern states, ran cheap excursion trains for prospective buyers, and brought hundreds of thousands of settlers onto the plains. Towns grew up around depots, and Kansas wheat could reach Chicago in a matter of days.

sources.title: Text B: The Railroad and the Mortgaged West
sources.attribution: Daniel Okafor-Reyes, historian, Mortgaged Prairie: Farmers, Carriers, and Power in the Trans-Mississippi West, 2011 (ALTON-composed, in the style of a historian of agrarian protest)
sources.body: Celebrations of the railroad as the settler's friend overlook who held power once the track was laid. Across much of the trans-Mississippi West, a single line served an entire district, and its managers set freight and grain storage charges as they pleased. Farmers who had borrowed to buy railroad land and new machinery found that the carrier could take much of a good harvest's value. The roads also sped the slaughter of the bison herds and carried the soldiers and settlers who pressed Plains nations onto reservations. The West the railroads built was tied into national markets, but on terms written by distant directors and their creditors.

items.stem: Thorne in Text A and Okafor-Reyes in Text B would most likely agree with which of the following statements about railroads in the West?

options.text: Railroads drew settlers westward and tied western farms to national markets.
options.label: key
options.why: Text A credits the railroads with bringing hundreds of thousands of settlers and moving Kansas wheat to Chicago; Text B grants that the railroad West was tied into national markets, though on unfair terms. Both accept the railroads' integrating role while disagreeing about who benefited.

options.text: Federal land grants and bond loans allowed railroad companies to charge farmers excessive freight rates.
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: Text B complains about rates but blames local monopoly, not federal aid, and Text A never mentions rates. Neither text links the subsidies to the rates.

options.text: Railroad managers set fair rates for western farmers because the companies depended on selling their land grants.
options.label: reversal
options.why: Text B argues the opposite: managers set charges as they pleased and took much of the harvest's value.

options.text: Private eastern and European investors built the western lines largely without assistance from Congress.
options.label: reversal
options.why: Text A argues the lines were creations of Washington and that without federal land and bonds few investors would have taken the risk.

facts: The Pacific Railway Act of 1862 granted land and federal bond loans to the Union Pacific and Central Pacific railroads.
The first transcontinental railroad was completed at Promontory Summit, Utah Territory, in 1869.

items.stem: Which of the following developments in the late nineteenth century would most directly support the argument Okafor-Reyes makes in Text B?

options.text: Midwestern farmers organized Granges in the 1870s and pressed states to regulate railroad and grain elevator rates.
options.label: key
options.why: Granger agitation produced state laws regulating railroad and elevator charges (upheld in Munn v. Illinois, 1877). It shows that farmers themselves saw carriers' control over freight and storage charges as a real grievance, which backs Text B's claim about railroad power.

options.text: Congress passed the Homestead Act in 1862, offering 160 acres of public land to settlers who lived on and improved it for five years.
options.label: true_but_not_responsive
options.why: The Homestead Act encouraged settlement but says nothing about railroad power over farmers, the core of Text B's argument.

options.text: Thousands of Chinese immigrants laid track for the Central Pacific through the Sierra Nevada under dangerous conditions and low wages.
options.label: true_but_not_responsive
options.why: Chinese railroad labor is accurate history but concerns construction, not the rates and debt imposed on settlers after the track was laid.

options.text: The Pacific Railway Act loaned federal bonds to railroad companies for each mile of track, enabling construction across thinly settled land.
options.label: misattributed
options.why: This evidence supports Thorne's argument in Text A about federal promotion, not Okafor-Reyes's argument about railroad power over farmers.

facts: The Grange (Patrons of Husbandry), founded in 1867, pushed state laws regulating railroad and grain elevator rates in the 1870s.
In Munn v. Illinois (1877), the Supreme Court upheld state regulation of grain elevator rates.

items.stem: The federal policies described in Text A are best understood in the context of which of the following?

options.text: Wartime Republican Congresses used federal land and credit to promote economic development in the West.
options.label: key
options.why: With Southern members gone after secession, the Republican-controlled Congress passed railroad aid and other development measures in 1862, the federal promotion Text A describes.

options.text: New Deal agencies financed large public works projects such as dams and highways to create jobs in the West.
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: New Deal public works came in the 1930s, decades after the railroad land grants and bond loans.

options.text: State governments in the 1820s and 1830s funded canals and turnpikes, such as the Erie Canal, to link interior farms to eastern ports.
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: State-funded internal improvements belong to the earlier market revolution and were state projects, not the federal grants Text A describes.

options.text: The dominance of laissez-faire ideas that discouraged government from aiding or regulating private business enterprise in the late 1800s.
options.label: reversal
options.why: Text A describes active federal subsidy of business, the opposite of a hands-off approach. Laissez-faire talk also sat alongside generous aid to railroads.

facts: In 1862 the Republican-controlled Congress passed the Pacific Railway Act, the Homestead Act, and the Morrill Land-Grant College Act.
Southern Democrats had left Congress after their states seceded in 1860-1861.

items.stem: The grievances described in Text B most directly contributed to which of the following later developments?

options.text: The Populist Party's 1892 call for government ownership of the railroads
options.label: key
options.why: Farmers' anger at railroad rates and debt, described in Text B, grew into the Farmers' Alliances and the People's Party, whose 1892 Omaha Platform called for government ownership of the railroads.

options.text: The Pendleton Act's 1883 creation of competitive examinations for some federal jobs
options.label: unrelated_development
options.why: Civil service reform answered the spoils system and the assassination of Garfield, not farmers' complaints about railroads.

options.text: The Chinese Exclusion Act's 1882 ban on the immigration of Chinese laborers
options.label: unrelated_development
options.why: Exclusion grew from nativism and labor competition on the West Coast, not from farmers' grievances against railroad rates and creditors.

options.text: The American Federation of Labor's organization of skilled craft workers into national trade unions
options.label: unrelated_development
options.why: The AFL, founded in 1886, organized skilled industrial workers around wages and hours, not indebted farmers protesting railroad power.

facts: The People's (Populist) Party's Omaha Platform of 1892 called for government ownership of the railroads.
The Populist Party grew out of the Farmers' Alliance movement of the 1880s.

input.title: A Kansas Farm Letter, 1933: Debt, Dust, and Depression on the Southern Plains

sources.title: Letter from a farm woman in southwestern Kansas to her congressman, March 1933
sources.attribution: Ruth Ann Delacroix, a fictional wheat farmer's wife near the fictional town of Wolf Creek, Kansas, letter to her district's representative in Congress, March 1933 (ALTON-composed, in the style of letters sent by Plains farm families to federal officials in the early 1930s)
sources.body: We broke out the last of the buffalo grass on our north quarter in 1919, when wheat brought better than two dollars a bushel and the government told us wheat would win the war. My husband mortgaged the place to buy a tractor and a one-way plow, and for some years the crops paid. Now wheat will not fetch thirty cents at the elevator, and the tractor note comes due just the same. The Farmers State Bank closed its doors in November with our savings inside. Since February the wind has not let up for more than four days together. Dirt sifts under the doors and lies in drifts along the fence rows, and the seed we drilled last fall is blown clean out of the ground. Three families on our road have loaded their trucks for California. I do not blame the weather alone. We were told to plow and borrow and plant, and we did as we were told.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes the most likely purpose of the letter?
facts: Many Plains farmers took on mortgage debt for land and machinery during and after the World War I wheat boom (1917-1920s).
Farm families in the early 1930s often wrote to federal officials asking for relief as prices collapsed.

options.text: To argue that farmers deserved federal help because they had been urged into the practices that ruined them
options.label: key
options.why: Writing to a member of Congress, the author connects her family's ruin to wartime calls to plow and plant and closes with the line about doing 'as we were told.' That framing is meant to justify federal help for distressed farmers, which is what Plains families were asking Washington for in the early 1930s.

options.text: To urge Congress to adopt the free coinage of silver that Populist farm organizations had demanded as a remedy for debt
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: Free silver was a Populist demand of the 1890s. The letter never mentions currency policy.

options.text: To persuade officials that the federal government should stay out of agriculture and leave prices to private markets
options.label: reversal
options.why: The author blames market collapse and debt, not government involvement, and is asking a federal official to act. This is the opposite of her view.

options.text: To discourage neighbors from moving to California by describing the low wages awaiting migrants in western fields
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: The letter mentions families leaving for California, but it is addressed to a congressman and says nothing about wages in California.

items.stem: Which of the following historical developments best supports the author's claim that farmers "were told to plow and borrow and plant"?
facts: During World War I (1917-1919), the federal government guaranteed a minimum price for wheat and urged farmers to increase production.
Calvin Coolidge vetoed the McNary-Haugen farm relief bills in 1927 and 1928.
The Hawley-Smoot Tariff was enacted in 1930.

options.text: During World War I, the federal government guaranteed wheat prices and called on farmers to grow more
options.label: key
options.why: Wartime federal policy guaranteed high wheat prices and urged maximum output, which led Plains farmers to plow up grassland and go into debt. This backs up the author's statement that the government said wheat would win the war.

options.text: The Agricultural Adjustment Act of 1933 paid farmers to take land out of production in order to raise crop prices
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The AAA came after this letter and paid farmers to cut production, so it cannot show they had been encouraged to expand.

options.text: The Hawley-Smoot Tariff of 1930 raised import duties sharply and led other nations to retaliate against American exports
options.label: true_but_not_responsive
options.why: Retaliation hurt farm exports, which helps explain low prices. It does not show that farmers had been urged to plow and borrow.

options.text: Coolidge vetoed the McNary-Haugen bills, which would have had the government buy surplus crops and sell them abroad
options.label: true_but_not_responsive
options.why: The vetoes show federal reluctance to support farm prices in the 1920s. They are not evidence that the government encouraged farmers to expand.

items.stem: The bank closing and low wheat prices described in the excerpt are best understood in the context of which of the following?
facts: American agriculture suffered from overproduction, falling prices, and heavy debt throughout the 1920s.
Thousands of banks, many of them small rural banks, failed between 1930 and 1933.
The Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation was created by the Banking Act of 1933.

options.text: Low crop prices and heavy farm debt in the 1920s that left rural banks weak even before the 1929 crash
options.label: key
options.why: Farm prices dropped after World War I, leaving farmers with debts they could not repay. Many rural banks were already weak when the Depression began, and thousands failed in the early 1930s, like the bank in the letter.

options.text: Federal deposit insurance rules that required small rural banks to close if their reserves fell below national standards
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: Federal deposit insurance did not exist until the Banking Act of 1933 created the FDIC. Its purpose was to protect depositors, not to close banks.

options.text: Widespread buying of corporate stock on margin by Plains farm families who lost their savings when the market collapsed
options.label: overstated
options.why: Margin buying fed the 1929 crash, but it was mostly an urban, middle- and upper-class activity. The letter ties the family's losses to farm prices and a bank failure, not to stocks.

options.text: Competition from new immigrant farm laborers from southern and eastern Europe that drove down Plains wheat prices
options.label: unrelated_development
options.why: The quota laws of the 1920s had already cut immigration sharply. Wheat prices fell because of overproduction and weak demand, not labor competition.

items.stem: The conditions described in the excerpt most directly contributed to which of the following developments later in the 1930s?
facts: The federal Shelterbelt Project began in 1934 to plant tree windbreaks across the Great Plains.
Congress created the Soil Conservation Service in 1935 to promote practices such as contour plowing.

options.text: Federal soil conservation programs that promoted contour plowing and the planting of shelterbelts
options.label: key
options.why: Topsoil blowing away after the grassland was plowed under led the New Deal to create the Shelterbelt Project in 1934 and the Soil Conservation Service in 1935. Both aimed to stop the kind of erosion the letter describes.

options.text: The Wagner Act of 1935, which guaranteed industrial workers the right to organize unions and bargain collectively
options.label: unrelated_development
options.why: The Wagner Act was a real New Deal law, but it dealt with industrial labor relations, not Plains farming or soil erosion.

options.text: The Great Migration of African Americans from the rural South to northern factories during World War I
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The Great Migration began before this letter and had different causes. It was not an effect of the Dust Bowl.

options.text: Federal campaigns urging Plains farmers to plow additional grassland and plant the largest possible wheat crops
options.label: reversal
options.why: In the 1930s, federal policy tried to cut farm output and conserve soil, which is the reverse of the wartime push to expand that the letter describes.

input.title: Sectional Arithmetic: Rethinking the Missouri Compromise

sources.title: The Missouri Bargain as Political Arithmetic
sources.attribution: Historian Corinna Westervelt, The Balance Line: Congress and the Sectional Ledger, 1819-1821, published 2014 (ALTON-composed, in the style of a political history monograph)
sources.body: Textbooks often present the settlement of 1820 as a triumph of statesmanship, but the bargain is better read as an admission that the Union now ran on arithmetic. When Representative James Tallmadge of New York moved in 1819 to bar the further introduction of enslaved people into Missouri, the House divided almost entirely along sectional lines, and the amendment died in the Senate. The vote exposed a structural fact. Northern population growth had given the free states a lasting majority in the House, while the slaveholding states could count on protection only so long as the Senate stayed evenly split, eleven states to eleven. The compromise preserved that parity by pairing Missouri with Maine and by drawing a line across the remaining western lands. In doing so, Congress did not resolve whether slavery should expand. It converted the question into a contest over how many states each section could claim.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes the author's central argument about the Missouri Compromise?

options.text: It turned the question of slavery's expansion into a contest to maintain sectional balance
options.label: key
options.why: The author says Congress did not resolve slavery's expansion but converted it into a contest over how many states each section could claim, preserving Senate parity.

options.text: It permanently resolved the dispute over slavery's expansion through the careful statesmanship of congressional leaders
options.label: reversal
options.why: The author explicitly rejects the statesmanship reading and says the question was not resolved.

options.text: It showed that Northern voters were united behind the immediate abolition of slavery in all existing states
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: The excerpt discusses limiting slavery in Missouri, not immediate abolition; immediatism became prominent only in the 1830s.

options.text: It demonstrated that the Senate rather than the House had become the main voice of free-state population growth
options.label: reversal
options.why: The author says population growth gave the free states a House majority, while the Senate's equal split protected slaveholding states.

facts: The Tallmadge Amendment of 1819 proposed barring further introduction of slaves into Missouri; it passed the House and failed in the Senate.
In 1819 the Union had eleven free and eleven slave states.
The Missouri Compromise of 1820 admitted Missouri as a slave state and Maine as a free state.

items.stem: Which of the following developments of the 1830s would best support the author's argument about the effects of the compromise?

options.text: Congress admitted Arkansas as a slave state and Michigan as a free state within months of each other
options.label: key
options.why: Admitting Arkansas (1836) and Michigan (1837) in tandem continued the practice of pairing states to keep Senate parity, as the author describes.

options.text: Congress passed the Indian Removal Act, authorizing exchanges of eastern lands for territories west of the Mississippi River
options.label: unrelated_development
options.why: Indian removal concerned Native land and federal power, not the balance of free and slave states in the Senate.

options.text: South Carolina declared the federal tariffs of 1828 and 1832 null and void within its borders, prompting the Force Bill
options.label: true_but_not_responsive
options.why: The Nullification Crisis was sectional but concerned tariffs and states' rights, not the pairing of new states to preserve balance.

options.text: Abolitionists founded the American Anti-Slavery Society and began large petition drives aimed at Congress
options.label: true_but_not_responsive
options.why: The rise of abolitionist organizing reflects moral reform, not the political arithmetic of admitting states in balanced pairs.

facts: Arkansas was admitted as a slave state in 1836 and Michigan as a free state in 1837.
The Indian Removal Act was passed in 1830.
The Nullification Crisis of 1832-1833 concerned the tariffs of 1828 and 1832.

items.stem: The congressional conflict described in the excerpt is best understood in the context of which broader development?

options.text: Westward migration after the War of 1812 that brought Louisiana Purchase territories toward statehood
options.label: key
options.why: Rapid settlement of the West after 1815, including slaveholders moving into Missouri, produced the statehood application that triggered the 1819 crisis.

options.text: The annexation of Texas and the war with Mexico, which added vast new territory in the Southwest to the nation
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: Texas annexation (1845) and the Mexican-American War (1846-1848) came decades after the Missouri crisis.

options.text: The Monroe Doctrine's warning to European powers against new colonization anywhere in the Western Hemisphere
options.label: unrelated_development
options.why: The Monroe Doctrine (1823) addressed foreign policy, not the domestic dispute over slavery in new states.

options.text: The growth of textile mills in New England that employed young women from farm families in towns like Lowell
options.label: true_but_not_responsive
options.why: Early industrialization was real but does not explain the dispute over admitting Missouri and balancing the Senate.

facts: Missouri, part of the Louisiana Purchase of 1803, applied for statehood in 1819 after rapid postwar settlement.
The Monroe Doctrine was announced in 1823.
Texas was annexed in 1845 and the Mexican-American War lasted from 1846 to 1848.

items.stem: The line drawn across the remaining western lands, as mentioned in the excerpt, was intended to

options.text: bar slavery in the rest of the Louisiana Purchase north of 36°30' latitude, except in Missouri
options.label: key
options.why: The Missouri Compromise prohibited slavery in the remaining Louisiana Purchase territory north of 36°30', with Missouri itself excepted.

options.text: allow the settlers of each western territory to decide by a popular vote whether slavery would be permitted there
options.label: misattributed
options.why: Popular sovereignty was associated with the Compromise of 1850 and the Kansas-Nebraska Act of 1854, which overturned the line.

options.text: prohibit slavery in all lands gained from Mexico, as proposed by northern members of the House of Representatives
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: This describes the Wilmot Proviso of 1846, which never became law and concerned the Mexican Cession, not Louisiana Purchase lands.

options.text: divide the Oregon Country between the United States and Great Britain along a line of latitude agreed upon by treaty
options.label: misattributed
options.why: The Oregon Treaty of 1846 set the 49th parallel boundary; it had nothing to do with slavery or the Missouri settlement.

facts: The Missouri Compromise of 1820 banned slavery in the Louisiana Purchase territory north of 36°30' latitude, except Missouri.
The Wilmot Proviso was proposed in 1846 and never passed the Senate.
The Kansas-Nebraska Act of 1854 effectively repealed the 36°30' restriction through popular sovereignty.

input.title: A Union Captain Defends the Emancipation Proclamation, 1863

sources.title: Letter from a Union officer to his brother in Ohio
sources.attribution: Captain Josiah Treadwell, a fictional company officer in an Ohio volunteer infantry regiment, letter to his brother from a camp in Louisiana across the river from Vicksburg, April 1863 (ALTON-composed, in the style of a Union soldier's letter home)
sources.body: Dear Brother, You write that our neighbors in Licking County call the President's proclamation a scheme to turn the war into an abolition crusade, and that some of them swear they will not fight for the negro. Let them come down here and see what it does. Since New Year's Day the colored people come into our lines by the score, whole families carrying their bundles, and they tell us where the rebel pickets stand and which roads will bear our wagons. The men among them dig our entrenchments and drive our teams, and now a regiment of them is drilling below camp under white officers. Every man who walks off a plantation is one less hand to raise corn for the rebel army or throw up its earthworks. I did not enlist to free slaves, and I will not pretend I did. But I mean to win, and this measure helps us win. Show this to anyone at the store who thinks otherwise. Your brother, Josiah

items.stem: Which of the following best describes Treadwell's purpose in writing the letter?
facts: The Emancipation Proclamation took effect on January 1, 1863.
Many Northern Democrats, especially Peace Democrats (Copperheads), opposed emancipation as a war aim in 1863.

options.text: To persuade doubters at home that emancipation served the Union war effort
options.label: key
options.why: Treadwell answers neighbors who call the proclamation an abolition crusade and asks his brother to show the letter to skeptics, arguing the measure helps the Union win. This reflects real Northern divisions over emancipation in 1863.

options.text: To urge Congress to pass a constitutional amendment abolishing slavery throughout the nation
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: The letter is addressed to his brother, not Congress, and says nothing of an amendment; the Thirteenth Amendment passed Congress only in 1865.

options.text: To protest the War Department's decision to place Black regiments under the command of white officers
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: Treadwell mentions white officers drilling a Black regiment only as evidence the policy is working; he raises no objection.

options.text: To support Peace Democrats who demanded an armistice and a negotiated settlement with the Confederacy
options.label: reversal
options.why: Treadwell insists he means to win the war; his argument runs against the antiwar and anti-emancipation views of Peace Democrats.

items.stem: Which of the following pieces of evidence would best support Treadwell's argument that the proclamation would help the Union win the war?
facts: The Emancipation Proclamation authorized the enlistment of African American men in the Union armed forces (1863).
About 180,000 African American men served in the Union army by the war's end in 1865.

options.text: By 1865 about 180,000 African American men had served in the Union army
options.label: key
options.why: Large-scale Black enlistment, made possible by the proclamation, added substantial manpower to Union forces, supporting Treadwell's claim that emancipation strengthened the Union military.

options.text: The proclamation exempted slaveholding border states such as Kentucky, Maryland, and Missouri
options.label: true_but_not_responsive
options.why: Accurate, but the exemption shows the policy's limits and political caution; it does not show the proclamation adding to Union military strength.

options.text: Mobs in New York City attacked Black residents during riots against the federal draft in July 1863
options.label: true_but_not_responsive
options.why: The draft riots reveal Northern hostility to the war and to emancipation, which tends to challenge rather than support Treadwell's optimism.

options.text: The Confederate Congress exempted from conscription one white man on plantations with twenty or more slaves
options.label: unrelated_development
options.why: This 1862 Confederate law fed class resentment in the South but was not a result of the proclamation and does not show emancipation aiding Union arms.

items.stem: The policy that Treadwell defends is best understood in the context of which of the following broader developments?
facts: Lincoln issued the preliminary Emancipation Proclamation in September 1862, after the Battle of Antietam, justifying it as a war measure under his authority as commander in chief.
The proclamation applied only to areas then in rebellion against the United States (1863).

options.text: Lincoln's use of presidential war powers to strike at Confederate resources
options.label: key
options.why: Lincoln justified emancipation as a military necessity under his war powers, aimed at taking away the enslaved labor that sustained the Confederacy, which is exactly the logic Treadwell describes.

options.text: Congressional Reconstruction's division of the former Confederacy into five military districts
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The Reconstruction Acts creating military districts came in 1867, years after the wartime proclamation.

options.text: The Republican platform of 1860, which pledged immediate abolition of slavery in every existing state
options.label: overstated
options.why: The 1860 Republican platform opposed the extension of slavery into the territories but did not promise to abolish it where it already existed.

options.text: The doctrine of popular sovereignty, which let territorial settlers vote on whether to permit slavery
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: Popular sovereignty was a prewar formula of the 1850s, tied to the Kansas-Nebraska Act, not the context for wartime emancipation.

items.stem: Besides the effects Treadwell describes, the Emancipation Proclamation contributed to which of the following developments during the Civil War?
facts: By making the abolition of slavery a Union war aim, the Emancipation Proclamation made Britain and France less willing to recognize the Confederacy (1863).
Kentucky and Maryland remained in the Union throughout the Civil War.

options.text: Reduced likelihood that Britain would recognize the Confederacy
options.label: key
options.why: Once the war was tied to ending slavery, antislavery opinion in Britain made it harder for the British government to recognize or aid the Confederacy.

options.text: The immediate freeing of all enslaved people held in the loyal border states of the Union
options.label: reversal
options.why: The proclamation specifically exempted the loyal border states; slavery there ended later, through state action and the Thirteenth Amendment.

options.text: A formal British alliance with the Union that added the Royal Navy to the blockade of Southern ports
options.label: overstated
options.why: Britain stayed officially neutral; the proclamation made recognition of the Confederacy less likely but produced no alliance with the Union.

options.text: Secession of Kentucky and Maryland, whose slaveholders joined the Confederacy in protest
options.label: reversal
options.why: Both border states stayed in the Union for the whole war; exempting them was meant to keep their loyalty.

input.title: A County Suffrage Leader Urges Ratification, 1919

sources.title: Address to a Legislative Committee on Ratification
sources.attribution: Mrs. Clara Vandermeer, chair of the Harlan County Equal Suffrage Association, speaking to a joint committee of a Midwestern state legislature called into session to consider ratification, autumn 1919 (ALTON-composed, in the style of a suffrage speech to state lawmakers)
sources.body: Gentlemen of the committee, I will not repeat the arguments you have heard for fifty years. I ask you only to look at the record of the last two. When the call came in 1917, the women of this county did not wait to be asked. We sold Liberty Bonds door to door, rolled bandages for the Red Cross, and took the places of our sons on the farms and in the shell plant at Millbrook. Our boys were told they crossed the ocean to make the world safe for democracy. Is it safe for democracy here, when the mothers who gave them up may not vote? Women already cast ballots in Wyoming, Colorado, and more than a dozen other states, and no home there has fallen. Congress has done its part. Now the question rests with you, and the nation will remember how this state answered.

items.stem: Which of the following best explains the purpose of the speaker in the excerpt?
facts: Congress passed the Nineteenth Amendment and sent it to the states in June 1919.
A constitutional amendment requires ratification by three-fourths of the states; the Nineteenth Amendment was ratified in August 1920.

options.text: To persuade state lawmakers to ratify a constitutional amendment that Congress had already sent to the states
options.label: key
options.why: The speaker says Congress has done its part and the question now rests with the state, matching the 1919 to 1920 ratification campaign for the Nineteenth Amendment.

options.text: To pressure members of Congress to pass a federal suffrage amendment after the Senate had repeatedly rejected it in wartime votes
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: The Senate did reject the amendment in 1918 and early 1919, but the speaker addresses state legislators and states that Congress has already acted.

options.text: To recruit county women to sell Liberty Bonds and volunteer with the Red Cross as the United States entered the First World War
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The speaker recounts wartime service as past evidence; she is not recruiting volunteers in 1917.

options.text: To protest the arrest and jailing of militant suffragists who had picketed outside the White House during the war
options.label: unrelated_development
options.why: The National Woman's Party pickets were real, but the excerpt says nothing about arrests or picketing.

items.stem: Which of the following developments would best support the speaker's claim that women's wartime service strengthened the case for woman suffrage?
facts: In September 1918 President Woodrow Wilson addressed the Senate urging passage of the woman suffrage amendment as a war measure.
The Sheppard-Towner Act providing federal funds for maternal and infant health was passed in 1921.

options.text: Woodrow Wilson's 1918 appeal to the Senate to approve woman suffrage as a measure necessary to win the war
options.label: key
options.why: Wilson's 1918 address explicitly tied women's war contributions to the justice of suffrage, the same link the speaker draws.

options.text: The Supreme Court's 1908 Muller v. Oregon ruling that upheld limits on women's working hours because of their physical differences
options.label: true_but_not_responsive
options.why: Muller was a real Progressive Era ruling on labor protection, but it says nothing about war service and rested on women's difference rather than civic contribution.

options.text: The founding in 1911 of a national association opposed to woman suffrage that warned voting would draw women away from the home
options.label: reversal
options.why: Anti-suffrage organizing would be evidence against, not for, the speaker's argument.

options.text: The Sheppard-Towner Act of 1921, which provided federal funds for maternal and infant health clinics in the states
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: This came after ratification and reflects women's use of the vote, not evidence that war service justified suffrage.

items.stem: The campaign described in the excerpt is best understood as part of which broader context of the early twentieth century?
facts: The Seventeenth Amendment, ratified in 1913, provided for the direct election of U.S. senators.
Progressive reformers promoted measures such as the initiative, referendum, recall, and direct primary to expand popular control of government.

options.text: Progressive efforts to make government more responsive to voters, such as the Seventeenth Amendment's direct election of senators
options.label: key
options.why: Woman suffrage was one of several Progressive Era reforms meant to broaden democratic participation, alongside the 1913 Seventeenth Amendment and state-level direct democracy measures.

options.text: Populist demands of the 1890s for the free coinage of silver, a graduated income tax, and government ownership of the railroads and telegraph lines
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: These were real Populist goals, but they were economic demands of the 1890s farmers' movement, not the context of the 1919 ratification fight.

options.text: New Deal programs of the 1930s that expanded federal relief, created Social Security, and protected workers' right to organize labor unions
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The New Deal came more than a decade after ratification.

options.text: Gilded Age urban political machines that traded city jobs, contracts, and favors for the votes and party loyalty of recently arrived immigrants
options.label: reversal
options.why: Progressive reformers, including many suffragists, opposed machine politics; machines were a target of reform, not its context of expansion.

items.stem: After the change urged in the excerpt was achieved in 1920, some suffrage activists most directly continued their efforts by doing which of the following?
facts: The National Woman's Party proposed an Equal Rights Amendment in 1923.
The Eighteenth Amendment establishing Prohibition was ratified in 1919, and the Equal Pay Act was passed in 1963.

options.text: Proposing an Equal Rights Amendment to bar legal discrimination against women on the basis of sex
options.label: key
options.why: The National Woman's Party, led by veterans of the suffrage campaign, introduced the Equal Rights Amendment in 1923 to extend legal equality beyond the vote.

options.text: Leading the national campaign for the Eighteenth Amendment to prohibit the manufacture and sale of alcohol
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: Prohibition was ratified in 1919, before the Nineteenth Amendment, so it was not a post-1920 continuation.

options.text: Pressing Congress to pass the Equal Pay Act requiring employers to pay men and women the same wages for the same work
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The Equal Pay Act was a 1963 achievement of a later era of women's activism.

options.text: Demanding that the Fifteenth Amendment be revised to ban voting discrimination based on sex as well as race
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: Debate over excluding sex from the Fifteenth Amendment split suffragists around 1869, not after 1920.

input.title: A Defense Town Faces the End of the Cold War

sources.title: Address on the city's economic future
sources.attribution: Ruth Galloway-Pena, mayor of Vista Arroyo, California (a fictional aerospace town), speech to the Vista Arroyo Chamber of Commerce, January 1992 (ALTON-composed, in the style of a local official's address to business leaders)
sources.body: Friends, for forty years this valley built the airplanes and missile guidance systems that kept the Soviets in check. When the President called for a stronger defense ten years ago, our payrolls doubled, and a machinist with a high school diploma could buy a house on Las Palmas Avenue. Last month the red flag came down over the Kremlin. I rejoice in that as much as anyone here; my father flew in Korea. But I would be failing you if I pretended that peace is free for Vista Arroyo. Congress is already talking about a peace dividend, and Washington will not keep buying bombers to fight an enemy that no longer exists. Halvorsen Aerospace has announced 1,800 layoffs. We cannot wait for the Pentagon to rescue us. I am asking every bank and business in this room to help us court new industries: commercial electronics, medical equipment, and trade with the nations of the Pacific.

items.stem: The mayor's main purpose in delivering the address was most likely
facts: The Soviet Union dissolved in December 1991.
After the Cold War ended, the United States reduced defense spending in the early 1990s, hurting defense-dependent regions such as Southern California.

options.text: to persuade local business leaders to help diversify a city economy dependent on military contracts
options.label: key
options.why: She speaks to the Chamber of Commerce and asks every bank and business to court new civilian industries because defense orders will shrink.

options.text: to lobby members of Congress to keep funding new bomber and missile programs so that aerospace jobs in the valley would be protected
options.label: reversal
options.why: She says Washington will not keep buying bombers and that the city cannot wait for the Pentagon; her audience is local business, not Congress.

options.text: to celebrate the collapse of Soviet communism and to urge local banks to finance economic aid and investment in the former Soviet republics
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: She welcomes the Soviet collapse, but she asks for investment in local industries and Pacific trade, not aid to former Soviet republics.

options.text: to protest a federal base closure commission decision and to organize residents to demand that the Pentagon reverse it before the layoffs
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: The excerpt mentions layoffs at a private contractor, not a base closure, and she rejects relying on the Pentagon.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes a claim the mayor makes in the excerpt?
facts: The Soviet Union dissolved in December 1991, ending the Cold War.
In the early 1990s, policymakers debated a peace dividend, meaning money saved through lower military spending.

options.text: The disappearance of the Soviet threat will likely reduce the federal military spending that sustains local jobs.
options.label: key
options.why: She links the end of the Soviet Union to talk of a peace dividend, fewer bomber purchases, and announced layoffs.

options.text: The defense buildup of the previous decade harmed the city by pulling skilled workers away from its civilian manufacturing industries.
options.label: reversal
options.why: She describes the buildup as a boom that doubled payrolls and let workers buy homes.

options.text: The collapse of the Soviet Union resulted mainly from economic pressure created by American military spending during the 1980s.
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: Historians debate this interpretation, and the mayor never explains why the Soviet Union collapsed.

options.text: Peace with the former Soviet Union will be temporary, so the city should prepare for a renewed arms competition in the coming decade.
options.label: reversal
options.why: She assumes the enemy no longer exists and urges a shift to civilian industries, not preparation for a new arms race.

items.stem: The rise in local defense payrolls that the mayor recalls from about ten years before her speech was most directly a result of
facts: President Ronald Reagan greatly increased military spending in the early 1980s.
The Reagan defense buildup included new weapons programs such as the B-1 bomber and the Strategic Defense Initiative (proposed 1983).

options.text: the Reagan administration's military buildup during the early 1980s
options.label: key
options.why: A speech given in 1992 points back to about 1982, when Reagan's large defense increases poured money into aerospace contractors.

options.text: the escalation of the Vietnam War and the expanded draft that increased defense contracting in the middle of the 1960s
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: Vietnam escalation happened in the mid-1960s, about twenty-five years before the speech, not ten.

options.text: the Strategic Arms Limitation Talks and detente policies of the 1970s, which shifted federal funds toward aerospace research
options.label: reversal
options.why: Detente and SALT tried to limit arms competition in the 1970s; they did not drive the defense boom of the early 1980s.

options.text: the space race after Sputnik, which led Congress to fund missile programs and science education in the late 1950s
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The response to Sputnik came in the late 1950s, decades before the period the mayor describes.

items.stem: Which of the following most directly contributed to the event the mayor describes as the red flag coming down over the Kremlin?
facts: Mikhail Gorbachev became Soviet leader in 1985 and introduced glasnost and perestroika.
The Soviet Union dissolved in December 1991.

options.text: Mikhail Gorbachev's reforms, which loosened political controls but failed to revive the Soviet economy
options.label: key
options.why: Glasnost and perestroika opened room for dissent and nationalist movements while the economy kept getting worse, which helped bring about the Soviet breakup in 1991.

options.text: The United Nations coalition victory over Iraq in the Persian Gulf War, which persuaded Soviet leaders to disband their own armed forces
options.label: overstated
options.why: The Gulf War of 1991 really happened, but it did not lead the Soviets to disband their military or cause the Soviet collapse.

options.text: The North American Free Trade Agreement, which joined the economies of North America and shut the Soviet bloc out of Western markets
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: NAFTA took effect in 1994, after the Soviet Union had already dissolved.

options.text: The detente agreements of the early 1970s, including SALT I, which ended the arms race and let Eastern European states leave the Warsaw Pact
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: Detente came nearly two decades earlier, did not end the arms race, and did not free Eastern Europe.

input.title: Radio, Automobiles, and the Limits of 1920s Prosperity

sources.title: A National Audience
sources.attribution: Harriet Ellery Voss, historian, Signals and Highways: Making a National Market, 1919-1932, 2011 (ALTON-composed, in the style of a cultural history of American consumerism)
sources.body: Between 1919 and 1929 the radio set and the motorcar did more to knit Americans into a single audience than any statute or sermon. Once broadcasters linked stations into coast-to-coast networks in the late 1920s, a family in rural Nebraska could hear the same dance band, ballgame, and soap advertisement as a family in Philadelphia. The Model T, its price cut again and again by the moving assembly line, carried farm families to town movie houses and chain stores. Installment plans let a clerk drive a car he could never have bought outright. Advertisers, sensing the new audience, sold not only goods but a common picture of the good life. Regional isolation gave way to a national marketplace of tastes.

sources.title: Prosperity on Credit
sources.attribution: Daniel Okoro Brandt, historian, The Mortgaged Decade: Farms, Factories, and Debt in the 1920s, 2016 (ALTON-composed, in the style of an economic and social history of the interwar years)
sources.body: Celebrations of a consumer republic in the 1920s tend to describe the view from a city apartment. Most farm households still lacked electric power at the decade's end, and many listened to battery radios, if they owned radios at all. Crop prices had collapsed after the wartime boom, so farm families who bought cars often bought them on credit they struggled to repay. In industrial towns, wages lagged behind the output of the factories, and installment debt filled the gap between what workers earned and what manufacturers needed to sell. The new goods were real, but the prosperity that carried them rested on borrowed money and was spread far more narrowly than the advertisements suggested.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes a difference between the arguments in Excerpt A and Excerpt B?

options.text: A stresses a new shared national culture, while B stresses uneven, credit-dependent prosperity
options.label: key
options.why: Voss argues radio and cars broke down regional isolation and created a national marketplace of tastes; Brandt argues the benefits were narrowly spread and rested on installment debt.

options.text: A claims consumer goods stayed confined to cities, while B claims they reached nearly every rural household
options.label: reversal
options.why: Reverses the excerpts: A describes goods reaching rural Nebraska, and B says most farm households lacked electricity.

options.text: Both argue that federal regulation of broadcasting and automobile sales was the main force behind the spread of new goods
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: Neither excerpt credits federal regulation; A credits technology, advertising, and credit, and B focuses on income and debt.

options.text: A blames installment buying for the Great Depression, while B sees credit as a sound basis for lasting growth
options.label: misattributed
options.why: A presents installment plans as opening access, and it is B, not A, that treats credit as a weakness.

facts: Installment buying of automobiles and appliances expanded widely in the 1920s.
Commercial radio networks, beginning with NBC in 1926, created national broadcast audiences in the late 1920s.

items.stem: Which of the following pieces of evidence would best support the argument in Excerpt B?

options.text: The share of national income going to the wealthiest Americans rose during the 1920s
options.label: key
options.why: Growing concentration of income backs Brandt's claim that prosperity was narrowly spread and that workers' purchasing power fell behind production.

options.text: Congress funded a large expansion of state highways through the Federal Aid Highway Act of 1921
options.label: true_but_not_responsive
options.why: Road building is real but supports A's picture of automobiles connecting regions, not B's argument about inequality and debt.

options.text: National magazines and syndicated advertising campaigns reached millions of readers across regions
options.label: true_but_not_responsive
options.why: National advertising supports A's argument about a shared national culture, not B's argument about narrow prosperity.

options.text: The Immigration Act of 1924 sharply reduced the number of newcomers from southern and eastern Europe
options.label: unrelated_development
options.why: Immigration restriction was a real 1920s controversy but does not speak to how consumer prosperity was distributed or financed.

facts: The share of national income held by the wealthiest Americans increased during the 1920s.
Farm prices fell sharply after World War I, leaving agriculture depressed through the 1920s.

items.stem: The spread of automobiles and radios described in both excerpts was most directly made possible by which of the following?

options.text: Rising industrial productivity from assembly lines and factory electrification
options.label: key
options.why: Mass production methods such as Ford's moving assembly line (1913) and electrified factories lowered costs and made cars and radios affordable to many consumers in the 1920s.

options.text: Rural Electrification Administration projects that extended power lines to farm households
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The REA was a New Deal agency created in 1935, after the decade described in the excerpts.

options.text: Continued federal direction of industry by the War Industries Board throughout the decade
options.label: overstated
options.why: The War Industries Board managed wartime production but was dissolved soon after World War I ended; it did not direct the 1920s economy.

options.text: Tariff reductions by Republican administrations that opened domestic markets to European goods
options.label: reversal
options.why: Republicans in the 1920s raised tariffs, for example with the Fordney-McCumber Tariff of 1922; they did not lower them.

facts: Henry Ford introduced the moving assembly line in 1913, sharply lowering the price of the Model T.
The Rural Electrification Administration was created in 1935.
The Fordney-McCumber Tariff of 1922 raised tariff rates.

items.stem: The developments described in Excerpt A were most similar to which later development?

options.text: The spread of television and car-centered suburbs in the decades after 1945
options.label: key
options.why: Like radio and the Model T in the 1920s, television and suburban automobile culture after World War II spread a shared national mass culture and consumer lifestyle.

options.text: The rise of the 1960s counterculture that rejected mainstream consumer values and conformity
options.label: reversal
options.why: The counterculture pushed back against the mass consumer culture A describes rather than resembling it.

options.text: The Great Society's federal programs that aimed to reduce poverty in Appalachia and inner cities
options.label: unrelated_development
options.why: Great Society antipoverty programs were government reforms, not the spread of new technology and shared consumer culture.

options.text: The Populist movement's campaign of the 1890s against railroad rates and tight money for farmers
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: Populism came earlier, not later, and its farm grievances look more like B's concerns than A's argument about national integration.

facts: Television ownership spread rapidly in the United States during the 1950s.
Automobile-dependent suburbs grew rapidly after 1945, aided by the Interstate Highway Act of 1956.

input.title: A Kansas Homesteader Addresses the Farmers' Alliance, 1890

sources.title: Address to a county meeting of the Farmers' Alliance
sources.attribution: Martha Ellery, a widowed homesteader of Sweetwater Township, speaking to a county meeting of the Farmers' Alliance in central Kansas, 1890 (ALTON-composed, in the style of a Gilded Age farm organization speech)
sources.body: Neighbors, I came to this quarter section in the spring of 1878 with my husband, two oxen, and a filing paper from the land office. The government asked only that we live on the land five years and improve it, and we did. We cut sod for a house, broke the prairie with a single plow, and lost our first crop to the grasshoppers. My husband is gone now, but the patent is in my name. Yet owning the land has not made me free. The railroad that crosses this county on land the nation gave it charges more to carry my wheat to Kansas City than the wheat brings at the elevator. The mortgage company back East takes its interest whether rain falls or not, and every dollar I owe grows heavier as prices sink. Do not tell me we have been idle. We have been alone. That is what this Alliance must end.

items.stem: Ellery's purpose in the excerpt was most likely to

options.text: persuade fellow farmers that their troubles came from economic forces requiring organized action
options.label: key
options.why: Ellery blames railroads and Eastern lenders rather than farmers' idleness and closes by saying the Alliance must end farmers' isolation. That fits the Farmers' Alliance push for cooperative and political action in the late 1880s and 1890s.

options.text: attract new settlers to western Kansas by stressing how easily homesteaders could gain title to good land
options.label: reversal
options.why: Land promoters and railroads did advertise this way, but Ellery stresses hardship and debt, which is the opposite of a recruiting pitch.

options.text: urge Congress to repeal the Homestead Act because its five-year residence rule had ruined small farmers
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: Ellery met the residence requirement and got her patent. She blames freight rates, mortgages, and falling prices, not the Homestead Act.

options.text: rally support for the gold standard by blaming paper money and silver coinage for the decline in farm prices
options.label: misattributed
options.why: Indebted farmers like Ellery generally wanted more money in circulation, such as free silver. Support for the gold standard came mostly from creditors and Eastern business interests.

facts: The Farmers' Alliance movement grew rapidly in the South and on the Great Plains in the late 1880s, promoting cooperatives and political action against railroads and lenders.
Plains farmers in the 1880s and 1890s commonly complained of high railroad freight rates and burdensome mortgage debt.

items.stem: Which of the following, if true, would most directly support Ellery's claim that her debts grew heavier over time?

options.text: General price levels and farm commodity prices fell steadily from the 1870s through the mid-1890s
options.label: key
options.why: Under deflation, a debt fixed in dollars has to be repaid with crops that sell for less and less, so its real burden rises. That is exactly what Ellery means by debts growing heavier as prices sink, and it describes the actual trend of the period.

options.text: Wheat prices rose sharply in the 1880s as European demand for American grain expanded after poor harvests abroad
options.label: reversal
options.why: Rising crop prices would make debts easier to repay, so this would undercut Ellery's claim. Grain prices generally fell in this period.

options.text: Barbed wire and steel plows allowed Plains farmers to fence and cultivate far larger acreages than before
options.label: true_but_not_responsive
options.why: New farm technology did expand Plains farming, but this fact does not show that the real burden of a fixed debt was increasing.

options.text: The Interstate Commerce Act of 1887 quickly forced railroads to cut freight rates on grain shipments across the West
options.label: overstated
options.why: The Interstate Commerce Commission was weak at first and did little to lower rates. Lower freight costs would not show debts growing heavier anyway.

facts: The United States experienced a long period of deflation from the 1870s to the mid-1890s, during which farm commodity prices generally declined.
The Interstate Commerce Act (1887) created the Interstate Commerce Commission, which initially had limited power to regulate railroad rates.

items.stem: Ellery's acquisition of the land described in the excerpt was made possible most directly by

options.text: federal laws passed during the Civil War that offered public land to settlers and aid to railroads
options.label: key
options.why: The Homestead Act of 1862 gave 160 acres to settlers who lived on the land and improved it for five years, as Ellery did. The Pacific Railway Acts of the same era gave land grants to railroads, which matches her mention of land the nation gave the railroad.

options.text: the Dawes Severalty Act, which divided reservation lands into individual allotments and opened surplus land to whites
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The Dawes Act was passed in 1887, nine years after Ellery filed her claim in 1878, and it dealt with reservation land, not public-domain homesteads.

options.text: the Northwest Ordinance, which set up a system for surveying western land and admitting new states to the Union
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The Northwest Ordinance of 1787 governed the Old Northwest. It did not grant free land to settlers on the Plains in the 1870s.

options.text: the Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo, which transferred vast western territories from Mexico to the United States
options.label: misattributed
options.why: The 1848 treaty transferred the Southwest and California. Central Kansas came mainly from the Louisiana Purchase, and the treaty did not give land to settlers.

facts: The Homestead Act (1862) granted 160 acres of public land to settlers who lived on and improved it for five years.
The Pacific Railway Acts (1862 and 1864) granted public land and loans to companies building the transcontinental railroad.

items.stem: The grievances expressed in the excerpt most directly contributed to which of the following developments in the 1890s?

options.text: The formation of a third party calling for government ownership of railroads and the free coinage of silver
options.label: key
options.why: Alliance farmers with grievances like Ellery's helped form the People's (Populist) Party. Its 1892 Omaha Platform demanded government ownership of railroads and free coinage of silver to reverse deflation.

options.text: The passage of state Granger laws establishing maximum rates that railroads and grain elevators could charge farmers
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The Granger laws came out of the Grange movement in the 1870s, before both this 1890 speech and the 1890s.

options.text: The creation of the Federal Reserve System to provide a more flexible currency and expand agricultural credit for farmers
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The Federal Reserve was created in 1913 during the Progressive Era, not in the 1890s.

options.text: The rapid growth of the Knights of Labor as industrial workers and farmers joined a single national union of producers
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The Knights of Labor peaked in the mid-1880s and declined quickly after the 1886 Haymarket affair. It was not growing in the 1890s.

facts: The People's (Populist) Party was formed in 1892; its Omaha Platform called for government ownership of railroads, free coinage of silver, and a graduated income tax.
State Granger laws regulating railroad and grain elevator rates were passed in the 1870s.

input.title: The Freedmen's Bureau Between Protection and Labor Discipline

sources.title: A historian on the Freedmen's Bureau and the Black Codes
sources.attribution: Harriet Vance Coleman, historian, The Contract and the Schoolhouse: Freedom's Bureau in the Cotton South, 2011 (ALTON-composed, in the style of a modern historical monograph)
sources.body: When Congress created the Bureau of Refugees, Freedmen, and Abandoned Lands in March 1865, it gave a small, underfunded agency a contradictory mission. Bureau agents were expected to shield freedpeople from the Black Codes that Southern legislatures passed in 1865 and 1866, laws that punished so-called vagrancy and allowed local courts to hire out unemployed Black men to planters. Agents did set aside some of these provisions and heard complaints in their own tribunals. Yet the same agents, most of them Union officers wary of fostering what they called dependence, pressed freedpeople to sign annual labor contracts with their former owners and sometimes ordered those who refused off the plantations. Agent reports from the cotton districts record far more contracts approved than wage complaints resolved. In the end, the Bureau's most lasting achievement lay less in its labor policy than in the schools it helped found, many of which outlived the agency itself.

items.stem: Which of the following developments would best support the author's claim that the Freedmen's Bureau had a contradictory mission?

options.text: Federal orders in 1865 directing the Bureau to restore abandoned lands to pardoned former Confederates
options.label: key
options.why: Under Johnson's pardon policy the Bureau, created partly to settle freedpeople on abandoned land, had to return that land to former owners and evict freedpeople, which shows the conflicting aims the author describes.

options.text: Congress renewing and expanding the Bureau's authority in 1866 by overriding President Andrew Johnson's veto of the bill
options.label: true_but_not_responsive
options.why: This happened, but it shows Congress backing the Bureau's protective role. It does not show the agency working against freedpeople's interests.

options.text: The founding of colleges such as Fisk and Howard with Bureau support to train Black teachers, ministers, and other professionals in the South
options.label: true_but_not_responsive
options.why: This supports the author's separate point about schools, not the claim that the Bureau's mission was contradictory.

options.text: The Homestead Act of 1862 offering western public land to settlers who lived on and improved a claim for five years
options.label: unrelated_development
options.why: This was a western land policy and was not part of how the Bureau dealt with freedpeople in the South.

facts: Congress created the Bureau of Refugees, Freedmen, and Abandoned Lands in March 1865.

In 1865 President Andrew Johnson's pardons led to the restoration of abandoned and confiscated lands to former Confederates, and the Bureau carried out evictions of freedpeople, including on the Sea Islands.

items.stem: Which of the following, if true, would most directly challenge the author's argument about the Freedmen's Bureau's labor policy?

options.text: Records showing Bureau agents often voided unfair contracts and won back wages for freedpeople
options.label: key
options.why: The author argues that the Bureau's labor policy mostly pushed freedpeople into contracts on planters' terms. Widespread evidence of agents protecting workers' wages would cut against that argument.

options.text: Evidence that most Bureau agents were Union army veterans who distrusted relief and feared freedpeople would become dependent
options.label: reversal
options.why: This would back up the author's explanation for why agents pushed contracts. It does not challenge the argument.

options.text: Reports that Southern legislatures dropped many Black Code provisions after Congress imposed Military Reconstruction in 1867
options.label: true_but_not_responsive
options.why: This concerns what state legislatures did, not how Bureau agents handled labor contracts.

options.text: Accounts showing northern groups like the American Missionary Association staffed many schools the Bureau helped build
options.label: true_but_not_responsive
options.why: This bears on the schools, not on the argument about labor policy.

facts: The Bureau operated its own tribunals to hear freedpeople's complaints, including disputes over labor contracts.
The American Missionary Association worked with the Freedmen's Bureau to found and staff schools for freedpeople.

items.stem: The Black Codes described in the excerpt are best understood in the context of which of the following?

options.text: Presidential Reconstruction, which let Southern governments led by ex-Confederates set the terms of freedom
options.label: key
options.why: Under Johnson's lenient plan in 1865 and 1866, restored Southern legislatures controlled by former Confederates passed the Black Codes to restrict freedpeople's labor and movement.

options.text: The Military Reconstruction Acts, which divided the former Confederacy into districts and required new state constitutions
options.label: reversal
options.why: The Military Reconstruction Acts of 1867 came after the Black Codes and were partly a reaction against them. They did not produce the codes.

options.text: The end of federal occupation after the Compromise of 1877, which returned Southern state governments to Democratic Redeemers
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The Black Codes were passed in 1865 and 1866, about a decade before 1877.

options.text: Enforcement of the Fugitive Slave Act of 1850, which required Northern officials to help return escaped enslaved people
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: This was an antebellum law about slavery and does not explain postwar codes aimed at freedpeople.

facts: Southern legislatures formed under President Andrew Johnson's Reconstruction plan passed Black Codes in 1865 and 1866.
Congress passed the Military Reconstruction Acts in 1867.

items.stem: The vagrancy and hiring-out provisions of the Black Codes described in the excerpt were most similar in purpose to which development of the late nineteenth century?

options.text: The spread of convict leasing, in which Southern states rented prisoners to private firms
options.label: key
options.why: Like the hiring-out provisions, convict leasing used the criminal law to supply forced labor, much of it Black, to private employers in the New South.

options.text: The Chinese Exclusion Act of 1882, which barred Chinese laborers from entering the United States for ten years
options.label: unrelated_development
options.why: This law kept workers out of the country. It did not use the courts to force residents to work for employers.

options.text: The Dawes Act of 1887, which divided reservation lands into individual allotments to promote Native assimilation
options.label: unrelated_development
options.why: This was a land and assimilation policy for Native Americans, not a way of forcing workers into labor through the courts.

options.text: Federal court injunctions against striking railroad workers during the Pullman Strike of 1894, enforced by troops
options.label: unrelated_development
options.why: This was a crackdown on organized strikers. It did not convict people for vagrancy and hire them out to private employers.

facts: Convict leasing spread across Southern states in the late nineteenth century, renting mostly Black prisoners to private companies and planters.
The Chinese Exclusion Act was passed in 1882 and the Dawes Act in 1887.

input.title: A Hill-County Defense of Tennessee's Evolution Law, 1925

sources.title: Letter to the editor on the Dayton trial
sources.attribution: Letter to the editor of the Harlan Creek Sentinel, a weekly newspaper in a rural Tennessee county, by Josiah Pruett, a farmer and Methodist lay preacher who served on the county school board, July 1925 (ALTON-composed, in the style of rural letters to the editor written during the Scopes trial)
sources.body: The city papers say we in the hill counties are ignorant because our legislature has forbidden the teaching that man descended from a lower order of animals. I answer that the people of this county pay the teacher's salary, build the schoolhouse, and send their children to sit in it. Have we no say in what is taught there? These professors and lawyers who have come down by train to Dayton speak of science as though it were a new religion, and they would have our boys and girls believe the Bible is a book of fables. I have watched young people go off to Chattanooga and Nashville and come home with bobbed hair, phonograph jazz, and no use for the church. A schoolroom that teaches a child he is kin to the ape will finish the work the picture show began. Let the great universities argue as they please. In our schools, the majority shall rule.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes the point of view expressed in the excerpt?
facts: In March 1925 Tennessee passed the Butler Act, banning the teaching in public schools that humans descended from a lower order of animals.
Protestant fundamentalists of the 1920s defended literal readings of the Bible against modernist and scientific ideas.

options.text: A rural Protestant defending majority control over public schools against urban modernist influence
options.label: key
options.why: Pruett insists that local taxpayers and the majority decide what is taught, defends the Bible against scientific challenges, and blames city influences, reflecting the rural fundamentalist side of 1920s cultural conflict.

options.text: A fundamentalist urging Congress to pass a federal law requiring Bible instruction in every public school of the nation
options.label: overstated
options.why: The author defends local and state authority over schools; he never calls for federal action or mandatory Bible instruction.

options.text: A Progressive reformer urging that trained professional experts, rather than local school boards, set the curriculum
options.label: reversal
options.why: The author rejects the authority of professors and university experts and defends local majority rule, the opposite of the Progressive faith in expertise.

options.text: A nativist calling for quota laws restricting immigration from southern and eastern European nations
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: Immigration restriction was a real 1920s cause, but the excerpt says nothing about immigrants or quotas.

items.stem: Which of the following pieces of evidence would best support the author's concern that young people were being drawn away from rural ways of life?
facts: The 1920 census reported for the first time that more Americans lived in urban areas than in rural areas.
Farm incomes fell during the 1920s as crop prices dropped after World War I.

options.text: Census figures from 1920 showing that, for the first time, most Americans lived in urban places
options.label: key
options.why: The 1920 census documented the shift of population toward cities, supporting the author's observation that young people were leaving for Chattanooga and Nashville and absorbing urban culture.

options.text: Statistics showing that farm incomes rose steadily through the 1920s as crop prices remained at their wartime highs
options.label: reversal
options.why: Farm prices and incomes fell after World War I; prosperity on the farm would also undercut rather than support a pull toward cities.

options.text: Reports that the Ku Klux Klan's membership grew into the millions during the early 1920s, including in northern states
options.label: true_but_not_responsive
options.why: The Klan revival was real, but its growth says nothing about young people leaving rural life for urban culture.

options.text: Court records showing that federal agents enforced the Volstead Act's ban on liquor sales more strictly in rural counties
options.label: unrelated_development
options.why: Prohibition enforcement is a separate 1920s controversy and does not show migration or changing youth culture.

items.stem: The controversy described in the excerpt is best understood in the context of which of the following broader developments of the 1920s?
facts: During the 1920s, radio, motion pictures, and mass-circulation magazines spread new urban cultural norms, including jazz and new styles for young women.
The Scopes trial of 1925 became a national symbol of conflict between traditional religious values and modern scientific ideas.

options.text: Clashes between traditional and modern values as mass media and cities spread new cultural norms
options.label: key
options.why: The author links evolution in the classroom to bobbed hair, jazz, and the picture show, placing the Dayton controversy within the broader 1920s conflict between traditionalists and modern urban culture.

options.text: Debates over American imperialism after the Spanish-American War, which divided voters over annexing the Philippines
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The debate over annexing the Philippines took place around 1898 to 1900 and has no connection to the school curriculum dispute.

options.text: The Red Scare after World War I, during which federal agents arrested and deported thousands of suspected radicals
