options.label: true_but_not_responsive
options.why: The Red Scare of 1919 to 1920 was real, but the excerpt concerns religion, science, and youth culture rather than political radicalism.

options.text: The Populist campaign for free silver coinage and government ownership of the railroads and telegraphs
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: Populism was a rural movement of the 1890s focused on economic grievances, not 1920s disputes over evolution and culture.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes the outcome of the 1925 trial in Dayton, Tennessee, mentioned in the excerpt?
facts: John Scopes was convicted in July 1925 of violating Tennessee's Butler Act and fined 100 dollars.
In 1927 the Tennessee Supreme Court set aside the conviction on a technicality, and the Butler Act stayed in force until 1967.
In Epperson v. Arkansas (1968) the U.S. Supreme Court struck down a state ban on teaching evolution.

options.text: The teacher was convicted under the state law, but the verdict was later set aside on a technicality
options.label: key
options.why: Scopes was found guilty and fined, and the Tennessee Supreme Court later reversed the conviction on a technicality over the fine, which left the law itself in place.

options.text: The United States Supreme Court struck down the state ban on teaching evolution as a violation of the First Amendment
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The Scopes case never reached the U.S. Supreme Court; the Court did not strike down an evolution ban until Epperson v. Arkansas in 1968.

options.text: The jury acquitted the teacher, and Tennessee lawmakers responded by repealing the ban on teaching evolution that year
options.label: reversal
options.why: Scopes was convicted, and Tennessee kept the Butler Act in force until 1967.

options.text: The trial ended in a mistrial after the defense persuaded the judge to admit testimony from many scientists
options.label: reversal
options.why: The judge excluded most expert scientific testimony, and the trial ended in a conviction, not a mistrial.

input.title: Public Power and Labor's Defeats, 1886-1894

sources.title: Courts, Soldiers, and the Limits of Labor Organizing
sources.attribution: Marguerite Ellsworth-Vance, historian, Iron Bargains: Workers, Courts, and Capital, 1877-1900, published 2011 (ALTON-composed, in the style of a modern labor historian's monograph)
sources.body: Historians have often explained the collapse of the Knights of Labor by pointing to its loose structure and its mixing of skilled and unskilled members. Those weaknesses were real, but they matter less than the way employers learned to borrow public power. After the bombing at Chicago's Haymarket Square in May 1886, prosecutors tied labor organizers to anarchism, and membership in the Knights fell sharply. At Homestead in 1892, the Carnegie Steel Company's managers relied on Pinkerton guards and then on the Pennsylvania state militia to reopen the works with nonunion men. Two years later, when the American Railway Union refused to handle Pullman cars, the federal government obtained a sweeping court injunction and sent army troops into Chicago. In each case, workers lost less to the market than to courts, soldiers, and public fear. The lesson unions drew was that organizing would succeed only if government stopped acting as an employer's ally.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes the author's main argument in the excerpt?
facts: The Haymarket bombing in Chicago occurred in May 1886, and the Knights of Labor declined sharply afterward.
The Homestead strike of 1892 and the Pullman strike of 1894 ended in defeats for the unions involved.

options.text: Labor's defeats owed more to employers' use of courts, troops, and police than to flaws within unions.
options.label: key
options.why: The author concedes internal weaknesses but argues employers 'learned to borrow public power,' citing prosecutors, militia, injunctions, and federal troops.

options.text: The Knights of Labor collapsed chiefly because it combined skilled and unskilled workers in one loosely governed organization.
options.label: reversal
options.why: This is the older explanation the author says matters less than employers' use of public power.

options.text: Strikes failed mainly because falling prices and recurring depressions weakened workers' bargaining position in labor markets.
options.label: reversal
options.why: The author says workers lost less to the market than to courts, soldiers, and public fear.

options.text: Unions lost because ethnic and religious divisions among new immigrant workers kept them from acting together.
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: Immigrant divisions were a real problem in the period, but the excerpt never mentions them.

items.stem: Which of the following pieces of evidence would most directly support the author's argument about the labor conflicts of the period?
facts: In In re Debs (1895), the Supreme Court upheld Eugene V. Debs's contempt conviction for violating the federal injunction issued during the Pullman strike.
The Interstate Commerce Act of 1887 created the Interstate Commerce Commission to oversee railroad rates.

options.text: In 1895 the Supreme Court upheld the contempt sentence of the union leader who defied the Pullman injunction.
options.label: key
options.why: In re Debs shows the highest court backing the injunction used to break the Pullman boycott, which supports the claim that government power, not the market, defeated labor.

options.text: Local Knights of Labor assemblies often struck without national approval, while leaders preferred arbitration and producer cooperatives.
options.label: true_but_not_responsive
options.why: This points to internal disorganization, the explanation the author downplays, so it would modify the argument rather than support it.

options.text: The American Federation of Labor grew in the 1890s by organizing skilled craft workers and focusing on wages and hours.
options.label: true_but_not_responsive
options.why: The AFL's growth suggests union structure mattered, which supports the older explanation, not the author's emphasis on state power.

options.text: The Interstate Commerce Act of 1887 created a federal commission to oversee railroad rates charged to shippers and farmers.
options.label: unrelated_development
options.why: Railroad rate regulation concerned shippers and farmers, not how the government acted in labor disputes.

items.stem: The labor conflicts described in the excerpt occurred most directly in the context of a period in which
facts: In the late nineteenth century, large corporations such as Carnegie Steel consolidated industries, and mechanization reduced the value of many workers' skills.
The National Labor Relations Board was created by the Wagner Act in 1935.

options.text: corporations grew in scale and mechanization reduced many workers' skills and bargaining power
options.label: key
options.why: Large industrial firms like Carnegie Steel and Pullman, along with deskilling through machines, set up the wage and control disputes behind Homestead and Pullman.

options.text: the National Labor Relations Board enforced workers' right to vote on union representation in their workplaces
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The NLRB came out of the 1935 Wagner Act, four decades after these strikes.

options.text: wartime federal boards mediated disputes in exchange for unions' promises not to strike in defense plants
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: Wartime labor boards and no-strike pledges belong to the world wars, not to 1886-1894.

options.text: state minimum wage and maximum hours laws had been upheld for most men employed in factories and mills
options.label: overstated
options.why: Hours and wage protections for most adult male workers did not exist in this era, and courts often struck such laws down.

items.stem: Which development of the twentieth century most directly reflected the change in government's role that, according to the author, unions concluded they needed?
facts: The Norris-La Guardia Act of 1932 restricted federal court injunctions in labor disputes.
The Wagner Act of 1935 protected workers' right to organize and bargain collectively, and union membership grew substantially in the late 1930s.
Despite the Clayton Act of 1914, courts continued to issue injunctions against unions in the 1920s.

options.text: Congress in the 1930s limited labor injunctions and protected collective bargaining, aiding union growth.
options.label: key
options.why: The Norris-La Guardia and Wagner Acts ended government's role as the employer's ally, which is the condition the author says unions saw as necessary, and union membership rose.

options.text: The Clayton Act of 1914 permanently ended the use of federal court injunctions against strikes, pickets, and boycotts.
options.label: overstated
options.why: The Clayton Act claimed to protect labor, but courts kept issuing injunctions against unions well into the 1920s.

options.text: The Taft-Hartley Act of 1947 allowed states to ban union shops and required union officers to sign anti-communist oaths.
options.label: reversal
options.why: Taft-Hartley put new restrictions on unions. It moved away from the pro-labor government stance the author describes.

options.text: Quota laws in the 1920s sharply reduced immigration from southern and eastern Europe, shrinking the pool of industrial labor.
options.label: unrelated_development
options.why: Immigration restriction did change the labor market, but it did not change government's role in labor disputes.

input.title: A Virginia Planter Against Hamilton's Financial Program, 1791

sources.title: Letter to the Freeholders of Amelia County
sources.attribution: Ezra Whitlock, a fictional planter and former militia captain, in a printed letter to the voters of Amelia County, Virginia, 1791 (ALTON-composed, in the style of an Anti-Federalist and early Republican address to constituents)
sources.body: Friends and neighbors: When our soldiers came home from the late war, they were paid in certificates, and many sold those papers for a few shillings on the pound to keep their families fed. Now the Secretary of the Treasury would have Congress redeem these papers at their full face value, so that the gentlemen of Philadelphia and New York who bought them up may grow rich on the labor of the men who earned them. Nor is this all. Virginia has paid down much of her own war debt, yet we are to be taxed to pay the debts of states that paid little. And now a national bank is chartered, though I search the Constitution in vain for any power to create a corporation. If Congress may do whatever it deems useful, the states are nothing, and the planter and the farmer will be ruled by a moneyed few.

items.stem: Whitlock's point of view in the excerpt was most likely shaped by which of the following?

options.text: Fear that federal policy favored northern financial interests over southern agrarian states
options.label: key
options.why: Whitlock contrasts Virginia's planters and farmers with speculators in Philadelphia and New York and objects to Virginia paying other states' debts. This matches the southern agrarian opposition to Hamilton's funding, assumption, and bank plans.

options.text: A belief that close commercial ties with Great Britain were essential to restoring American credit abroad
options.label: reversal
options.why: Wanting close trade ties with Britain to restore credit was a Federalist position tied to Hamilton. Whitlock is attacking that program, not defending it.

options.text: Support for a loose interpretation of the Constitution that would let Congress fund roads and canals
options.label: reversal
options.why: Whitlock reads the Constitution strictly and rejects implied powers ('I search the Constitution in vain'). Loose construction is the view he opposes.

options.text: Fear that the British would continue occupying forts in the Northwest Territory, threatening frontier settlers
options.label: true_but_not_responsive
options.why: British troops did stay in the northwestern forts until Jay's Treaty, but the excerpt is about finance and the Constitution, not frontier security.

facts: In 1790 Hamilton proposed funding the national debt at face value and having the federal government assume state war debts.
Virginia and some other southern states had already paid off much of their Revolutionary War debt by 1790, so they objected to assumption.

items.stem: Which of the following, if true, would most directly support the author's claim about who would profit from redeeming the war certificates at full value?

options.text: Records showing that northern investors had bought most soldiers' certificates at steep discounts
options.label: key
options.why: Whitlock claims that speculators who bought the certificates cheaply would get rich at the expense of the veterans who first held them. Evidence that northern investors held most of the paper after buying it below face value supports that claim directly. Historically, much of the debt had in fact passed to speculators by 1790.

options.text: Records showing that Virginia and several other southern states had already levied taxes to retire much of their war debt
options.label: true_but_not_responsive
options.why: This backs Whitlock's separate complaint about assuming state debts. It says nothing about who held the federal certificates.

options.text: Reports that the Bank of the United States expanded credit and steadied the value of paper currency in commercial cities
options.label: unrelated_development
options.why: This is about how the bank performed, not about who owned the certificates. If anything, it weakens the author's case against the bank.

options.text: Testimony that most original holders still kept their certificates and would receive full payment from the Treasury
options.label: reversal
options.why: If the original holders still had their certificates, they would get the profit, not speculators. This would refute the author's claim.

facts: By 1790 many Revolutionary War debt certificates had been sold by original holders, including veterans, to speculators at a fraction of face value.
Congress approved funding the debt at face value in 1790, paying the current holders of the certificates.

items.stem: The arguments in the excerpt are best understood in the context of which of the following broader developments?

options.text: Disputes over the reach of federal power that helped produce the first political parties
options.label: key
options.why: The fights over Hamilton's funding plan, assumption, and the national bank, along with strict versus loose readings of the Constitution, helped split national politics into Federalists and Democratic-Republicans in the 1790s.

options.text: Complaints that the Articles of Confederation left Congress unable to levy taxes or repay its war debts
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: Those complaints belong to the 1780s, under the Articles. The excerpt is responding to a program adopted under the Constitution.

options.text: Sectional quarrels over extending slavery into the western territories that were settled by the Missouri Compromise of 1820
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The Missouri crisis came about thirty years later, and it concerned slavery's expansion, not federal finance.

options.text: Outrage over the XYZ Affair and the undeclared naval war with France during the presidency of John Adams
options.label: true_but_not_responsive
options.why: The XYZ Affair and the Quasi-War deepened party conflict later in the 1790s. They involved foreign policy, not the 1790-1791 financial debates in the excerpt.

facts: Disagreements over Hamilton's financial program in the early 1790s contributed to the rise of the Federalist and Democratic-Republican parties.
Congress chartered the First Bank of the United States in 1791 after a cabinet debate over strict versus loose construction of the Constitution.

items.stem: Which of the following was part of the 1790 compromise that secured congressional approval for federal assumption of state debts, the policy Whitlock criticizes?

options.text: Placement of the permanent national capital on the Potomac River, near southern states
options.label: key
options.why: Under the Compromise of 1790, enough southern congressmen supported assumption in exchange for putting the permanent national capital on the Potomac River.

options.text: Adoption of the three-fifths clause counting enslaved people for representation and direct taxes
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The three-fifths clause was agreed to at the Constitutional Convention in 1787. It had nothing to do with assumption.

options.text: Passage of the Bill of Rights to reassure Antifederalists who feared a strong central government
options.label: true_but_not_responsive
options.why: Congress proposed the Bill of Rights in 1789 to address concerns raised during ratification. It was not a trade for votes on assumption.

options.text: Admission of Missouri as a slave state and Maine as a free state to preserve sectional balance
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: That was the Missouri Compromise of 1820. It dealt with slavery and statehood, not war debts.

facts: The Compromise of 1790 linked congressional approval of federal assumption of state debts to locating the permanent national capital on the Potomac River.
The national capital moved to the District of Columbia in 1800.

input.title: Electoral Arithmetic and Lower South Secession, 1860-1861

sources.title: Excerpt on the Lower South's response to the election of 1860
sources.attribution: Marian Delacroix-Hale, historian, The Arithmetic of Disunion: Electoral Fear and the Lower South, 1860-1861, published 2009 (ALTON-composed, in the style of a modern historian's monograph)
sources.body: Secessionists in the Lower South did not wait for Abraham Lincoln to do anything; they acted on what his victory revealed. The returns of November 1860 showed that a party with almost no presence south of the Ohio River could capture the presidency on free-state votes alone. Lincoln's name did not even appear on the ballot in most slaveholding states, yet he won a clear majority of the electoral college. To planters in South Carolina, Mississippi, and Alabama, the arithmetic mattered more than the man. A Republican administration would control federal appointments, including the postmasters who decided what mail reached Southern towns, and it would block slavery's expansion into the western territories. Secession conventions framed their decision as a defense of slavery against a permanent northern majority. That the states of the Upper South rejected immediate secession that winter suggests the fear was strongest where slavery was most concentrated.

items.stem: Which of the following would best support the author's argument that Lower South secessionists did not wait for Lincoln to take any action as president?

options.text: South Carolina voted to secede in December 1860, months before Lincoln took office in March 1861.
options.label: key
options.why: South Carolina's convention acted in December 1860, and six more Lower South states followed before the March 1861 inauguration, so secession came before Lincoln could do anything in office, as the author argues.

options.text: Lincoln's April 1861 call for 75,000 volunteers after Fort Sumter prompted Virginia and three other states to secede.
options.label: true_but_not_responsive
options.why: This is accurate, but it concerns the Upper South reacting to a presidential action. It does not show the Lower South moving before Lincoln acted.

options.text: The Emancipation Proclamation of 1863 declared enslaved people in areas still in rebellion against the United States to be free.
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The proclamation came two years after secession, so it cannot be evidence about why the Lower South left the Union in 1860-1861.

options.text: The Kansas-Nebraska Act of 1854 opened northern territories to slavery through popular sovereignty, angering many Northerners.
options.label: unrelated_development
options.why: The act helped produce the Republican Party, but it says nothing about when Lower South states seceded compared with Lincoln's actions in office.

facts: South Carolina adopted an ordinance of secession on December 20, 1860.
Lincoln was inaugurated in March 1861, after seven Lower South states had seceded.

items.stem: The secession of Virginia, North Carolina, Tennessee, and Arkansas in the spring of 1861 would most likely modify the author's argument by suggesting that

options.text: for some slave states, the use of federal force after Fort Sumter, not the election, was decisive
options.label: key
options.why: These Upper South states seceded only after Fort Sumter and Lincoln's call for troops. That suggests coercion, more than the electoral arithmetic the author stresses, pushed them out, which adds a qualification to the argument.

options.text: the Upper South had been more eager than the Deep South to leave the Union from the moment results were known
options.label: reversal
options.why: The Upper South turned down immediate secession in the winter of 1860-1861. The Deep South moved first.

options.text: Lincoln's victory had played no role at all in the decisions of any slaveholding state to leave the Union in 1860 and 1861
options.label: overstated
options.why: The later secessions qualify the argument but do not overturn it. The Lower South plainly reacted to the election result.

options.text: Upper South states had largely abandoned slavery by 1861 and seceded mainly to protect their tariff-protected industries
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: Slavery was still strong in Virginia, North Carolina, and Tennessee in 1861, and tariff protection of industry was not what drove their secession.

facts: Confederate forces fired on Fort Sumter in April 1861, and Lincoln then called for 75,000 volunteers.
Virginia, North Carolina, Tennessee, and Arkansas seceded after Lincoln's call for troops in 1861.

items.stem: The election result described in the excerpt was most directly shaped by which of the following developments of the 1850s?

options.text: The collapse of the Whig Party and the rise of a Republican Party based almost entirely in free states
options.label: key
options.why: After the Whigs fell apart in the mid-1850s, the antislavery-extension Republican Party grew up as a purely Northern party. That is why it could win the presidency with almost no Southern support.

options.text: The rise of the Know-Nothing Party, which replaced the Democrats as the main national party in the slave states
options.label: overstated
options.why: The Know-Nothings had a short burst of strength in the mid-1850s but never replaced the Democrats in the South, and they had faded by 1860.

options.text: The continued competition of Whigs and Democrats for voters in both the North and the South throughout the decade
options.label: reversal
options.why: The Second Party System's two parties competing in both sections broke down in the 1850s. It was not a context that lasted to 1860.

options.text: The Supreme Court's Dred Scott decision, which upheld Congress's power to ban slavery in all of the western territories
options.label: reversal
options.why: Dred Scott v. Sandford (1857) ruled that Congress could not ban slavery in the territories. That is the opposite of what this option says.

facts: The Whig Party collapsed in the mid-1850s, and the Republican Party formed in 1854 in opposition to the expansion of slavery.
Dred Scott v. Sandford (1857) held that Congress lacked power to prohibit slavery in the territories.

items.stem: The secessionists' effort, described in the excerpt, to shield a sectional interest from a northern-dominated federal government most resembled which earlier development?

options.text: South Carolina's attempt in 1832 to nullify federal tariffs it considered unconstitutional
options.label: key
options.why: In the Nullification Crisis, South Carolina claimed state power to reject federal law in order to protect Southern interests from a national majority. That is the same pattern of state resistance the secessionists followed in 1860.

options.text: Western Pennsylvania farmers' armed resistance in 1794 to a federal excise tax on whiskey production
options.label: unrelated_development
options.why: The Whiskey Rebellion was local resistance to a tax. It was not an official state action claiming sovereignty to protect a sectional interest.

options.text: Congressman David Wilmot's 1846 proposal to bar slavery from any territory acquired from Mexico in the war
options.label: reversal
options.why: The Wilmot Proviso was the kind of federal limit on slavery's expansion that secessionists feared. It did not resist such limits.

options.text: President Andrew Jackson's removal of federal deposits from the Second Bank of the United States in 1833
options.label: unrelated_development
options.why: This was an exercise of federal executive power in the Bank War. It was not a state effort to resist a national majority.

facts: In 1832 South Carolina declared the federal tariffs of 1828 and 1832 null and void within the state.
The Wilmot Proviso (1846) proposed banning slavery in territory gained from Mexico.

input.title: Making Slavery by Statute in the Chesapeake

sources.title: Law and Labor in Colonial Virginia
sources.attribution: Corinne Haverford Pike, historian, Statutes of Bondage: Law and Labor in the Tidewater, 1660-1740, a fictional monograph, 2018 (ALTON-composed, in the style of a social history of colonial law)
sources.body: Historians once read the Chesapeake's slave laws as a record of a system already in place. The statute books suggest the reverse. Legislators built hereditary racial slavery step by step, and they kept pace with the labor market. In 1662 the Virginia assembly declared that a child's condition followed that of the mother, which cut enslaved children off from any claim through a free English father. Five years later it ruled that baptism did not alter bondage, closing a door some Africans had used to petition for freedom. These early acts came when enslaved Africans were still a minority of the colony's bound laborers. The decisive measures came later. Fewer English servants were crossing the ocean, and private traders, freed in 1698 from a royal company's monopoly, carried thousands of captives up the York and Rappahannock rivers. In those years the assembly gathered its scattered statutes into the comprehensive code of 1705. Law did not merely follow slavery; it gave the institution its permanent, racial shape.

items.stem: Which of the following pieces of evidence would best support the author's claim that Virginia's slave laws kept pace with changes in the colony's labor market?

options.text: A decline in English servant arrivals in the late 1600s alongside a rise in imports of enslaved Africans
options.label: key
options.why: The author ties the 1705 code to fewer English servants and more captives arriving. In the late seventeenth century, better conditions in England cut the supply of indentured servants, and Chesapeake planters turned more and more to enslaved Africans. That is exactly the pattern the argument needs.

options.text: Growing numbers of free farmers raising wheat for export from Pennsylvania and the other middle colonies by the 1700s
options.label: true_but_not_responsive
options.why: Middle-colony grain farming did grow, but it describes another region's labor system and says nothing about how Chesapeake labor shifts shaped Virginia law.

options.text: Spanish reliance on the encomienda system to compel the labor of indigenous peoples in New Spain during the 1500s
options.label: unrelated_development
options.why: The encomienda was a real Spanish labor system, but it belongs to a different empire and an earlier century, so it cannot show Virginia lawmakers responding to their own labor market.

options.text: Revivals of the 1740s Great Awakening that drew increasing numbers of enslaved people into evangelical Protestant churches
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The Great Awakening came decades after the 1705 code and concerns religion, not the labor-supply changes the author links to lawmaking.

facts: The supply of English indentured servants to the Chesapeake declined in the late 1600s while imports of enslaved Africans rose.
Virginia consolidated its slave laws into a comprehensive code in 1705.

items.stem: Which of the following pieces of evidence would most directly modify the author's argument that law gave slavery in Virginia its permanent, racial shape?

options.text: Court records showing some Africans in Virginia held in lifelong servitude during the 1640s
options.label: key
options.why: If Africans were already held for life before the 1662 statute, then custom and practice were creating lifelong racial bondage before the law did. That would qualify the claim that legislation gave slavery its shape and suggest the law partly confirmed existing practice.

options.text: Records of free Africans, such as Anthony Johnson, owning land and servants on Virginia's Eastern Shore at midcentury
options.label: reversal
options.why: Free Black landowners at midcentury show that racial status was still fluid before the slave codes. That supports, rather than modifies, the author's view that law hardened slavery later.

options.text: Evidence that planters turned increasingly to enslaved Africans after Bacon's Rebellion exposed the dangers of armed former servants
options.label: reversal
options.why: The planters' move away from servants after the 1676 rebellion fits the author's story of lawmakers responding to a changing labor force, so it backs up the argument instead of qualifying it.

options.text: A 1688 petition by Germantown Quakers in Pennsylvania condemning the buying and selling of human beings
options.label: true_but_not_responsive
options.why: The Germantown protest is real, but it is moral criticism from another colony and does not bear on whether Virginia law created or followed slavery.

facts: Some Africans in Virginia were held in lifelong servitude in the 1640s, before the colony passed statutes defining slavery (for example, the 1640 sentence of John Punch to serve for life).
Anthony Johnson, a free man of African descent, held land on Virginia's Eastern Shore in the mid-1600s.
Bacon's Rebellion occurred in Virginia in 1676.

items.stem: The arrival of enslaved Africans in the Chesapeake described in the excerpt is best understood in the context of which broader development?

options.text: An Atlantic economy linking colonial tobacco exports to English markets under the Navigation Acts
options.label: key
options.why: Chesapeake demand for enslaved labor came from tobacco, a staple crop that the Navigation Acts directed to English markets. The slave trade into the York and Rappahannock rivers was one part of this mercantilist Atlantic trading system.

options.text: A British campaign to suppress the transatlantic slave trade, culminating in Parliament's abolition act of 1807
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: Britain's abolition campaign came about a century later and worked against the expansion of the trade described in the excerpt.

options.text: Colonial assemblies' growing refusal to accept any form of imperial regulation of their commerce with other nations
options.label: overstated
options.why: Colonists often evaded trade laws under salutary neglect, but before 1754 they did not reject all imperial regulation. Tobacco planters worked within the Navigation Acts system.

options.text: The exchange of plants, animals, and diseases between the Eastern and Western hemispheres after 1492
options.label: too_broad
options.why: The Columbian Exchange is a very broad backdrop. It does not explain the specific commercial system, tobacco exports within the British mercantile empire, that drove the Chesapeake slave trade.

facts: England's Navigation Acts, beginning in 1651 and 1660, required enumerated colonial goods such as tobacco to be shipped to England.
The Royal African Company's monopoly on the English slave trade was ended in 1698, opening the trade to independent merchants.

items.stem: Which of the following later developments in the British colonies most closely continued the pattern of lawmaking described in the excerpt?

options.text: South Carolina's adoption of a harsher slave code after the Stono Rebellion of 1739
options.label: key
options.why: South Carolina's Negro Act of 1740 tightened control over enslaved people in a colony with a large enslaved population. It continued the pattern of colonial assemblies using comprehensive statutes to define and enforce racial slavery.

options.text: The Georgia trustees' decision in the 1730s to prohibit slavery in their new colony south of Carolina
options.label: reversal
options.why: Georgia's early ban went the opposite way from the Virginia pattern, restricting slavery instead of building it into law. The ban was lifted around 1750.

options.text: Pennsylvania's passage of a gradual emancipation law during the War for Independence in 1780
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: Gradual emancipation came in the revolutionary era and began dismantling slavery, so it neither falls in the period nor continues the pattern.

options.text: The growth of New England's shipbuilding and fishing economy, which relied heavily on family and wage labor
options.label: unrelated_development
options.why: New England's maritime economy was a real regional development, but it has nothing to do with legislatures writing slave codes.

facts: The Stono Rebellion took place in South Carolina in 1739, and the colony passed the Negro Act of 1740 in response.
Georgia's trustees banned slavery in 1735, and the ban was repealed around 1750.

input.title: Furnace and Furrow: Coerced Labor in the New South

sources.title: Labor and Growth in the New South
sources.attribution: Miriam Castellane, historian, Furnace and Furrow: Labor and Capital in the Georgia Piedmont, 1870-1900, published 2011 (ALTON-composed, in the style of a modern academic monograph on Southern labor history)
sources.body: Boosters of the New South promised that railroads, cotton mills, and coal mines would free the region from its dependence on a single crop. Yet the labor arrangements behind this growth bound Black and poor white Southerners more tightly than the promoters admitted. In the cotton districts, sharecroppers who signed contracts each January pledged their share of the coming harvest to a furnishing merchant under the crop-lien system, and many ended the year owing more than when they began. In the mines, brickyards, and turpentine camps, states leased prisoners, most of them Black men convicted of vagrancy or petty theft, to private companies that paid the state a fee and housed them in brutal conditions. Industrial progress and agricultural debt, in short, were not opposites but partners. Both depended on workers who had little power to bargain, to move, or to refuse.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes the historian's main argument in the excerpt?
facts: Under the crop-lien system after the Civil War, Southern tenants and sharecroppers pledged future crops to merchants for supplies on credit, often falling into debt.
Southern states leased convicts, disproportionately Black, to private companies in the late nineteenth century.

options.text: Economic growth in the New South depended on labor systems that sharply restricted workers' freedom.
options.label: key
options.why: The historian argues that industrial progress and agricultural debt were partners, both resting on workers with little power to bargain, move, or refuse, which matches the history of crop liens and convict leasing.

options.text: Southern industrialization in the 1880s largely ended the region's reliance on cotton by drawing sharecroppers into mill and mine jobs.
options.label: reversal
options.why: The excerpt says boosters promised an end to single-crop dependence but that coercive arrangements persisted; cotton stayed dominant in much of the South.

options.text: Convict leasing was chiefly a creation of Northern investors who used Southern prisons to evade the wage demands of organized labor.
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: The excerpt describes states leasing prisoners to private companies but makes no claim about Northern investors or union wage demands.

options.text: Sharecropping offered freedpeople a gradual path to landownership that industrial wage work in Southern cities could not provide.
options.label: reversal
options.why: The historian stresses that sharecroppers often sank deeper into debt, not that they moved toward owning land.

items.stem: Which of the following pieces of evidence would most directly support the historian's argument about workers in the New South?
facts: Southern states passed Black Codes in 1865-1866 that included vagrancy laws allowing those unable to pay fines to be hired out.
Plessy v. Ferguson (1896) upheld a Louisiana law requiring separate railroad cars.

options.text: Southern laws after 1865 that punished vagrancy and allowed those unable to pay fines to be hired out
options.label: key
options.why: Vagrancy laws that turned unemployment into a crime and fed people into forced labor directly support the claim that workers had little power to refuse or move.

options.text: The rapid expansion of railroad mileage across the former Confederate states during the 1880s, financed heavily by outside investors
options.label: true_but_not_responsive
options.why: Railroad growth is real and part of New South development, but it shows economic expansion, not the coercive labor conditions at the core of the argument.

options.text: The Supreme Court's 1896 ruling in Plessy v. Ferguson upholding a Louisiana law requiring separate railroad cars for Black passengers
options.label: true_but_not_responsive
options.why: Plessy concerns legal segregation in public accommodations, not the labor arrangements of sharecropping and convict leasing.

options.text: The founding of Tuskegee Institute in Alabama in 1881 to train Black students in agricultural and industrial trades
options.label: unrelated_development
options.why: Tuskegee's founding concerns Black education and self-help, not evidence that workers were bound by debt or forced labor.

items.stem: The labor arrangements described in the excerpt expanded most directly in the context of which of the following?
facts: Following the Compromise of 1877, federal troops were withdrawn from the South and Democratic 'Redeemer' governments controlled Southern states.
The Freedmen's Bureau did not carry out large-scale land redistribution; President Andrew Johnson returned most confiscated land to former owners in 1865.

options.text: The return of Democratic Redeemer governments to power in Southern states as Reconstruction ended
options.label: key
options.why: Redeemer governments cut public spending, expanded convict leasing, and passed laws favoring landowners and merchants, providing the political setting for the systems in the excerpt.

options.text: The Freedmen's Bureau's widespread redistribution of confiscated plantation land to formerly enslaved families
options.label: reversal
options.why: Land redistribution largely failed; most confiscated land went back to former owners, which is why freedpeople turned to sharecropping.

options.text: The Great Migration of Black Southerners to Northern industrial cities that left planters short of field laborers
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The Great Migration began around World War I, well after these labor systems took hold in the 1870s and 1880s.

options.text: The Populist Party's capture of Congress and the presidency on a platform of federal ownership of the railroads
options.label: overstated
options.why: The Populists called for government railroad ownership in 1892 but never won control of Congress or the presidency, and they challenged rather than created these conditions.

items.stem: Which of the following best explains why sharecropping became widespread in the South in the decades after the Civil War?
facts: After the Civil War, most freedpeople did not receive land, and many planters had land but little cash, leading to sharecropping arrangements.
The Fifteenth Amendment (1870) barred denial of the vote on the basis of race and contained no economic guarantees.

options.text: Freedpeople lacked land and capital, while landowners lacked cash to pay wages.
options.label: key
options.why: Sharecropping traded labor for a share of the crop, suiting landless freedpeople and cash-poor planters after emancipation and the war's destruction.

options.text: The Homestead Act of 1862 moved most landless Southern farmers onto free federal land in the Great Plains.
options.label: overstated
options.why: Few landless Southerners, Black or white, got homesteads in the West; most stayed in the South as tenants and sharecroppers.

options.text: The Fifteenth Amendment required states to guarantee formerly enslaved people a share of the crops they raised.
options.label: misattributed
options.why: The Fifteenth Amendment dealt with voting rights and said nothing about crop shares or labor contracts.

options.text: Large numbers of European immigrants settled in the rural South and demanded tenant contracts over wage labor.
options.label: unrelated_development
options.why: Most European immigrants in this period went to Northern and Midwestern cities, not the rural South.

input.title: Veterans, Mortgages, and the Unequal Suburb

sources.title: A historian on GI Bill housing benefits in postwar Ohio
sources.attribution: Dorothea Lindqvist, historian, Paper Deeds: Veterans, Mortgages, and the Making of a Suburban County, 2009 (ALTON-composed, in the style of a modern historian's monograph; author, book, and development are fictional)
sources.body: Historians often call the Servicemen's Readjustment Act of 1944 a ladder into the middle class. In the tract developments that went up outside Cleveland after 1946, though, the ladder was missing rungs. The law's loan guarantees let a veteran buy a two-bedroom house in a place like Brookfield Acres with little or no down payment, and the monthly payments often came to less than city rents. Yet the act left approval to local banks and Veterans Administration offices. Those offices followed Federal Housing Administration appraisal rules that rated mixed or Black neighborhoods as poor risks, and builders wrote racial restrictions into their sales contracts. Of the first 3,100 VA-backed mortgages recorded in the county, fewer than 40 went to Black veterans. So the suburbs that federal money built were more than a reward for service. They came out of policy choices that turned equal wartime sacrifice into unequal postwar wealth.

items.stem: Which of the following pieces of historical evidence would best support the author's argument in the excerpt?
facts: Levitt and Sons began building Levittown, New York, in 1947.
Levittown's builders initially refused to sell homes to African American buyers, including veterans.

options.text: Levittown, New York, opened in 1947 and at first barred sales to African American buyers, veterans included.
options.label: key
options.why: The excerpt argues that federally backed suburbs shut out Black veterans. The racial exclusion at Levittown, the best-known postwar development built with federal mortgage support, is direct evidence for that claim.

options.text: The law paid college tuition and living stipends that let millions of veterans enroll in universities and trade schools.
options.label: true_but_not_responsive
options.why: This is accurate about the GI Bill, but it deals with education benefits. It does not speak to the author's claim about unequal access to housing.

options.text: The Federal-Aid Highway Act of 1956 funded thousands of miles of interstate roads that made long daily commutes from suburbs practical.
options.label: true_but_not_responsive
options.why: Highways help explain why suburbs grew. They say nothing about racial inequality in who could buy suburban homes.

options.text: In Shelley v. Kraemer in 1948 the Supreme Court ruled that state courts could not enforce racially restrictive housing covenants.
options.label: reversal
options.why: The ruling shows government acting against housing discrimination, so if anything it complicates the author's claim instead of supporting it.

items.stem: Which of the following findings, if documented, would most weaken the author's argument about postwar suburban housing?
facts: The Servicemen's Readjustment Act of 1944 guaranteed home loans for veterans.
Federal Housing Administration appraisal practices in the 1930s and 1940s rated Black and racially mixed neighborhoods as high lending risks.

options.text: Records showing that Black and white veterans in the county won VA loan approvals at similar rates for comparable homes
options.label: key
options.why: The author's argument depends on unequal approval of VA-backed mortgages. Evidence of equal approval rates would undercut the central claim that policy choices turned shared sacrifice into unequal wealth.

options.text: Records showing that monthly mortgage payments in Brookfield Acres were lower than the rents charged for apartments in Cleveland
options.label: true_but_not_responsive
options.why: The excerpt already grants this point. Cheap payments explain why suburbs appealed to buyers but do not touch the claim about unequal access.

options.text: Records showing that local bank officers relied on Federal Housing Administration maps that rated Black neighborhoods as hazardous risks
options.label: reversal
options.why: This finding would strengthen the argument, because it ties federal appraisal rules directly to discriminatory lending.

options.text: Records showing that builders cut costs by assembling houses in stages with specialized crews, much like an automobile assembly line
options.label: unrelated_development
options.why: Mass-production building methods are real, but they have nothing to do with who was approved for loans or barred from buying.

items.stem: The rapid construction of housing developments like the one described in the excerpt after 1946 was most directly a response to which of the following?
facts: After World War II, millions of returning servicemen faced a severe housing shortage.
Marriage and birth rates rose sharply after 1945, beginning the baby boom.

options.text: A severe housing shortage as returning veterans married and started families
options.label: key
options.why: Almost no homes were built during the Depression and the war. Demobilization, a wave of marriages, and the baby boom then created heavy demand, which builders met with tract housing paid for through GI Bill mortgages.

options.text: New Deal public housing programs that had already moved most urban working families into federally owned apartments
options.label: overstated
options.why: New Deal public housing existed but housed only a small share of urban families. It did not satisfy demand or set off the suburban boom.

options.text: The Federal-Aid Highway Act of 1956, which created the interstate system that first allowed workers to commute by car
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The suburban boom began about a decade before 1956. Commuting by car was already common, so the act sped up suburban growth rather than starting it.

options.text: Wartime price controls and rationing that were extended into the 1950s to restrain consumer demand for durable goods
options.label: reversal
options.why: Most controls and rationing ended soon after the war. Pent-up savings then fed a consumer boom, the opposite of restrained demand.

items.stem: The pattern of suburban growth described in the excerpt contributed most directly to which of the following developments in the 1950s and 1960s?
facts: In the 1950s and 1960s, many white middle-class families moved from central cities to suburbs.
This movement reduced urban tax bases and left poverty concentrated in many central cities.

options.text: Shrinking tax bases and growing concentrations of poverty in many central cities
options.label: key
options.why: Federally backed suburbs drew mostly white middle-class families out of cities while minority residents were largely kept out. Cities lost revenue and were left with concentrated poverty, which helped produce the urban crisis of the 1960s.

options.text: A revival of downtown department stores as suburban families drove into cities for most of their weekly shopping
options.label: reversal
options.why: Suburbanization drew shopping away from downtowns toward suburban shopping centers and malls, so downtown retail declined.

options.text: An expansion of Works Progress Administration projects to build roads, schools, and parks in new suburban towns
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The WPA was a New Deal agency that shut down in 1943, before the postwar suburban boom began.

options.text: A large migration of African Americans from Northern cities back to the rural South in search of affordable farmland
options.label: reversal
options.why: In these decades the Great Migration was still bringing African Americans into Northern and Western cities. Movement back toward the South came later and went mainly to Southern cities, not farmland.

input.title: Debt, Money, and the Omaha Platform

sources.title: A Historian Reinterprets the Populist Revolt
sources.attribution: Ingrid Solvang, historian, Bushels and Ballots: Debt, Money, and the Plains Revolt, 1874-1896, chapter on the 1892 Omaha convention, published 2009 (ALTON-composed, in the style of a modern historian of agrarian protest)
sources.body: An older generation of scholars pictured the Populists as backward-looking farmers chasing a vanished agrarian past. The record from the wheat and cotton belts tells a different story. From the 1870s to the mid-1890s, prices for staple crops drifted steadily downward, while the debts farmers had taken on to buy land, machinery, and seed stayed fixed in dollars that grew more valuable each year. A Kansas farmer who borrowed in 1880 found that repaying his mortgage in 1890 took far more bushels of wheat than he had planned for. Railroad rates, set by companies that faced no competition along many branch lines, took another share. When delegates gathered at Omaha in 1892, their demands for an expanded currency, a graduated income tax, and public ownership of the railroads rested on a precise diagnosis of these pressures. The Populists did not reject the modern economy. They asked the national government to manage it in the interest of producers.

items.stem: Which of the following, if presented as evidence, would most directly support the author's claim that the Populists did not reject the modern economy?

options.text: Farmers' Alliances set up cooperative marketing exchanges and proposed federal warehouses offering low-interest loans on stored crops.
options.label: key
options.why: Cooperative exchanges and the subtreasury plan show agrarian reformers trying to use modern marketing, credit, and federal institutions to their advantage, which supports the claim that they sought to manage the modern economy instead of escaping it.

options.text: Some Populist orators blamed the farmers' troubles on a shadowy conspiracy of eastern and foreign bankers, voicing it in sharply moralistic and apocalyptic language.
options.label: reversal
options.why: Conspiratorial rhetoric is the kind of evidence the older interpretation used to portray Populists as backward-looking, so it would tend to challenge the author's claim, not support it.

options.text: The Grange was founded in 1867 as a fraternal society that held picnics, lectures, and social gatherings to ease the isolation of rural families.
options.label: true_but_not_responsive
options.why: The Grange's social role is accurate but says nothing about whether agrarian reformers accepted or rejected the modern market economy.

options.text: Large bonanza farms in the Dakota Territory employed hundreds of seasonal laborers and steam-powered threshers to harvest wheat for export.
options.label: unrelated_development
options.why: Bonanza farms show the commercialization of agriculture but reveal nothing about the outlook or program of the Populist movement.

facts: The Southern Farmers' Alliance proposed a subtreasury plan in the late 1880s for federal warehouses and low-interest loans on stored crops.
Farmers' Alliances organized cooperative buying and marketing exchanges in the 1880s.

items.stem: Which of the following developments would historians most likely use to modify the author's portrayal of the Populist program as a broad plan for national economic management?

options.text: The People's Party endorsed Democrat William Jennings Bryan in 1896, and the campaign centered on free silver while setting aside other demands.
options.label: key
options.why: Fusion with the Democrats in 1896 narrowed the movement to the single issue of free silver, dropping much of the Omaha Platform. This qualifies the author's picture of a broad program for managing the economy.

options.text: Congress passed the Interstate Commerce Act in 1887, creating a federal commission to require that railroad rates be reasonable and publicly posted.
options.label: true_but_not_responsive
options.why: The act shows federal interest in regulating railroads but says nothing about how broad or narrow the Populist program was, so it does not modify the author's portrayal.

options.text: The Panic of 1893 drove crop prices still lower, set off a wave of farm foreclosures across the plains, and deepened rural support for a greatly expanded national money supply.
options.label: reversal
options.why: Worsening farm distress after 1893 fits the author's explanation of agrarian grievances, so it would support the argument instead of modifying it.

options.text: The Seventeenth Amendment, ratified in 1913, adopted the Populist call for the direct election of United States senators by the voters of each state.
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: This later Progressive Era reform carried out a Populist goal, so it supports the movement's influence. It also comes after the period in question and does not qualify how broad the Populist program was in the 1890s.

facts: In 1896 the People's Party nominated Democrat William Jennings Bryan for president, and his campaign focused on free silver.
William McKinley defeated Bryan in 1896, and the People's Party declined afterward.

items.stem: The falling crop prices and growing burden of debts described in the excerpt were most directly connected to which of the following?

options.text: Federal monetary policy, including the Coinage Act of 1873 and the 1879 resumption of gold-backed specie payments, restricted the money supply.
options.label: key
options.why: Ending the coinage of the silver dollar in 1873 and returning to specie payments in 1879 tied the currency to gold. The money supply grew more slowly than output, which caused deflation and raised the real value of farm debts.

options.text: The Sherman Silver Purchase Act of 1890 required the Treasury to buy millions of ounces of silver each month and pay for it with notes redeemable in coin.
options.label: reversal
options.why: The Silver Purchase Act was a modest inflationary concession to silver interests, so it worked against deflation instead of causing it.

options.text: The Federal Reserve System, created in 1913 to manage the nation's currency and credit, raised interest rates sharply and tightened lending to rural banks.
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The Federal Reserve did not exist until 1913, so it could not explain deflation between the 1870s and the 1890s.

options.text: Protective tariffs such as the McKinley Tariff of 1890 raised the prices farmers paid for manufactured goods while offering almost nothing to protect the prices of their crops sold abroad.
options.label: true_but_not_responsive
options.why: Tariffs were a real farm grievance, but they raised the cost of goods farmers bought. They do not explain the general fall in prices and the rising real value of debts.

facts: The Coinage Act of 1873 ended the coinage of the standard silver dollar, which critics called the Crime of '73.
Under the Specie Resumption Act of 1875, the government resumed redeeming paper money in gold coin in 1879.

items.stem: The approach described in the final sentence of the excerpt most closely resembles which later twentieth-century federal policy?

options.text: The Agricultural Adjustment Act of 1933 paid farmers to reduce production of staple crops in order to raise farm prices.
options.label: key
options.why: Like the Populist demands, the New Deal's AAA used national government power to manage the agricultural economy for the benefit of farm producers.

options.text: Treasury Secretary Andrew Mellon's tax program in the 1920s lowered income tax rates on the highest earners to encourage private investment.
options.label: reversal
options.why: Mellon's tax cuts went in the opposite direction from the Populist call for a graduated income tax and federal intervention for producers.

options.text: The National Origins Act of 1924 set strict immigration quotas that favored newcomers from northern and western Europe over other regions.
options.label: unrelated_development
options.why: Immigration restriction has nothing to do with federal management of the economy for producers.

options.text: The Eighteenth Amendment, ratified in 1919, prohibited the manufacture, sale, and transportation of intoxicating liquors throughout the United States.
options.label: unrelated_development
options.why: Prohibition was a moral reform aimed at alcohol, not an effort to manage the economy in the interest of agricultural producers.

facts: The Agricultural Adjustment Act of 1933 paid farmers to cut production to raise crop prices.
The Omaha Platform of 1892 called for an expanded currency, a graduated income tax, and government ownership of railroads.

input.title: The Crisis of 1798: Sedition, Opposition, and State Resolutions

sources.title: The Crisis of 1798 and the Problem of Opposition
sources.attribution: Historian Corinne Haldane Voss, from the published Wexford Lectures on the Early Republic, delivered at Linton College, 2011 (ALTON-composed, in the style of a historian's interpretive lecture)
sources.body: We usually tell the story of 1798 as a clash between liberty and repression, but the deeper conflict was over whether an organized opposition could exist at all. Federalists in Congress, alarmed by the XYZ Affair and the undeclared naval war with France, lengthened the residency requirement for citizenship to fourteen years. They allowed the president to deport aliens he judged dangerous, and they made it a crime to publish false, scandalous, and malicious writing against the government. Nearly every prosecution under the Sedition Act fell on Republican printers or politicians, among them the Vermont congressman Matthew Lyon. The Kentucky and Virginia Resolutions, drafted in secret by Thomas Jefferson and James Madison, replied that the laws were unconstitutional and that states could judge federal overreach. No other state legislature endorsed them. The Republicans won their real victory at the ballot box in 1800, yet the constitutional theory they had advanced outlived the party quarrel that produced it.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes the main argument of the excerpt?

options.text: The central issue was whether an organized political opposition could legitimately exist.
options.label: key
options.why: Voss says the deeper conflict of 1798 was over whether an organized opposition could exist at all, and she supports this by noting that prosecutions fell almost entirely on Republicans.

options.text: The Kentucky and Virginia Resolutions rallied most state legislatures to oppose the Federalist laws.
options.label: reversal
options.why: The excerpt says no other state legislature endorsed the resolutions. Historically, several northern legislatures rejected them outright.

options.text: The laws mainly reflected Federalist fears of a sudden wave of immigration from Ireland and Germany.
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: The excerpt explains the laws through the crisis with France and partisan conflict. It says nothing about a wave of immigration from particular countries.

options.text: The Sedition Act prosecutions permanently silenced the Republican press until the end of the decade.
options.label: overstated
options.why: The excerpt describes prosecutions but makes no claim that they silenced the opposition. In fact, Republicans kept publishing and won the election of 1800.

facts: Congress passed the Alien and Sedition Acts in 1798 during the Quasi-War with France.
Vermont congressman Matthew Lyon was convicted under the Sedition Act in 1798.
Other state legislatures did not endorse the Kentucky and Virginia Resolutions of 1798, and several northern states rejected them.

items.stem: Which of the following facts would most directly support the excerpt's argument that the Sedition Act served Federalist partisan purposes?

options.text: The Sedition Act was set to expire in March 1801, when Adams's term as president ended.
options.label: key
options.why: Setting the law to lapse when the Federalist administration's term ended suggests it was meant to protect Federalists in power, not to protect the government as such. That supports Voss's partisan reading.

options.text: Washington's Farewell Address of 1796 warned Americans against the dangers of a spirit of faction.
options.label: true_but_not_responsive
options.why: This is true, but a general warning against faction does not show that the Sedition Act was written or enforced to benefit one party.

options.text: The Naturalization Act of 1790 had allowed free white immigrants to become citizens after two years.
options.label: true_but_not_responsive
options.why: This is true and shows how much the 1798 law lengthened residency, but it says nothing about the Sedition Act targeting the Republican opposition.

options.text: The Bill of Rights, ratified in 1791, prohibited Congress from abridging freedom of speech or press.
options.label: true_but_not_responsive
options.why: This is true and bears on whether the act was constitutional, but it does not show that the act was aimed at one party.

facts: The Sedition Act of 1798 was written to expire on March 3, 1801, the end of John Adams's term.
The Bill of Rights, including the First Amendment, was ratified in 1791.

items.stem: The conflict described in the excerpt is best understood in the context of which broader development of the 1790s?

options.text: Party divisions arising from disputes over Hamilton's financial program and the Jay Treaty
options.label: key
options.why: Federalists and Democratic-Republicans formed in the 1790s around disputes over Hamilton's national bank and debt plans and over foreign policy, such as the Jay Treaty. The fight of 1798 grew out of this first party system.

options.text: Western farmers' armed resistance to the federal whiskey excise, which troops put down in 1794
options.label: true_but_not_responsive
options.why: The Whiskey Rebellion was real and tested federal authority. However, it was a single episode of resistance to a tax, not the broader party conflict that explains the laws of 1798 and the response to them.

options.text: Federalist and Antifederalist arguments in state conventions over ratifying the new Constitution in 1788
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The ratification debates came a decade earlier. Federalists and Democratic-Republicans were new parties that formed after the Constitution took effect.

options.text: Evangelical revivals of the Second Great Awakening that encouraged democratic challenges to established elites
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The Second Great Awakening reached its height in the early 1800s. It was a religious movement, not the political context of the 1798 laws.

facts: Disputes over Alexander Hamilton's financial program in the early 1790s helped divide Federalists from Democratic-Republicans.
The Jay Treaty with Britain (1794-1795) sharpened party divisions.

items.stem: The constitutional theory advanced in the resolutions, as described in the excerpt, most directly anticipated which later development in the first half of the 1800s?

options.text: South Carolina's declaration in 1832 that federal tariff laws were void within the state
options.label: key
options.why: South Carolina's Ordinance of Nullification of 1832 relied on the compact theory of the 1798 resolutions, which held that states could judge whether federal laws were constitutional.

options.text: The Supreme Court's assertion in Marbury v. Madison (1803) of its power to strike down federal laws
options.label: misattributed
options.why: Marbury placed the power to judge constitutionality in the federal courts, not in the states, so it does not continue the resolutions' claim.

options.text: The Supreme Court's ruling in McCulloch v. Maryland (1819) that states could not tax a national bank
options.label: reversal
options.why: McCulloch affirmed federal supremacy over the states, which is the opposite of the state authority the resolutions claimed.

options.text: The Missouri Compromise of 1820, which admitted Maine and Missouri together to preserve the sectional balance in the Senate
options.label: unrelated_development
options.why: The Missouri Compromise was a congressional settlement over slavery's expansion. It did not assert that a state could declare federal law void.

facts: South Carolina passed the Ordinance of Nullification in 1832, declaring the tariffs of 1828 and 1832 void in the state.
Nullifiers drew on the compact theory of the Kentucky and Virginia Resolutions of 1798.
Marbury v. Madison (1803) established judicial review by federal courts.

input.title: Allegiance and Survival: The Revolution as a Civil War

sources.title: Choosing Sides in the Revolutionary Countryside
sources.attribution: Excerpt from Hollis T. Wendover, Neighbors at Arms: Allegiance and Survival in the Revolutionary Countryside, a fictional study published in 2011 (ALTON-composed, in the style of a social historian of the American Revolution)
sources.body: Historians once sorted colonists neatly into Patriots and Loyalists, assuming each man chose his side after reading pamphlets on natural rights or weighing his ties to the Crown. The records of the war years tell a messier story. In the Carolina and New York backcountry, many families declared an allegiance only when an army or a militia company appeared at the door, and some changed sides more than once. Local committees of safety demanded oaths, disarmed suspected Tories, and seized their property, so that political loyalty became a question of survival. Old quarrels over land titles, debts, and church membership often decided which side a farmer took. For enslaved people, and for Native nations such as many of the Iroquois, the question was rarely abstract principle. It was which side seemed more likely to secure their freedom or their land. The Revolution was a war for independence, but it was also a civil war fought among neighbors.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes the main argument of the excerpt?
facts: The American Revolution (1775-1783) divided colonists into Patriots, Loyalists, and many who tried to stay neutral.

options.text: Allegiance in the war often depended on local conditions and survival more than on political principle.
options.label: key
options.why: The author says choices came when armies arrived, under committee pressure, and from local quarrels, calling the war a civil war among neighbors.

options.text: Most colonists sided with the Patriots after Enlightenment ideas about natural rights convinced them that British rule was illegitimate.
options.label: reversal
options.why: The author rejects the older view that colonists picked sides after reading pamphlets on natural rights.

options.text: Loyalists were chiefly royal officeholders and wealthy merchants whose commercial ties to Britain determined their political choices.
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: The excerpt focuses on backcountry farmers, enslaved people, and Native nations, not elite officeholders or merchants.

options.text: The war was fought mainly by professional armies, leaving most farm families in the backcountry largely untouched by the fighting.
options.label: reversal
options.why: The author stresses that the war reached backcountry homes directly through armies, militias, and committees.

items.stem: Which of the following pieces of evidence would best support the author's claim that the Revolution was also a civil war fought among neighbors?
facts: At the Battle of Kings Mountain in South Carolina in October 1780, Patriot militia defeated Loyalist militia; almost all combatants on both sides were Americans.
France formally allied with the United States in 1778.

options.text: At Kings Mountain in 1780, nearly all the soldiers on both sides were American Patriot and Loyalist militiamen.
options.label: key
options.why: A major battle fought almost entirely between American militias on opposing sides directly shows colonists fighting one another.

options.text: France's 1778 alliance with the United States supplied troops, loans, and a navy that helped the Continental Army defeat Britain.
options.label: true_but_not_responsive
options.why: Accurate, but it concerns international aid against Britain, not conflict among colonists.

options.text: Thomas Paine's Common Sense sold widely in 1776 and persuaded many readers that independence was justified by reason and nature.
options.label: reversal
options.why: Evidence that ideas persuaded colonists would challenge, not support, the author's emphasis on local and practical motives.

options.text: The siege of Yorktown in 1781 ended with the surrender of a British army to combined American and French forces under Washington.
options.label: true_but_not_responsive
options.why: Accurate, but it describes the defeat of a British army, not neighbors fighting neighbors.

items.stem: The choices of Native nations described in the excerpt are best understood in the context of which broader development?
facts: The Proclamation of 1763 restricted colonial settlement west of the Appalachian Mountains.
During the Revolution most Iroquois nations sided with Britain, although the Oneida and Tuscarora largely supported the Patriots.

options.text: Many Native nations saw Britain as a check on settlers, since the Proclamation of 1763 had restricted settlement west of the Appalachians.
options.label: key
options.why: Because Britain had tried to limit westward settlement after 1763, many Native nations saw a British victory as the best way to protect their lands, which fits the excerpt's point about land.

options.text: The Northwest Ordinance of 1787 pledged that Native lands would never be taken without consent, leading Native nations to trust the new United States government.
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The ordinance came after the war, so it could not shape wartime choices, and its promises did not earn lasting Native trust.

options.text: The Iroquois Confederacy remained united behind the Patriot cause because the Albany Plan of Union had earlier tied the Six Nations to colonial governments.
options.label: reversal
options.why: The Iroquois split during the war, with most nations siding with Britain, and the Albany Plan was never adopted.

options.text: Spanish missions in New Mexico and California drew coastal and Pueblo peoples into labor systems that tied their survival to Catholic religious orders.
options.label: unrelated_development
options.why: Spanish missions in the Southwest and Pacific coast had nothing to do with eastern Native nations' choices in the Revolution.

items.stem: Which of the following was a direct result of the wartime treatment of suspected Loyalists described in the excerpt?
facts: During and after the Revolution, roughly 60,000 or more Loyalists left the United States, many settling in Nova Scotia, New Brunswick, and Quebec.
The Alien and Sedition Acts (1798) targeted immigrants and critics of the Adams administration.
Shays' Rebellion (1786-1787) was led by indebted western Massachusetts farmers, many of them Revolutionary War veterans.

options.text: Tens of thousands of Loyalists left the United States, many of them resettling in British Canada.
options.label: key
options.why: Facing oaths, disarmament, and confiscated property, large numbers of Loyalists left, many for British North America.

options.text: Congress passed the Alien and Sedition Acts in 1798 chiefly to punish former Loyalists who had kept their property after the war.
options.label: misattributed
options.why: The acts targeted immigrants and Democratic-Republican critics of the Adams administration, not former Loyalists.

options.text: Shays' Rebellion in 1786 was led by dispossessed Loyalists demanding that Massachusetts return their confiscated farms.
options.label: misattributed
options.why: The rebels were indebted farmers, many of them Patriot veterans, protesting taxes and foreclosures.

options.text: Former Loyalists became the core of the Federalist Party, using it to push for the return of confiscated property.
options.label: overstated
options.why: The Federalists formed in the 1790s around Hamilton's program; former Loyalists were not the party's base.

input.title: The Contract with America and Divided Government in the 1990s

sources.title: Excerpt A: A historian on the Contract's lasting influence
sources.attribution: Corinne Haldane, The Hundred Days That Lasted: Congress and the Conservative Turn, 2011 (ALTON-composed, in the style of a political historian of the late twentieth century)
sources.body: When House Republicans unveiled their Contract with America on the Capitol steps in September 1994, many commentators dismissed it as campaign theater. They were mistaken. That November, voters gave Republicans control of both chambers of Congress, and the new House majority was the party's first in forty years. During the first hundred days of 1995, the House voted on every item in the Contract. More important, the document changed the terms of national debate. A Democratic president who had campaigned on an active federal government soon found himself bargaining over how quickly, not whether, to balance the federal budget. The Contract did not need to become law in its entirety to succeed. It moved the political center of gravity decisively to the right, and that shift outlasted the men who drafted it.

sources.title: Excerpt B: A historian on the limits of the Republican Revolution
sources.attribution: Theodore Okafor-Lind, Gridlock and Bargain: Divided Government in the Clinton Years, 2015 (ALTON-composed, in the style of a historian of American political institutions)
sources.body: People often remember the Republican landslide of 1994 as a revolution, but its legislative record was thinner than its rhetoric. A constitutional amendment imposing congressional term limits failed in the House, and the balanced budget amendment fell short in the Senate. When Speaker Newt Gingrich's majority clashed with the White House over spending in the winter of 1995 to 1996, two partial shutdowns of the federal government followed, and most voters blamed congressional Republicans. Bill Clinton won reelection comfortably the next year. What emerged was less a conservative triumph than an uneasy bargaining relationship. Each side claimed credit for compromises neither had wanted, and partisan distrust in Washington deepened with every round.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes a similarity and a difference between the two excerpts?

options.text: Both describe the 1994 elections as giving Republicans power in Congress, but they disagree about whether a lasting conservative policy shift resulted.
options.label: key
options.why: Haldane and Okafor-Lind both treat the 1994 Republican takeover of Congress as their starting point. Haldane argues the Contract moved politics durably to the right, while Okafor-Lind argues its record was thin and that it led to bargaining and deeper partisanship.

options.text: Both argue that the Contract with America failed mainly because President Clinton vetoed nearly all of its bills, but they disagree about how the public viewed those vetoes.
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: Neither excerpt says vetoes caused the Contract to fail. Haldane does not think it failed at all, and Okafor-Lind points to defeated amendments and the shutdowns.

options.text: Okafor-Lind argues that the new Republican majority transformed national policy for decades, while Haldane contends that its accomplishments were mostly symbolic and quickly reversed by Democrats.
options.label: reversal
options.why: This swaps the two arguments. Haldane is the one who stresses lasting change, and Okafor-Lind is the one who questions how much the majority achieved.

options.text: Haldane emphasizes debates over foreign policy after the collapse of the Soviet Union, while Okafor-Lind stresses how new computer technology was reshaping the economy and the workforce.
options.label: unrelated_development
options.why: Both excerpts deal with congressional politics and the federal budget. Neither discusses post-Cold War foreign policy or the technology economy.

facts: Republicans won majorities in both the House and Senate in the 1994 midterm elections; it was their first House majority since the 1954 elections.
House Republican candidates released the Contract with America in September 1994.

items.stem: Which of the following developments in the late 1990s would most directly support Haldane's argument over Okafor-Lind's?

options.text: Clinton's 1996 signing of a law replacing Aid to Families with Dependent Children with time-limited block grants
options.label: key
options.why: The 1996 welfare reform law (PRWORA) ended AFDC, an entitlement dating to the New Deal, and replaced it with TANF block grants that had work requirements and time limits. A Democratic president signing a long-standing conservative goal supports Haldane's claim that the political center moved right.

options.text: The Supreme Court's 1998 decision striking down the line-item veto power that the Republican Congress had granted the president in 1996
options.label: reversal
options.why: A Contract measure being struck down shows the Contract's limits. That fits Okafor-Lind's view of a thin record better than Haldane's.

options.text: The House of Representatives' vote in December 1998 to impeach President Clinton on charges of perjury and obstruction of justice
options.label: true_but_not_responsive
options.why: The impeachment shows the deepening partisan distrust Okafor-Lind describes. It does not show a lasting rightward shift in policy.

options.text: Congressional approval in 1993 of the North American Free Trade Agreement through a coalition of Republicans and moderate Democrats
options.label: wrong_period
