options.why: NAFTA passed in 1993, before the Contract and the 1994 elections, so it cannot show that the Contract had any effect.

facts: In 1996 Clinton signed the Personal Responsibility and Work Opportunity Reconciliation Act, which replaced AFDC with Temporary Assistance for Needy Families.
The Supreme Court struck down the Line Item Veto Act in Clinton v. City of New York (1998).

items.stem: Which of the following provides the most direct context for the 1994 election results that both excerpts describe?

options.text: Voter frustration after the Clinton administration's plan for universal health insurance collapsed in Congress
options.label: key
options.why: Clinton's health care reform plan failed in Congress in 1994. Together with the 1993 tax increase, that failure fed criticism of 'big government' and helped Republicans win control of Congress that November.

options.text: Public outrage over the Iran-Contra affair, in which officials secretly sold arms to Iran to fund the Nicaraguan Contras
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The Iran-Contra affair came to light in 1986 under Reagan, about eight years before the 1994 elections, and it hurt Republicans, not Democrats.

options.text: Lingering anger over the Watergate scandal, which had driven a Republican president from office and badly discredited his party
options.label: reversal
options.why: Watergate (1972 to 1974) helped Democrats in the 1974 midterms. It did not help Republicans win in 1994.

options.text: Growing opposition to the war in Iraq, which had turned public opinion against the administration's handling of foreign affairs
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The Iraq War began in 2003, and opposition to it helped Democrats retake Congress in 2006, not Republicans in 1994.

facts: The Clinton administration's health care reform proposal failed in Congress in 1994.
Republicans gained control of both houses of Congress in the November 1994 midterm elections.

items.stem: The agenda described in Haldane's excerpt most directly continued which earlier development in United States politics?

options.text: The 1980s conservative effort under Reagan to cut taxes, reduce regulation, and shrink federal social spending
options.label: key
options.why: The Contract's calls for balanced budgets, tax cuts, and a smaller federal government carried forward the conservative program of the Reagan years, including the 1981 tax cuts and deregulation.

options.text: The Great Society's commitment to using federal funds and new agencies to fight poverty and expand access to health coverage
options.label: reversal
options.why: The Contract tried to roll back federal social programs of the kind the Great Society created, such as Medicaid and the antipoverty programs, not extend them.

options.text: The New Deal coalition's support for federal labor protections, large public works programs, and a strong political role for unions
options.label: reversal
options.why: The Contract opposed the activist federal government that the New Deal coalition stood for.

options.text: The Progressive Era campaign to build federal regulatory agencies that would police large corporations and protect consumers from fraud
options.label: reversal
options.why: The Contract aimed to reduce federal regulation, while Progressives worked to expand it.

facts: Ronald Reagan signed major income tax cuts in the Economic Recovery Tax Act of 1981 and pursued deregulation in the 1980s.
The Contract with America (1994) called for a balanced budget amendment, tax cuts, and reductions in the size of the federal government.

input.title: A Western Memorial for Roads, Canals, and a Home Market, 1829

sources.title: Memorial of the Farmers and Mechanics of Elk Prairie, Indiana
sources.attribution: Petition sent to the United States Congress by residents of the fictional town of Elk Prairie, Indiana, December 1829 (ALTON-composed, in the style of a western petition to Congress)
sources.body: To the Honorable the Senate and House of Representatives: The undersigned farmers, millers, and mechanics of Elk Prairie respectfully represent that the produce of our fields finds no market worth the name. A barrel of flour that brings five dollars at Baltimore fetches scarcely two at our landing. The difference goes to the wagoner and to the long, dangerous passage by flatboat to New Orleans. The great canal of New York has shown what one work of internal improvement can do, for the farmers of that state's western counties now sell their grain at prices close to those of the seaboard. We therefore pray that Congress carry the Cumberland Road westward across our state and lend its aid to the proposed canal joining the Wabash to Lake Erie. We ask no favor for one section alone. The Pittsburgh manufacturer, protected by the tariff, will buy our pork and wheat, and we will buy his iron and glass. In this way the Union will be bound together by interest as well as by affection.

items.stem: Which of the following best explains the purpose of the memorial?

options.text: To persuade Congress that federally funded transportation would tie western farms to national markets
options.label: key
options.why: The petitioners ask Congress to extend the Cumberland Road and aid a Wabash-Lake Erie canal so that their crops can reach markets at better prices. This reflects western interest in federal internal improvements in the 1820s.

options.text: To protest that the protective tariff enriched northeastern manufacturers at the expense of western and southern agricultural producers
options.label: reversal
options.why: This was the Southern complaint against the tariffs of the 1820s. The memorial instead praises the tariff for building up a manufacturing home market that would buy western crops.

options.text: To urge federal removal of Native American nations from the Old Northwest so that white settlers could claim and farm their fertile lands
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: Indian removal was a real policy in this period, but the memorial says nothing about Native land. Its requests concern roads, canals, and markets.

options.text: To demand that the Second Bank of the United States extend more generous credit to western farmers facing falling crop prices
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: Westerners did resent the Bank after the Panic of 1819, but the memorial never mentions banking or credit. Its complaint is about the cost of transportation.

facts: The National (Cumberland) Road was a federally funded road begun at Cumberland, Maryland, in 1811 and later extended westward toward Ohio, Indiana, and Illinois.
In the 1820s western farmers commonly shipped produce by flatboat down the Ohio and Mississippi Rivers to New Orleans.

items.stem: Which of the following developments would most directly support the memorial's argument that better transportation would raise the value of western farm produce?

options.text: The sharp drop in freight costs between Buffalo and New York City after the Erie Canal opened in 1825
options.label: key
options.why: The Erie Canal cut freight costs between the Great Lakes and New York City by roughly ninety percent. That raised the value of upstate and western produce, which is the evidence the memorial points to.

options.text: The rapid growth of cotton exports from the Deep South after the invention of the cotton gin in the 1790s made short-staple cotton profitable
options.label: unrelated_development
options.why: The growth of cotton exports was real, but it came from a new processing technology and the spread of slavery, not from improved transportation of western produce.

options.text: The rise in the number of New England textile mills after the Embargo of 1807 and the War of 1812 cut off imports of British cloth
options.label: true_but_not_responsive
options.why: This shows the growth of domestic manufacturing. It says nothing about whether transportation raised farm prices in the West.

options.text: The increase in voter turnout after many states eliminated property qualifications for white male voters during the 1820s and 1830s
options.label: unrelated_development
options.why: The expansion of the white male franchise was real, but it was a political change and gives no evidence about transportation and crop prices.

facts: The Erie Canal, connecting the Hudson River to Lake Erie, was completed in 1825.
The Erie Canal reduced freight costs between Buffalo and New York City by roughly 90 percent.

items.stem: The memorial was most likely written in the context of which of the following?

options.text: Debates over whether the Constitution allowed federal spending on roads and canals within states
options.label: key
options.why: From Madison's 1817 veto of the Bonus Bill to Jackson's 1830 Maysville Road veto, leaders argued over whether Congress had the power to fund internal improvements. That is the debate this 1829 petition enters.

options.text: Disputes between Federalists and Democratic-Republicans over Jay's Treaty and the nation's trade relations with Great Britain
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The fight over Jay's Treaty took place in the mid-1790s, decades before this petition, and it concerned foreign trade, not internal transportation.

options.text: Conflicts over the annexation of Texas and whether slavery would expand into lands acquired after the war with Mexico
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: These conflicts belong to the mid-1840s and the period after 1848, well after the 1829 memorial.

options.text: Arguments over the Missouri Compromise and whether Congress should keep a balance between the numbers of free and slave states
options.label: unrelated_development
options.why: The Missouri crisis was a real sectional dispute of 1819 and 1820, but it was about slavery's expansion, not about federal aid for transportation.

facts: President James Madison vetoed the Bonus Bill for internal improvements in 1817 on constitutional grounds.
President Andrew Jackson vetoed the Maysville Road bill in 1830, arguing that federal funding of a road lying entirely within one state was improper.

items.stem: The memorial's vision of manufacturers and farmers buying each other's goods most closely reflects which of the following economic programs?

options.text: Henry Clay's plan pairing a protective tariff with a national bank and internal improvements
options.label: key
options.why: Clay's American System aimed to build a national home market by protecting manufacturing, keeping a national bank, and funding transportation. The memorial pairs the tariff with roads and canals in the same way.

options.text: Thomas Jefferson's agrarian ideal of independent yeoman farmers selling their surplus crops freely to European buyers
options.label: reversal
options.why: Jefferson's agrarian vision looked to foreign markets and distrusted manufacturing, while the memorial welcomes a protected domestic industry as the farmer's customer.

options.text: Alexander Hamilton's Report on Manufactures, which Congress enacted in full with federal bounties for new industries in the 1790s
options.label: overstated
options.why: Hamilton did propose aid to manufacturing in 1791, but Congress never adopted most of the report, and it came a generation before this memorial.

options.text: The Jacksonian program of limited federal power that vetoed national funding for local roads and dismantled the national bank
options.label: reversal
options.why: Jacksonians opposed the federal activism the memorial requests. Jackson's vetoes and his war on the Bank cut against the American System.

facts: Henry Clay promoted the American System in the 1810s and 1820s: a protective tariff, a national bank, and federally funded internal improvements.
Congress chartered the Second Bank of the United States in 1816 and passed a protective tariff the same year.

input.title: The Cherokee Strategy of Law and Print, 1820s-1830s

sources.title: A historian on the Cherokee case against removal
sources.attribution: Harriet Vandermolen, historian, from Paper Sovereignty: The Cherokee Nation and the Limits of Law, 1817-1839, a book based on her lectures at Calder Springs College, 2011 (ALTON-composed, in the style of a scholarly monograph on Native American history)
sources.body: By the late 1820s the Cherokee Nation had built what its leaders believed was an unanswerable case for remaining in the Southeast. It adopted a written constitution in 1827, printed a bilingual newspaper at its capital of New Echota, and sent delegations to Washington carrying petitions signed by thousands. These were not gestures of surrender to white ways but a deliberate strategy: to meet the United States on the ground of law and print, where the Cherokee could argue as a sovereign nation bound to the republic by treaty. The strategy produced a striking courtroom victory, yet it could not protect Cherokee land. The decisive forces lay outside the courtroom: Georgia's hunger for territory, sharpened after gold was found in the hills in 1829, and a national government whose executive had no intention of defending treaty rights against a state. Legal standing, it turned out, depended on someone willing to enforce it.

items.stem: Which of the following would best support the author's claim that the Cherokee Nation's legal standing depended on someone willing to enforce it?
facts: In Worcester v. Georgia (1832) the Supreme Court ruled that Georgia law had no force within Cherokee territory.
President Andrew Jackson's administration did not act to compel Georgia to comply with the Worcester ruling.

options.text: After Worcester v. Georgia (1832), the Jackson administration made no effort to force Georgia to obey the ruling.
options.label: key
options.why: The excerpt refers to a courtroom victory that could not protect Cherokee land. Worcester was that victory, and the executive's refusal to enforce it is direct evidence that legal rights meant little without enforcement.

options.text: Sequoyah's syllabary, completed in 1821, allowed thousands of Cherokee to read and write in their own language within a few years.
options.label: true_but_not_responsive
options.why: Cherokee literacy supports the author's description of a strategy built on print. It says nothing about whether courts or the executive enforced Cherokee rights.

options.text: The Indian Removal Act passed Congress in 1830 only after a close vote, with many Northern members and some missionaries speaking against it.
options.label: true_but_not_responsive
options.why: The close vote shows that removal was controversial. It is not evidence about the enforcement of a court ruling, which is the claim the question asks about.

options.text: Seminole fighters in Florida resisted removal through years of armed warfare against the United States Army in the late 1830s.
options.label: unrelated_development
options.why: Seminole armed resistance was a different strategy pursued by a different nation. It does not bear on the failure to enforce the Cherokee's legal victory.

items.stem: Which of the following would most directly modify the author's portrayal of the Cherokee as pursuing a single deliberate strategy of resisting removal through law and print?
facts: In 1835 a minority Cherokee faction, the Treaty Party, signed the Treaty of New Echota, ceding Cherokee lands in the Southeast in exchange for land west of the Mississippi.
Principal Chief John Ross and the majority of Cherokee opposed the treaty.

options.text: In 1835 a minority faction of Cherokee leaders signed the Treaty of New Echota, ceding the nation's land in the Southeast.
options.label: key
options.why: The Treaty of New Echota shows that the Cherokee were divided, and that some leaders gave up on legal resistance and chose negotiated removal. That complicates the picture of one unified strategy.

options.text: Principal Chief John Ross carried petitions signed by thousands of Cherokee to Washington and protested removal before Congress throughout the 1830s.
options.label: reversal
options.why: Ross's petition campaigns are an example of the legal and political strategy the author describes. They support the portrayal rather than modify it.

options.text: Northern missionaries who lived among the Cherokee, some of whom were jailed by Georgia, publicly opposed removal in the 1830s.
options.label: true_but_not_responsive
options.why: Missionary opposition concerns white allies of the Cherokee. It does not show disagreement among the Cherokee about strategy.

options.text: Some wealthy Cherokee owned plantations worked by enslaved African Americans, following the agricultural patterns of their white neighbors.
options.label: true_but_not_responsive
options.why: Plantation slaveholding among elite Cherokee is accurate. It describes economic adaptation, not a split over how to resist removal.

items.stem: Georgia's demand for Cherokee territory described in the excerpt is best understood in the context of which broader development of the early 1800s?
facts: After the invention of the cotton gin in 1793, short-staple cotton cultivation spread rapidly across the Deep South in the early 1800s.
The spread of cotton increased demand for fertile land and for enslaved labor in the Southern interior.

options.text: The expansion of cotton cultivation into the Deep South, which raised demand for fertile land and enslaved labor
options.label: key
options.why: In the early 1800s the cotton boom drove white Southerners to push for Native lands in Georgia, Alabama, and Mississippi. This land hunger explains Georgia's pressure on the Cherokee alongside the 1829 gold discovery.

options.text: The Free-Soil movement, which sought to keep slavery out of the western territories gained from Mexico after the war
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The Free-Soil movement began in 1848, after Cherokee removal. It was also about slavery in the West, not about Southern demand for Native land.

options.text: The growth of commercial wheat farming in the Old Northwest, as canals such as the Erie Canal linked farms to Eastern markets
options.label: unrelated_development
options.why: This was a real part of the market revolution, but it took place in the Old Northwest. It does not explain Georgia's push for Cherokee land.

options.text: Federal laws granting free 160-acre homesteads to settlers who agreed to live on and improve western public land for five years
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The Homestead Act was passed in 1862, decades after removal, so it could not have shaped Georgia's demands in the 1820s and 1830s.

items.stem: Which later development most closely resembles the pattern in the excerpt, in which Native land guaranteed by treaty was taken after valuable resources were discovered on it?
facts: The Fort Laramie Treaty of 1868 recognized the Black Hills as part of the Great Sioux Reservation.
After gold was confirmed in the Black Hills in 1874, the United States took control of the region in 1877.

options.text: The seizure of the Black Hills from the Lakota in the 1870s after gold was found on land promised by treaty
options.label: key
options.why: As in Georgia after 1829, the discovery of gold on treaty-guaranteed land led to pressure from settlers and the federal government. The Lakota lost the land despite the 1868 treaty.

options.text: The Indian Reorganization Act of 1934, which ended allotment and restored a measure of tribal self-government on reservations
options.label: reversal
options.why: The 1934 act moved federal policy toward protecting tribal land and government, which is the opposite of the pattern of dispossession.

options.text: The Proclamation of 1763, which barred British colonists from settling on Native lands west of the Appalachian Mountains
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The Proclamation came before removal, not after, and it tried to limit settlement on Native land rather than allow it to be taken.

options.text: The Northwest Ordinance of 1787, which pledged that Native lands and property would never be taken without the Indians' consent
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The Ordinance came earlier, and its pledge of good faith runs against the pattern. It is not a later case of land being taken after a resource discovery.

input.title: Trade, Mills, and Jobs in a Piedmont County, 1990-2006

sources.title: Employment and Exports to Mexico, Alder Fork County, North Carolina, 1990-2006
sources.attribution: Prepared by the fictional Alder Fork County Workforce Board for a public hearing on trade and local jobs, 2007. ALTON-composed illustrative data, not real statistics (ALTON-composed, in the style of a county workforce report)
sources.body: The table shows the number of jobs in three sectors of a textile-producing county in the Carolina Piedmont and the value of county-made goods shipped to Mexico in selected years before and after the North American Free Trade Agreement took effect in January 1994.

columns: County goods shipped to Mexico (millions of dollars)

items.stem: Which of the following most directly contributed to the change in textile and apparel mill jobs shown in the table between 1994 and 2002?
facts: The North American Free Trade Agreement took effect on January 1, 1994, phasing out most tariffs among the United States, Canada, and Mexico.
After NAFTA, many labor-intensive manufacturers, including apparel firms, shifted production to lower-wage locations such as Mexico.

options.text: Lower tariffs among the United States, Canada, and Mexico encouraged firms to shift labor-intensive production to lower-wage sites
options.label: key
options.why: The table shows mill jobs falling from 8,900 in 1994 to 3,800 in 2002, right after NAFTA took effect in 1994 and removed trade barriers, which made relocating apparel and textile work to lower-wage Mexico profitable.

options.text: Rising union membership in Southern mill towns pushed wages above levels that firms could sustain, prompting a wave of plant closures in the region
options.label: reversal
options.why: Union membership was falling in the 1990s, and Southern textile mills had long had very few union members, so this gets the trend backward.

options.text: The Arab oil embargo sharply raised energy costs, making it unprofitable for American factories to keep running power-hungry looms and dye works
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The OAPEC oil embargo happened in 1973-1974, two decades before the 1994-2002 drop shown in the table.

options.text: Federal deregulation of the airline and trucking industries lowered shipping costs and drew mill workers away from factories into transportation careers
options.label: unrelated_development
options.why: Transportation was deregulated mostly in the late 1970s and early 1980s. It did not cause textile jobs to move abroad, and the table shows no shift of workers into transportation.

items.stem: Which of the following pieces of evidence from the table would best support a speaker at the 2007 hearing who argued that expanded trade under NAFTA harmed the county's industrial workforce?
facts: NAFTA went into effect in 1994.
Critics of NAFTA, including many labor unions, argued that it would cost American manufacturing jobs.

derived.desc: Percent change in textile and apparel mill jobs, 1994 to 2002
Ratio of goods shipped to Mexico, 2006 to 1990
Increase in service and retail jobs, 1990 to 2006

options.text: Textile and apparel mill jobs fell by more than half between 1994 and 2002
options.label: key
options.why: Mill jobs went from 8,900 to 3,800 (down about 57 percent) in the years right after NAFTA took effect. This directly backs the claim that the county's industrial workers were hurt.

options.text: The value of county goods shipped to Mexico nearly quadrupled from 1990 to 2006, rising every year listed
options.label: reversal
options.why: Shipments grew from 14 to 55 million dollars. NAFTA supporters would cite this rising export figure, so it works against the speaker's argument instead of supporting it.

options.text: Service and retail employment rose steadily across the period, adding about 7,600 jobs between 1990 and 2006
options.label: true_but_not_responsive
options.why: The number is correct, but service job growth does not show harm to industrial workers. If anything, it could be used to answer the speaker's argument.

options.text: Other manufacturing jobs grew between 1990 and 1998, rising from 3,100 to 3,600 positions during the decade
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: These numbers show manufacturing jobs growing during the early years of NAFTA. They do not support a claim that trade under the agreement harmed industrial workers.

items.stem: The overall employment trends shown in the table are best understood in the context of which broader development in the United States from the 1980s to the 2000s?
facts: From the 1980s onward, the share of U.S. workers in manufacturing declined while service-sector and information-based employment grew.
Deindustrialization and growing global economic integration reshaped many U.S. regional economies in the late twentieth century.

options.text: The shift of American jobs away from manufacturing and toward service work as the economy became more global
options.label: key
options.why: The table shows mill and factory jobs shrinking while service and retail jobs rose from 11,800 to 19,400. This matches the nationwide move toward a service economy within a more integrated world economy in Period 9.

options.text: The Sun Belt boom, as federal defense contracts and new highways drew factories and skilled industrial workers into Southern counties
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The Sun Belt boom built on defense spending was mostly a development of the 1950s-1970s. It also brought manufacturing into the region, the opposite of the factory losses in the table.

options.text: The growth of federal social programs under the Great Society, which created many new public-sector jobs in poor rural counties of the South
options.label: unrelated_development
options.why: The Great Society came in the mid-1960s. Its programs do not account for mill closures or private service-job growth in the 1990s and 2000s.

options.text: The end of the Cold War, which closed military bases and defense plants and thereby became the main reason Southern textile employment collapsed
options.label: overstated
options.why: Defense cuts in the 1990s did hit some local economies, but they were not the main force behind job losses in textiles, a consumer industry hurt by foreign competition and trade liberalization.

items.stem: The pattern in textile and apparel employment shown in the table was most similar to which development of the 1970s and early 1980s?
facts: In the 1970s and early 1980s, steel and auto employment in the Northeast and Midwest declined sharply as plants closed amid foreign competition, a region later called the Rust Belt.
During this period, many manufacturers relocated production to the South, the West, or overseas.

options.text: The loss of steel and auto jobs in Northeastern and Midwestern cities as plants closed amid foreign competition
options.label: key
options.why: Like the textile losses in the table, Rust Belt deindustrialization in the 1970s and early 1980s meant a long decline in an established industry as firms faced foreign competition and moved production elsewhere.

options.text: The rapid growth of factory employment in Southern and Western cities as manufacturers left high-wage unionized regions for lower-cost labor
options.label: reversal
options.why: This describes manufacturing jobs growing in the Sun Belt, the opposite of the steep fall in mill jobs in the table.

options.text: The rise in employment for women in the workforce as rising living costs and the feminist movement drew millions into paid jobs
options.label: true_but_not_responsive
options.why: More women did enter the workforce in the 1970s, but that was an overall rise in employment. It does not resemble one industry's jobs shrinking.

options.text: The expansion of manufacturing employment during the Second World War as federal contracts drove factory production to record levels nationwide
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: This is from the 1940s, not the 1970s, and it describes a boom in industrial jobs, not a decline.

input.title: The Northern Revolt of 1854: Kansas-Nebraska and the Republican Coalition

sources.title: Courthouse Crowds and the Making of the Republican Party
sources.attribution: Corinne Haldane, historian, from Courthouse Crowds: The Northern Revolt of 1854, a study of anti-Nebraska meetings in the Old Northwest, 2009 (ALTON-composed, in the style of a modern political historian)
sources.body: Historians once credited the Republican Party's birth to a rising tide of abolitionist conviction, but the record of 1854 points elsewhere. When Stephen Douglas's Kansas-Nebraska bill repealed the Missouri Compromise ban on slavery north of 36 degrees 30 minutes, Northern voters who had never joined an antislavery society filled courthouses and church halls to denounce what they called a broken bargain. At meetings from Wisconsin to Ohio, speakers said less about the enslaved than about the farmer and mechanic who would be shut out of the West if slaveholders claimed it first. Former Whigs, Free Soilers, and anti-Nebraska Democrats found common ground in that grievance, even as many remained indifferent or hostile to Black equality. Within two years this coalition had displaced the Whigs and outpaced the nativist Know-Nothings across much of the North. Its cement was resistance to slavery's spread, not a crusade to end slavery where it already stood.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes the author's main argument in the excerpt?
facts: The Kansas-Nebraska Act (1854) repealed the Missouri Compromise restriction on slavery north of 36 degrees 30 minutes by applying popular sovereignty to Kansas and Nebraska.
The Republican Party formed in 1854 from a coalition of former Whigs, Free Soilers, and anti-Nebraska Democrats opposed to the expansion of slavery.

options.text: Northern anger over opening western territory to slavery, more than abolitionism, united the early Republican coalition.
options.label: key
options.why: The author states the coalition's cement was resistance to slavery's spread rather than a crusade to end slavery, and that many members were not abolitionists.

options.text: The Republican Party grew directly out of abolitionist societies that demanded immediate emancipation throughout the Southern states.
options.label: reversal
options.why: This is the older view the author explicitly rejects; she notes most participants had never joined an antislavery society.

options.text: Nativist hostility toward Irish and German Catholic immigrants was the main force that held the early Republican coalition together.
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: The author presents the nativist Know-Nothings as rivals the Republicans outpaced, not as the source of Republican unity.

options.text: Douglas designed the Kansas-Nebraska Act chiefly to weaken the Whigs and strengthen Democratic control of Congress and the presidency.
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: The excerpt says nothing about Douglas's motives; it focuses on Northern reactions to the act.

items.stem: Which of the following pieces of evidence would best support the author's argument about what held the Republican coalition together?
facts: The Republican platform of 1860 denied the authority of Congress or a territorial legislature to give legal existence to slavery in any territory.
The 1860 Republican platform also affirmed the right of each state to order and control its own domestic institutions.

options.text: The 1860 Republican platform opposed slavery in the territories but affirmed each state's right to control its own institutions.
options.label: key
options.why: A platform that barred slavery's expansion while disclaiming interference with slavery in existing states directly confirms that free-soil, not abolition, defined the party.

options.text: William Lloyd Garrison's followers continued to denounce the Constitution as a proslavery compact and urge Northern separation from slaveholders.
options.label: true_but_not_responsive
options.why: Garrisonian radicalism stood apart from party politics and says nothing about what united Republican voters.

options.text: Know-Nothing candidates swept state offices in Massachusetts in 1854 by appealing to fears of Catholic immigrants and their influence.
options.label: true_but_not_responsive
options.why: Know-Nothing success shows nativism's appeal in a rival movement; it would complicate rather than support the claim about the Republican coalition.

options.text: The Liberty Party nominated James Birney for president in 1840 and 1844 on a platform that put opposition to slavery at its center.
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: This earlier third party predates the Kansas-Nebraska crisis and cannot show what united Republicans after 1854.

items.stem: The controversy over the Kansas-Nebraska Act described in the excerpt is best understood in the context of which broader development?
facts: The Missouri Compromise (1820) and the Compromise of 1850 were earlier attempts to settle whether slavery would expand into western territories.
The Mexican Cession following the Mexican-American War (1848) reopened the question of slavery in the territories.

options.text: Recurring conflict over whether slavery would expand into western lands as the United States acquired and organized territory
options.label: key
options.why: The act reopened the territorial slavery question that the Missouri Compromise, the Wilmot Proviso debate, and the Compromise of 1850 had tried to settle.

options.text: Debates over federal funding for roads and canals that divided supporters of Henry Clay's American System from Jacksonian Democrats
options.label: unrelated_development
options.why: Internal improvements debates were a Period 4 economic issue, not the context for the fight over slavery in Kansas and Nebraska.

options.text: Rising Irish and German immigration to Northern cities, which fueled competition for factory jobs and nativist political movements
options.label: true_but_not_responsive
options.why: Immigration shaped Know-Nothing politics, but it does not explain the dispute over repealing the Missouri Compromise line.

options.text: Southern resistance to protective tariffs, which led South Carolina in 1832 to declare federal tariff laws null and void within its borders
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The nullification crisis was an earlier dispute over tariffs and federal power, not over slavery in the territories.

items.stem: The political realignment described in the excerpt most directly contributed to which of the following developments later in the period?
facts: Abraham Lincoln won the 1860 presidential election without carrying any slave state.
South Carolina seceded in December 1860, followed by other Deep South states before Lincoln's inauguration in March 1861.

options.text: The secession of Deep South states after Lincoln won the presidency in 1860 without carrying any slave state
options.label: key
options.why: The sectional Republican coalition elected Lincoln with Northern votes alone, which Deep South states treated as grounds for secession.

options.text: The Supreme Court's ruling in Dred Scott v. Sandford that Congress had no power to bar slavery from federal territories
options.label: misattributed
options.why: The 1857 ruling came from the Taney Court's own reasoning and undercut the Republican program; the realignment did not produce it.

options.text: The breakup of the national Whig Party into hostile sectional factions following its heavy defeat in the presidential election of 1852
options.label: reversal
options.why: Whig collapse helped make room for the Republican Party; it was a cause of the realignment, not a result.

options.text: The passage of a strengthened Fugitive Slave Act that required Northern citizens to assist federal officials in capturing escaped slaves
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The Fugitive Slave Act was part of the Compromise of 1850, before the Kansas-Nebraska Act and the Republican Party existed.

input.title: A Friar's Plea from New Spain: Disease, Livestock, and Labor

sources.title: Letter from a Franciscan friar to the Council of the Indies
sources.attribution: Fray Andrés de Valcárcel, a fictional Franciscan friar serving in a Native town in central New Spain, letter to the Council of the Indies in Spain, 1578 (ALTON-composed, in the style of sixteenth-century missionary reports)
sources.body: Most Powerful Lords: I write from the town of San Miguel Tecalco, where I have served the Indians for nineteen years. When I came, this valley held some four thousand households. After the great sickness of these two years past, I count fewer than nine hundred. The old men say their grandfathers knew no such pestilence before the Christians came, and I believe them, for the Spaniards of the town fall ill and most recover, while the natives die whole houses at once. Meanwhile the cattle and sheep of the estancias multiply beyond number. They break into the maize fields at night, and the few who remain cannot guard them. I beg Your Lordships to order the herds kept far from the Indian towns and to lighten the tribute and labor owed by the survivors, for the dead cannot pay, and the living are made to pay for them.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes the purpose of the letter in the excerpt?
facts: Spanish colonists in sixteenth-century New Spain raised large herds of European cattle and sheep that damaged Native farmland.
Native communities in New Spain owed tribute and labor to Spanish colonists and the Crown under the encomienda and related systems in the 1500s.

options.text: To persuade royal officials to shield Native towns from livestock and ease the burdens on survivors
options.label: key
options.why: The friar asks the Council to keep herds away from Indian towns and to lighten tribute and labor, a common missionary appeal to the Crown on behalf of Native communities.

options.text: To justify expanding encomienda grants to Spanish settlers whose estates had lost their Native workers
options.label: reversal
options.why: The friar wants to reduce demands on Native survivors, the opposite of extending colonists' claims to their labor.

options.text: To request soldiers from the viceroy to suppress a Native uprising against Franciscan missions in the valley
options.label: unrelated_development
options.why: The letter describes disease and livestock damage, not armed resistance, and it is addressed to the Council of the Indies, not the viceroy.

options.text: To encourage the Crown to ship more American maize and cattle hides to Castile to profit from abundant harvests
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: The letter mentions maize fields being ruined, not surplus harvests, and makes no case for exports.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes a claim the author makes in the excerpt?
facts: European diseases such as smallpox killed Native peoples of the Americas at much higher rates than Europeans because Native populations had no prior exposure, beginning after 1492.
Central Mexico suffered severe epidemics in the sixteenth century, including a major outbreak in the late 1570s.

options.text: The sickness killed Native people at far higher rates than it killed the Spanish colonists
options.label: key
options.why: The friar contrasts Spaniards who 'fall ill and most recover' with natives who 'die whole houses at once.'

options.text: Spaniards and Natives suffered the sickness equally, so labor shortages burdened every community alike
options.label: reversal
options.why: The excerpt stresses that mortality was very unequal between the two groups.

options.text: Spanish livestock carried the pestilence into Native towns when the herds broke into the maize fields at night
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: The friar discusses livestock and disease as separate harms; he never says the animals spread the sickness.

options.text: Native survivors should be relieved of tribute entirely and allowed to leave the towns for Spanish estates
options.label: overstated
options.why: He asks only that tribute and labor be lightened, not abolished, and says nothing about moving to Spanish estates.

items.stem: The conditions described in the excerpt are best understood in the context of which of the following broader processes?
facts: After Columbus's voyages beginning in 1492, plants, animals, and diseases moved between the Eastern and Western Hemispheres in what is called the Columbian Exchange.
Europeans brought cattle, sheep, and horses to the Americas in the sixteenth century.

options.text: The exchange of plants, animals, and pathogens between hemispheres that followed Columbus's voyages
options.label: key
options.why: Old World diseases and livestock changing Native populations and land use are core parts of the Columbian Exchange.

options.text: The rise of the triangular trade linking British North American rum, African captives, and Caribbean sugar
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: That British-centered Atlantic trade developed in the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries and does not explain epidemics and herds in 1570s New Spain.

options.text: The competition among Catholic and Protestant European states that followed the Reformation in the sixteenth century
options.label: true_but_not_responsive
options.why: Religious rivalry did shape European colonization, but it does not account for disease and livestock in Native towns.

options.text: The search by French and English navigators for a Northwest Passage to the markets of Asia
options.label: unrelated_development
options.why: Northern exploration had nothing to do with conditions in central New Spain.

items.stem: The population decline described in the excerpt most directly contributed to which of the following developments in the Spanish colonies in the sixteenth century?
facts: As Native populations fell in the 1500s, Spanish colonists increasingly imported enslaved Africans for labor in the Americas.
The Spanish New Laws of 1542 limited the encomienda system but did not end Native forced labor; labor drafts such as the repartimiento continued.
The Pueblo Revolt took place in 1680.

options.text: Growing importation of enslaved Africans to supply labor in place of Native workers
options.label: key
options.why: Mass Native deaths created labor shortages, and the Spanish increasingly relied on enslaved Africans in the sixteenth century.

options.text: The Crown's complete abolition of Native forced labor through the New Laws issued in 1542
options.label: overstated
options.why: The New Laws limited the encomienda, but Native forced labor continued through labor drafts like the repartimiento, as the friar's complaint about labor shows.

options.text: The Pueblo Revolt that drove Spanish colonists out of New Mexico for more than a decade
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The Pueblo Revolt took place in 1680, in the seventeenth century, and had different causes.

options.text: The development of fur-trading partnerships with Native peoples like those the French formed along the St. Lawrence
options.label: misattributed
options.why: Fur-trade alliances describe French colonization, not the Spanish response to labor shortages.

input.title: Workforce Change at a New England Textile Mill, 1834-1854

sources.title: Operatives at the Haddon Falls Manufacturing Company, Massachusetts, 1834-1854
sources.attribution: Payroll summary prepared by a fictional company agent, Josiah Pell, for the corporation's Boston directors, Haddon Falls, Massachusetts, 1855; ALTON-composed illustrative data, not real statistics (ALTON-composed, in the style of a Lowell-system corporation payroll report)
sources.body: The table summarizes the size and makeup of the workforce, the number of looms tended by each weaver, and the average weekly pay of women operatives after the deduction for company board, at a fictional Massachusetts cotton mill organized on the Lowell model.

columns: Native-born New England women (percent of workforce)
Average weekly pay of women after board (dollars)

items.stem: The change in the number of looms tended per weaver shown in the table most directly reflects which of the following processes?
facts: In the 1830s and 1840s Lowell-system mill owners increased the number of machines each operative tended (the speedup and stretch-out) while cutting piece rates, prompting turnouts in 1834 and 1836.
Massachusetts did not enact a ten-hour law for women and children until 1874.

derived.desc: Increase in looms per weaver 1834 to 1854
Change in weekly pay after board 1834 to 1854

options.text: Mill owners intensified the pace of work to cut labor costs as competition in cloth production grew
options.label: key
options.why: Looms per weaver double while pay after board falls, matching the speedup and stretch-out that Lowell-system owners imposed in the 1830s and 1840s as cloth prices fell and competition rose.

options.text: State laws limiting the workday to ten hours forced owners to raise output per worker during shorter shifts
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: Ten-hour petitions failed in the 1840s; Massachusetts passed a ten-hour law only in 1874, long after the period of the table.

options.text: Collective bargaining agreements negotiated by national unions raised productivity in exchange for higher weekly wages
options.label: reversal
options.why: Mill operatives had no collective bargaining contracts in this era, and the table shows pay falling, not rising.

options.text: The adoption of interchangeable parts in federal armories allowed weavers to repair looms without machinists
options.label: unrelated_development
options.why: Interchangeable parts in armories were a real development but do not explain weavers being assigned more looms.

items.stem: Which of the following would best support an argument, based on the table, that working conditions for women mill operatives worsened during the 1840s?
facts: In 1845 the Lowell Female Labor Reform Association, led by mill women, petitioned the Massachusetts legislature for a ten-hour workday, prompting a legislative hearing.
In 1840 President Martin Van Buren set a ten-hour day for laborers on federal public works.

options.text: Mill women petitioned the Massachusetts legislature in 1845 for a ten-hour workday
options.label: key
options.why: The 1845 ten-hour petitions organized by mill women show operatives themselves protesting longer hours and heavier work, corroborating the rising loom assignments and falling pay in the table.

options.text: Mill magazines written by operatives published essays praising the opportunities for self-improvement in mill towns
options.label: reversal
options.why: Literary magazines celebrating mill life would tend to challenge, not support, a claim that conditions worsened.

options.text: Martin Van Buren set a ten-hour day for laborers on federal public works projects in 1840
options.label: true_but_not_responsive
options.why: The order applied to federal workers, not private textile mills, so it says nothing about mill conditions.

options.text: Mill corporations built supervised boardinghouses and required operatives to attend church
options.label: true_but_not_responsive
options.why: Boardinghouse supervision was part of the original Lowell design from the 1820s and does not show change for the worse in the 1840s.

items.stem: Which of the following best explains the change in the share of Irish-born workers at the mill between 1846 and 1854, as shown in the table?
facts: The Irish potato famine (1845-1852) caused a mass migration of poor Irish to the United States, many settling in northeastern cities and mill towns.
The Chinese Exclusion Act was passed in 1882.
The Know-Nothing (American) Party of the 1850s opposed Catholic immigration.

derived.desc: Change in Irish-born share 1846 to 1854 (percentage points)

options.text: Famine in Ireland drove large numbers of poor migrants to northeastern cities
options.label: key
options.why: The potato famine beginning in 1845 sent hundreds of thousands of Irish to the Northeast, giving mill owners a pool of workers willing to accept lower pay, which matches the sharp rise after 1846.

options.text: Federal immigration law restricted entry from Asia, steering employers toward European laborers
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: Federal restriction of Asian immigration came with the Chinese Exclusion Act of 1882, decades after the table.

options.text: The Know-Nothing movement urged manufacturers to hire newly arrived Catholic immigrants
options.label: reversal
options.why: The Know-Nothings were nativists hostile to Catholic immigrants, not promoters of hiring them.

options.text: Gold discoveries in California drew many New England men westward after 1848
options.label: true_but_not_responsive
options.why: The Gold Rush did draw men west, but the mill workforce was mostly women, and the rush does not explain the influx of Irish workers.

items.stem: The change in the makeup of the mill workforce shown in the table is most similar to which development in the later nineteenth century?
facts: From the 1880s to the 1910s, American industries increasingly relied on immigrant workers from southern and eastern Europe.
The Homestead Act was passed in 1862.

derived.desc: Decline in native-born women share 1834 to 1854 (percentage points)

options.text: Late-nineteenth-century factories came to rely heavily on immigrants from southern and eastern Europe
options.label: key
options.why: Like the replacement of Yankee mill women by Irish immigrants, later industrial employers turned to new immigrant groups from southern and eastern Europe as a low-wage workforce.

options.text: Large numbers of women took jobs in defense plants as men left for military service during the Second World War
options.label: reversal
options.why: This was native-born women entering industrial work in the twentieth century, the opposite of the table's trend of native-born women leaving.

options.text: Formerly enslaved people in the South entered sharecropping and tenant farming arrangements with landowners after the Civil War
options.label: unrelated_development
options.why: Sharecropping was an agricultural labor system in the South, not a shift toward immigrant factory labor.

options.text: Settlers claimed western land under the Homestead Act of 1862, expanding family farming on the Great Plains
options.label: unrelated_development
options.why: Homesteading concerned western land settlement and farming, not changes in the makeup of the industrial workforce.

input.title: A Virginia Veteran on the Proclamation Line, 1764

sources.title: Letter from a backcountry surveyor and former militia captain
sources.attribution: Josiah Haverill, a surveyor in Augusta County, Virginia, who served as a provincial militia captain in the French and Indian War, letter to a business associate in Williamsburg, 1764 (ALTON-composed, in the style of a colonial frontier letter)
sources.body: I served four campaigns against the French and their Indian allies, and was promised, as were all who enlisted under the governor's proclamation of 1754, a share of lands upon the Ohio. Now word comes from London that the King has drawn a line along the heads of the rivers, and that no subject may settle or survey beyond it. We are told this is to quiet the Indians after the late troubles at Detroit and Fort Pitt. But who bled to clear that country? Not the ministers at Whitehall. Ten thousand regulars are to remain among us, and Parliament now speaks of a stamp duty to support them. So we are to be taxed for an army that keeps us out of the very lands our blood purchased. I cannot think the Crown means to treat its American subjects as tenants rather than as Englishmen.

items.stem: The author's point of view in the excerpt is best described as that of

options.text: A colonial veteran who believed military service had earned colonists a right to western lands
options.label: key
options.why: Haverill cites his four campaigns and the 1754 land promise and argues that colonists' blood purchased the Ohio lands now closed by the Proclamation of 1763.

options.text: A royal official defending the boundary line as the surest way to avoid renewed warfare with American Indian nations
options.label: reversal
options.why: This states the Crown's justification, which the author reports only in order to reject it.

options.text: A Patriot leader calling on the colonies to declare independence and form a separate republican government
options.label: overstated
options.why: The author still calls himself an Englishman and appeals to the Crown. Colonists did not seriously call for independence until 1775-1776.

options.text: A Quaker pacifist objecting to the stationing of soldiers on moral grounds
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: The author is a soldier, and his objection is about paying for troops and losing land, not about the morality of war.

facts: The Proclamation of 1763 barred colonial settlement west of the Appalachian Mountains.
Virginia's governor promised land bounties in the Ohio country to volunteers in 1754.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes the author's main argument in the excerpt?

options.text: Colonists were being made to pay for an army that also barred them from lands they had helped win
options.label: key
options.why: The author's central complaint is that colonists will be taxed for troops who enforce the boundary that shuts them out of western lands.

options.text: Parliament should admit elected colonial delegates so that Americans could consent to any new stamp duty
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: The author mentions the stamp duty but never proposes colonial representation in Parliament.

options.text: The Crown should negotiate new treaties with Indian nations to purchase lands beyond the mountains for settlers
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: The excerpt proposes no treaty or purchase. It argues that the colonists already earned the land through war.

options.text: Regular troops were needed in the West to protect settlers from attacks such as those at Detroit
options.label: reversal
options.why: The author resents the stationing of regulars and does not defend it.

facts: Britain decided in 1763 to keep about 10,000 regular troops in North America.
Prime Minister George Grenville announced a proposed stamp duty in 1764, and Parliament passed the Stamp Act in 1765.

items.stem: The British policies described in the excerpt are best understood in the context of

options.text: Britain's effort to govern and pay for a greatly enlarged empire after defeating France
options.label: key
options.why: After the Treaty of Paris (1763), Britain held vast new territory and a large war debt. It responded with the Proclamation Line, a standing army in America, and new colonial taxes.

options.text: Britain's response to colonial boycotts and the Boston Massacre that followed the Townshend Acts of 1767
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The excerpt is from 1764, years before the Townshend Acts (1767) and the Boston Massacre (1770).

options.text: Britain's effort to win Iroquois support for a plan of colonial union proposed at the Albany Congress
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The Albany Congress met in 1754 at the start of the war. Its plan of union was never adopted and does not explain the postwar policies in the letter.

options.text: Britain's competition with Spain for Florida, which Spain had gained from Britain at the end of the war
options.label: reversal
options.why: In 1763 Spain gave Florida to Britain, not the other way around. The boundary dispute in the letter is about the trans-Appalachian West.

facts: The Treaty of Paris of 1763 transferred Canada and lands east of the Mississippi from France to Britain, and Florida from Spain to Britain.
The Seven Years' War left Britain with a large national debt.

items.stem: The conflict over western settlement on American Indian lands described in the excerpt continued most directly in which development of the 1790s?

options.text: Warfare between the United States and an Ohio Country Indian confederacy, ended by the Treaty of Greenville
options.label: key
options.why: White settlers kept pushing into the Ohio Country, which led to the Northwest Indian War. After the Battle of Fallen Timbers (1794), the Treaty of Greenville (1795) opened much of present-day Ohio to settlement.

options.text: The Whiskey Rebellion, in which western Pennsylvania farmers took up arms against a federal excise tax on distilled spirits
options.label: true_but_not_responsive
options.why: This was a 1790s frontier protest, but it was about a tax. It was not a conflict over settling Indian lands.

options.text: The forced relocation of southeastern Indian nations to lands west of the Mississippi River under the Indian Removal Act
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The Indian Removal Act passed in 1830, not in the 1790s.

options.text: The Quasi-War, an undeclared naval conflict with France that followed the XYZ Affair and the seizure of American ships
options.label: unrelated_development
options.why: The Quasi-War was a maritime and diplomatic conflict, and it had nothing to do with western settlement.

facts: The Northwest Indian War ended with the Battle of Fallen Timbers in 1794 and the Treaty of Greenville in 1795.
The Indian Removal Act was passed in 1830.

input.title: Revival and Reform in a Canal Town: Two Interpretations

sources.title: Excerpt A
sources.attribution: Ellen R. Marsh, historian, Fire Along the Canal: Revival and Reform in Western New York (fictional book), 2004 (ALTON-composed, in the style of a social historian of American religion)
sources.body: In the winter of 1831 the Presbyterian and Methodist congregations of Cayuga Falls, a canal town in western New York, held protracted meetings that ran for weeks. Preachers told converts plainly that sin was a choice and that a changed heart could be chosen too. That message carried beyond the meetinghouse. Within two years the town had a temperance society whose pledge rolls included canal boatmen and their wives, a female moral reform auxiliary, and a small antislavery society that sent petitions to Congress. Women, who made up most of the converts, wrote the petitions and gathered the signatures door to door. Reform in Cayuga Falls was not imposed from above. It was the work of ordinary people who had come to believe that they, and their nation, could be made perfect.

sources.title: Excerpt B
sources.attribution: Thomas A. Okafor, historian, Order in the Counting House: Class and Conversion in the Canal Towns (fictional book), 2011 (ALTON-composed, in the style of a labor and economic historian)
sources.body: The revival that swept Cayuga Falls arrived just as the town was being remade by the canal. Master craftsmen who had once housed and fed their journeymen now hired wage hands by the week and went home at night to separate neighborhoods. The leading converts were these employers, along with merchants and their families. Having lost the household authority that once governed workers' drinking and idleness, they sought a new kind of control. Mill owners and boatyard proprietors preferred to hire men who had signed the temperance pledge, and Sunday schools taught punctuality alongside Scripture. The reform societies spoke the language of Christian benevolence, but they also served a new commercial class that wanted a sober, disciplined, and dependable labor force.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes a key difference between the two excerpts' interpretations of reform in Cayuga Falls?
facts: Revivalists of the Second Great Awakening in the 1820s and 1830s emphasized free will and the possibility of moral perfection.
Temperance, moral reform, and antislavery societies multiplied in the 1830s, many drawing on evangelical converts.

options.text: Marsh traces reform to converts' faith in moral perfection, while Okafor stresses employers' desire for a disciplined workforce.
options.label: key
options.why: Excerpt A ends by crediting ordinary people who believed they could be made perfect; Excerpt B argues that reform served a commercial class seeking sober, dependable labor.

options.text: Marsh argues that reform was led mainly by wealthy merchants and mill owners, while Okafor argues that it was led by canal boatmen and other wage-earning laborers.
options.label: reversal
options.why: Reverses the excerpts: Marsh stresses ordinary people and women, while Okafor identifies employers and merchants as the leading converts.

options.text: Marsh claims that the revivals pulled converts away from political life, while Okafor claims that the revivals led converts directly into antislavery petition campaigns to Congress.
options.label: reversal
options.why: It is Marsh, not Okafor, who describes the antislavery petitions; Okafor does not discuss petitions at all.

options.text: Marsh focuses on the influence of itinerant Methodist preachers from the South, while Okafor focuses on Catholic immigrants arriving to dig and operate the canal.
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: Neither excerpt mentions Southern preachers or Catholic immigrants; both focus on local congregations and town residents.

items.stem: Which of the following developments of the period would best support Okafor's argument in Excerpt B?
facts: During the market revolution of the early 1800s, wage labor in workshops and factories increasingly replaced the artisan apprenticeship system in which journeymen lived in masters' households.
Charles Grandison Finney led major revivals in western New York in the 1820s and early 1830s, preaching that individuals could choose salvation.

options.text: The spread of wage labor in manufacturing, which weakened the older apprentice system that bound workers to masters' households
options.label: key
options.why: Okafor argues that employers lost household authority over workers as wage labor spread and turned to reform as a new form of control; the market revolution's shift to wage labor supports this.

options.text: The leadership of women in antislavery societies, where female converts organized petition drives and raised money to support abolitionist newspapers and lecturers
options.label: true_but_not_responsive
options.why: A real development, but it supports Marsh's emphasis on ordinary converts and women, not Okafor's class-control argument.

options.text: Charles Finney's preaching that individuals could freely choose salvation, which encouraged many converts to believe that American society itself could be perfected
options.label: true_but_not_responsive
options.why: Finney's free-will theology supports Marsh's argument about religious conviction driving reform rather than Okafor's economic explanation.

options.text: The founding of utopian communities such as Brook Farm, where reformers withdrew from commercial society entirely to experiment with cooperative living and shared labor
options.label: unrelated_development
options.why: Utopian withdrawal from commercial society does not show employers using reform to discipline wage workers, so it does not support Okafor's claim.

items.stem: The revivals and reform societies described in both excerpts are best understood in the context of which broader development of the early nineteenth century?
facts: The Erie Canal opened in 1825, linking the Hudson River to Lake Erie and spurring rapid commercial and population growth in western New York.
Western New York became known as the burned-over district because of the frequency of revivals there in the 1820s and 1830s.

options.text: Rapid commercial and population growth in western New York after the Erie Canal opened in 1825
options.label: key
options.why: Both excerpts place Cayuga Falls in a canal town being transformed by commerce; the Erie Canal's opening made western New York the burned-over district of revivals and reform.

options.text: The renewed religious enthusiasm of the First Great Awakening, which spread through the colonies following the preaching tours of George Whitefield
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The First Great Awakening occurred in the 1730s and 1740s, roughly a century before the 1831 revivals described.

options.text: The rise of nativist movements opposing the arrival of large numbers of Irish Catholic immigrants during the famine years of the late 1840s
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: Famine-era Irish immigration and the nativist reaction came after the early 1830s events in the excerpts, and neither excerpt concerns immigrants.

options.text: The spread of Transcendentalist thought among New England writers who rejected organized churches in favor of individual intuition and nature
options.label: true_but_not_responsive
options.why: Transcendentalism was a real current of the period, but the excerpts describe church-based evangelical revivals in western New York, not New England philosophy that turned away from churches.

items.stem: The kind of reform activism described in Excerpt A most directly contributed to which later development in the 1840s?
facts: The Liberty Party, formed by antislavery reformers, nominated James G. Birney for president in 1840.
The House of Representatives adopted a gag rule in 1836 to table antislavery petitions without debate; it was repealed in 1844.

options.text: The formation of the Liberty Party, which ran an antislavery candidate for president in 1840
options.label: key
options.why: Excerpt A describes converts forming antislavery societies and petitioning Congress; such evangelical abolitionism fed directly into the Liberty Party's founding and its 1840 presidential campaign.

options.text: The adoption of the House gag rule, which automatically tabled the antislavery petitions sent to Congress by local reform societies
options.label: reversal
options.why: The gag rule was a reaction against abolitionist petitioning by opponents of abolition, adopted in 1836 rather than the 1840s, not a product of reformers' activism.

options.text: The expansion of the cotton economy into Texas and the Southwest, as planters moved enslaved laborers onto newly annexed lands
options.label: unrelated_development
options.why: Cotton expansion was driven by planters and world demand for cotton, not by Northern evangelical reform, which opposed the spread of slavery.

options.text: The Democratic Party's embrace of evangelical moral reform, including support for state laws to restrict alcohol and keep the Sabbath
options.label: reversal
options.why: Jacksonian Democrats generally opposed using government to enforce evangelical moral reform; reformers were more often associated with the Whigs.

input.title: Passenger Arrivals at Mendell Bay, California, 1876-1886

sources.title: Foreign Passenger Arrivals Recorded at the Port of Mendell Bay, California, Selected Years, 1876-1886
sources.attribution: Annual return of the customs collector for the fictional port of Mendell Bay, California; ALTON-composed illustrative data, not real statistics (ALTON-composed, in the style of a federal customs district report)
sources.body: The table gives the number of arriving passengers of Chinese nationality and the number of all other foreign passengers landed at a fictional Pacific port in selected years from 1876 to 1886.

items.stem: The change in Chinese arrivals at the port between 1882 and 1884 shown in the table most directly reflects which of the following?

options.text: A federal law suspending the entry of Chinese laborers into the United States
options.label: key
options.why: The table shows Chinese arrivals collapsing from 2,050 in 1882 to 15 in 1884. The Chinese Exclusion Act of 1882 suspended the immigration of Chinese laborers, which explains the drop.

options.text: An informal diplomatic agreement in which Japan agreed to stop issuing passports to laborers bound for the United States
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The Gentlemen's Agreement of 1907-1908 came about twenty-five years later and applied to Japanese laborers, not Chinese ones.

options.text: The completion of the transcontinental railroad, which ended the demand for Chinese track crews in the West
options.label: true_but_not_responsive
options.why: The railroad was finished in 1869. Chinese arrivals went on for more than a decade afterward and peaked in 1882, so it cannot explain the sudden drop after 1882.

options.text: The economic depression following the Panic of 1893, which reduced demand for immigrant labor across the nation
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The Panic of 1893 came a decade after the drop. A nationwide depression also would not explain why arrivals of other foreign passengers held steady.

facts: Congress passed the Chinese Exclusion Act in 1882, suspending the immigration of Chinese laborers for ten years.
The transcontinental railroad was completed in 1869.

derived.desc: Percent change in Chinese arrivals, 1882 to 1884

items.stem: Which of the following claims is best supported by the data in the table?

options.text: Restrictions after 1882 cut Chinese arrivals while other foreign arrivals stayed roughly steady
options.label: key
options.why: Chinese arrivals fell by more than 99 percent between 1882 and 1884. Other foreign arrivals went only from 3,300 to 3,000 between 1882 and 1886, about a 9 percent decline. The restriction targeted one national group.

options.text: Chinese arrivals rose steadily throughout the decade as railroad and mining employers recruited workers from Guangdong
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: Chinese arrivals fell from 1876 to 1880, jumped in 1881-1882, and then collapsed. That is not a steady rise.

options.text: Federal restriction reduced arrivals of all foreign passengers at the port by more than half between 1882 and 1886
options.label: overstated
options.why: Other foreign arrivals dropped only about 9 percent, from 3,300 to 3,000. The steep decline applies to Chinese arrivals alone.

options.text: Chinese passengers made up the majority of all foreign arrivals at the port in every year shown in the table
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: Chinese arrivals were fewer than other foreign arrivals in every year shown. In 1876, for example, the figures were 520 against 1,900.

facts: The Chinese Exclusion Act of 1882 applied specifically to Chinese laborers, not to European immigrants.
Immigration from Europe remained high through the 1880s.

derived.desc: Percent change in other foreign arrivals, 1882 to 1886
Percent change in Chinese arrivals, 1882 to 1884

items.stem: The restriction of Chinese arrivals shown in the table after 1882 is best understood in the context of which broader development of the late nineteenth century?

options.text: Agitation by western workers who blamed Chinese labor for low wages during the depression of the 1870s
options.label: key
options.why: In the hard times after the Panic of 1873, groups such as the Workingmen's Party of California blamed Chinese workers for driving down wages. Their pressure helped win passage of exclusion in 1882.

options.text: The Know-Nothing movement, which organized politically against Irish and German Catholic immigrants arriving in eastern port cities
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The Know-Nothings peaked in the mid-1850s and targeted Catholic immigrants in the East, not Chinese laborers on the West Coast in the 1880s.

options.text: Federal efforts to assimilate American Indians by dividing reservation land into individual allotments under the Dawes Act
options.label: unrelated_development
options.why: The Dawes Act of 1887 dealt with Native American land and assimilation. It was not a cause of Chinese immigration restriction.

options.text: The rise of Social Darwinist thought that defended the fortunes of industrialists as the natural result of competition
options.label: true_but_not_responsive
options.why: Social Darwinism was real in this period, but in that form it justified concentrated wealth. The labor-driven campaign behind Chinese exclusion is the more direct context.

facts: The Panic of 1873 began a severe economic depression in the 1870s.
The Workingmen's Party of California, organized in 1877, campaigned against Chinese labor.

items.stem: How did the policy reflected in the table relate to federal immigration policy in the early twentieth century?

options.text: It set a precedent for barring immigrants by national origin, later broadened in the quota laws of the 1920s
options.label: key
options.why: Chinese exclusion was the first major federal law to restrict immigration by nationality. Exclusion was extended in 1892 and made permanent in 1902, and the 1920s quota acts carried restriction by national origin much further.

options.text: It was reversed within a decade when Congress restored open entry for Chinese laborers to meet western labor demand
options.label: reversal
options.why: Congress extended exclusion with the Geary Act in 1892 and made it permanent in 1902. It was not repealed until 1943.

options.text: It led Congress to abolish all federal immigration screening, leaving inspection of arrivals to individual state governments
options.label: reversal
options.why: Federal control of immigration grew instead. The federal government took over inspection and opened Ellis Island in 1892.

options.text: It prompted the Supreme Court to rule that children born in the United States to Chinese parents could not claim citizenship
options.label: reversal
options.why: In United States v. Wong Kim Ark (1898), the Supreme Court held that a person born in the United States to Chinese parents was a citizen under the Fourteenth Amendment.

facts: The Geary Act of 1892 extended Chinese exclusion, which was made permanent in 1902 and repealed in 1943.
The Immigration Act of 1924 set national-origins quotas.
In United States v. Wong Kim Ark (1898), the Supreme Court ruled that a U.S.-born child of Chinese parents was a citizen.

input.title: A Deacon's Worry: Church Membership and the Town in Massachusetts Bay, 1660

sources.title: Letter on the State of the Church at Hadleigh Falls
sources.attribution: Letter from Nathaniel Pruett, a fictional deacon of the church at the fictional town of Hadleigh Falls, Massachusetts Bay Colony, to the elders of a neighboring church, 1660 (ALTON-composed, in the style of a seventeenth-century New England church letter)
sources.body: At our last town meeting, held in the meetinghouse the second Monday of March, the inhabitants voted forty pounds for our minister's maintenance and laid out the new lots beyond the mill brook. Yet I observed with grief how few at that meeting may stand as members of the church. Our fathers came into this wilderness to plant churches in covenant with God, and they gathered ours of those who could declare the work of grace upon their souls. Their sons now till the land, sit on the town's committees, and keep the Sabbath soberly, but most have never related any such experience before the congregation. Their children therefore go unbaptized. If the covenant be not opened to such persons, I fear that within one generation our church will be a small remnant amid a town of strangers to it, and this commonwealth will lose its godly foundation.

items.stem: The author's point of view in the excerpt is best described as that of
facts: Puritan congregations in Massachusetts Bay required a public account of a conversion experience for full church membership in the 1630s-1650s.
Many second-generation New Englanders did not seek or achieve full church membership, which created concern among church leaders by the 1650s.

options.text: A church officer worried that strict membership rules endangered the church's place in the town
options.label: key
options.why: Pruett, a deacon, grieves that few townsmen are church members and fears the church will become a small remnant. That fits the real worry of Puritan leaders as second-generation colonists failed to qualify for full membership.

options.text: A dissenter who sought freedom of conscience for those who rejected the colony's established Congregational churches
options.label: reversal
options.why: The author wants to keep the established church strong and the commonwealth godly. He is not seeking freedom from it, as dissenters such as the founders of Rhode Island did.

options.text: A merchant who complained that religious restrictions were hindering the town's growing trade in the Atlantic world
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: The excerpt says nothing about trade. The author is a church officer, and he cares about baptism and covenant, not commerce.

options.text: A royal official who hoped to place the Puritan colony under the closer supervision of the English crown
options.label: misattributed
options.why: Crown officials did press Massachusetts after the Restoration, but the author is a local deacon worried about church membership, not about crown authority.

items.stem: Which of the following pieces of evidence would best support the concern the author expresses in the excerpt?
facts: Admissions to full church membership declined among second-generation colonists in mid-seventeenth-century Massachusetts.
The First Great Awakening revivals reached New England in the 1730s and 1740s.
Anne Hutchinson was banished from Massachusetts Bay in 1638.

options.text: Records showing that fewer second-generation colonists were admitted to full church membership
options.label: key
options.why: The author fears that the sons of the founders are not becoming full members. Evidence of falling admissions among the second generation would directly support that fear, and such a decline did occur in mid-seventeenth-century New England.

options.text: Accounts showing that revival preachers of the 1740s drew large crowds and many new converts in New England towns
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The Great Awakening came about eighty years after the letter. Its surge of conversions would cut against a forecast of decline, so it does not support the 1660 concern.

options.text: Court records showing that Anne Hutchinson was banished from Massachusetts Bay for challenging the colony's ministers
options.label: unrelated_development
options.why: The Hutchinson case of 1638 was about dissent and the authority of ministers. It says nothing about whether second-generation colonists were joining the church.

options.text: Ship lists showing that most Puritan migrants of the 1630s arrived in family groups rather than as single laborers
options.label: true_but_not_responsive
options.why: Puritans did mostly migrate in families, but how they arrived does not show whether their children later qualified for church membership.

items.stem: The town meeting described in the excerpt reflects which of the following features of seventeenth-century New England?
facts: New England towns held town meetings in which inhabitants voted on local matters such as dividing land and paying ministers in the seventeenth century.
