Virginia's headright system granted 50 acres for each person whose passage a settler paid.
Proprietary colonies such as Pennsylvania (1681) and Carolina (1663) were granted to individual proprietors or groups of proprietors.

options.text: Local self-government in which town inhabitants decided land divisions and ministers' support
options.label: key
options.why: The excerpt describes inhabitants voting money for the minister and laying out new lots. New England town meetings handled exactly these local decisions.

options.text: Direct rule by royal governors who appointed town officers and collected taxes for the Church of England
options.label: reversal
options.why: In 1660 Massachusetts governed itself under its charter, and towns chose their own officers. Its churches were Congregational, not Anglican.

options.text: The headright system, which granted fifty acres of land to settlers who paid for a laborer's passage
options.label: misattributed
options.why: The headright system belonged to the Chesapeake colonies. New England towns divided land among inhabitants by town vote.

options.text: Proprietary land grants made by a single owner who sold lots to settlers and set terms of local government
options.label: misattributed
options.why: Proprietary arrangements describe colonies such as Pennsylvania or Carolina. They do not fit the town-centered land system of Massachusetts Bay.

items.stem: Concerns like those expressed in the excerpt most directly contributed to which of the following developments in the decade after the letter was written?
facts: A synod of Massachusetts ministers endorsed the Half-Way Covenant in 1662, allowing baptized but unconverted members to have their children baptized.
Rhode Island received a royal charter in 1663 that guaranteed liberty of conscience.
The Dominion of New England was created in 1686, and Massachusetts passed its school law in 1647.

options.text: Synod approval of the Half-Way Covenant, permitting baptism of the children of baptized nonmembers
options.label: key
options.why: The author fears that children of baptized but unconverted parents go unbaptized and asks that the covenant be opened. The 1662 synod's Half-Way Covenant was the direct answer to that problem.

options.text: Rhode Island's royal charter of 1663, which guaranteed liberty of conscience in religious matters to all of the colony's inhabitants
options.label: unrelated_development
options.why: The charter falls within the decade, but it came from Rhode Island's own tradition of religious tolerance. It was not a response to falling membership in Massachusetts churches.

options.text: Creation of the Dominion of New England, which vacated colonial charters and restricted the holding of town meetings
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The Dominion came in 1686, well after the decade in question. It grew out of royal efforts at imperial control, not concerns about church membership.

options.text: A Massachusetts law requiring towns of fifty households to hire a schoolmaster to teach children to read
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The school law was passed in 1647, before the letter, so it could not have resulted from the concerns of 1660.

input.title: A New Jersey Petition for Gradual Abolition, 1796

sources.title: Address to the New Jersey Legislature on Gradual Emancipation
sources.attribution: Address of the Freehold Township Friends of Liberty to the New Jersey legislature, drafted by Elias Vreeland, a Monmouth County farmer and Revolutionary War veteran, 1796 (ALTON-composed, in the style of a post-Revolutionary antislavery petition)
sources.body: Gentlemen, we who address you tilled our fields under the threat of British arms, and some of us carried muskets at Monmouth beside Black men who fought for a liberty they do not yet enjoy. The Declaration of our independence holds that all men are created equal and are endowed with a right to liberty. How can a state that bled for that principle still hold many thousands of persons in bondage? We do not ask you to strip any citizen of the servants he now holds, for we respect property lawfully acquired under our former laws. We ask only that every child hereafter born of an enslaved mother be declared free upon reaching mature years, after serving long enough to repay the cost of his rearing. Our neighbors across the Delaware adopted such a course sixteen years ago, and their commonwealth has suffered neither ruin nor disorder. Let New Jersey no longer lag behind her sister states in honoring the cause for which we fought.

items.stem: The address's proposal that only children born after the law's passage be freed was most likely intended to
facts: Northern gradual abolition laws, beginning with Pennsylvania's in 1780, typically freed only children born after passage and left those already enslaved in bondage.
The U.S. Constitution (1787) barred Congress from prohibiting the importation of enslaved people before 1808.

options.text: reassure slaveholding legislators that abolition would respect existing property rights
options.label: key
options.why: The authors say they will not strip any citizen of servants he now holds and that they respect lawfully acquired property. Gradual laws in the North were written this way to win over legislators who worried about slaveholders' losses.

options.text: satisfy Quaker reformers who demanded that all enslaved people in the state be freed at once without compensation
options.label: reversal
options.why: The address rejects immediate emancipation outright, and calls for immediate, uncompensated abolition came mainly in the 1830s.

options.text: persuade Congress to use its new constitutional authority to end the importation of enslaved Africans before 1808
options.label: misattributed
options.why: The address is directed to a state legislature and concerns emancipation within the state. The Constitution also barred Congress from banning the slave trade before 1808.

options.text: win support for a plan to resettle freed Black children in a colony in West Africa once they came of age
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: The address says nothing about colonization. Organized colonization efforts such as the American Colonization Society came later, in 1816.

items.stem: Which of the following pieces of evidence would best support the authors' claim that a gradual plan would not ruin slaveholders?
facts: Pennsylvania's Act for the Gradual Abolition of Slavery (1780) freed no one already enslaved, and children born to enslaved mothers after the act had to serve until age 28.
Massachusetts court decisions in the early 1780s (the Quock Walker cases) effectively ended slavery there under the 1780 state constitution.
The Northwest Ordinance (1787) prohibited slavery in the Northwest Territory.

options.text: Pennsylvania's 1780 act freed no one already enslaved and bound enslaved mothers' children to serve until 28
options.label: key
options.why: This shows that the 'neighbors across the Delaware' left owners' current labor force in place and gave them decades of service from children, which supports the claim that slaveholders suffered no ruin.

options.text: The Northwest Ordinance of 1787 barred slavery from the territory north of the Ohio River, where few slaveholders had yet settled with their laborers
options.label: true_but_not_responsive
options.why: The Ordinance is accurate, but it applied to a federal territory with few slaveholders. It says nothing about how a gradual plan affected owners in an established state.

options.text: Massachusetts court rulings in the early 1780s held slavery incompatible with the state constitution's declaration of rights, ending it quickly
options.label: reversal
options.why: The Massachusetts rulings ended slavery quickly through the courts, not gradually. That is the opposite of a plan built to protect owners' existing property.

options.text: The cotton gin, invented in 1793, made short-staple cotton profitable and sharply raised the market value of enslaved laborers in the Deep South
options.label: unrelated_development
options.why: The cotton gin changed the Southern economy. It offers no evidence about how gradual emancipation affected Northern slaveholders.

items.stem: The address is best understood in the context of which broader development in the era of the American Revolution?
facts: Revolutionary-era natural rights ideals, expressed in the Declaration of Independence (1776), led some Americans to challenge slavery and other inherited hierarchies.
The Second Great Awakening and immediatist abolitionism arose mainly in the early-to-mid nineteenth century, especially the 1820s and 1830s.

options.text: Revolutionary claims of natural rights led some Americans to question slavery and other inherited hierarchies
options.label: key
options.why: The address appeals to the Declaration and to wartime sacrifice. This fits the way Revolutionary ideals led to Northern abolition laws, more manumissions, and challenges to other hierarchies.

options.text: Evangelical revivals of the Second Great Awakening inspired reformers to demand the immediate, uncompensated emancipation of all enslaved people
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The Second Great Awakening and immediatism came decades later, and the address calls for gradual emancipation, not immediate.

options.text: The new federal Constitution granted Congress authority to abolish slavery within any state that petitioned for national assistance
options.label: misattributed
options.why: The Constitution gave Congress no power to abolish slavery inside the states. Abolition in the North came through state action, which is why the address goes to a state legislature.

options.text: Expanding factory production in New England created a demand for free wage labor that made slave ownership unprofitable in the North
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: Factory growth in New England belongs mainly to the Market Revolution after 1810. The address also makes an ideological case, not an economic one.

items.stem: Gradual abolition laws like the one proposed in the address contributed most directly to which development in the early 1800s?
facts: Free Black communities in Northern cities grew in the early 1800s and founded independent institutions, including the African Methodist Episcopal Church, organized in Philadelphia in 1816.
Several Northern states restricted Black voting in the early 1800s, for example New York's 1821 constitution set a property requirement for Black men only.
The 1808 federal ban applied to the international slave trade; the interstate slave trade continued and grew.

options.text: The growth of free Black communities in Northern cities that founded their own churches and mutual aid societies
options.label: key
options.why: As gradual laws took effect, free Black populations grew in Northern cities and built independent institutions, such as the AME Church organized in Philadelphia in 1816.

options.text: The steady expansion of voting rights for free Black men in Northern states, which by the 1830s enjoyed suffrage on equal terms with whites
options.label: reversal
options.why: Northern states often restricted Black voting during this period. New York's 1821 constitution and Pennsylvania's 1838 constitution are examples, so this is the opposite of what happened.

options.text: The Missouri Compromise of 1820, which prohibited slavery in all federal territories and admitted Missouri as a free state alongside Maine
options.label: overstated
options.why: The Compromise admitted Missouri as a slave state and Maine as a free state. It barred slavery only in the Louisiana Purchase lands north of 36 degrees 30 minutes.

options.text: Congressional abolition of the slave trade between states in 1808, which halted the sale of enslaved people from the Upper South to the Deep South
options.label: misattributed
options.why: The 1808 ban covered only the international slave trade. The domestic trade from the Upper South to the Deep South grew after that.

input.title: Rival Responses to the Dred Scott Decision, 1857

sources.title: A Southern Editor Greets the Ruling
sources.attribution: Editorial by Lucius Harrow, editor of the Coosa Valley Sentinel, a newspaper in a fictional Alabama town, March 1857 (ALTON-composed, in the style of a Southern Democratic newspaper editorial)
sources.body: The Supreme Court has at last spoken, and the agitators of the North must bow. The Chief Justice and a majority of his brethren have declared what every Southern man has long known: the Constitution protects the slave as property in every territory of the Union, and Congress never possessed the power to shut our people out of the common domain. The Missouri line, which for a generation insulted the South, is struck down as void. Let the Black Republicans rave; they rave against the supreme law of the land. A citizen of Alabama may now carry his servants to Kansas with the same security as his horses. This judgment should close the question forever, and every true friend of the Union ought to accept it as final.

sources.title: A Northern Lawyer Answers the Ruling
sources.attribution: Speech by Silas Wendover, a lawyer, at a Republican meeting in the fictional town of Marlow Ferry, Ohio, April 1857 (ALTON-composed, in the style of a Northern Republican public address)
sources.body: Fellow citizens, we are told that a majority of the judges in Washington have settled the matter and that we must now be silent. I say the decision settles nothing but the designs of those who procured it. Dred Scott lived for years on free soil in Illinois and in the northern territory, yet the Court leaves him in bondage and declares that no person of African descent, though born on this soil and free, may claim the rights of a citizen. If Congress cannot keep slavery out of Kansas, what will prevent the next ruling from carrying it into Ohio? Our remedy is not riot but the ballot. Elect men who will hold the territories for free labor, and in time the Court itself will change.

items.stem: The authors of both excerpts would most likely agree that the Supreme Court's ruling in the Dred Scott case

options.text: denied Congress the power to prohibit slavery in the federal territories
options.label: key
options.why: Harrow celebrates that Congress 'never possessed the power' to exclude slaveholders and that the Missouri line is void; Wendover laments that 'Congress cannot keep slavery out of Kansas.' The 1857 ruling did hold the Missouri Compromise ban unconstitutional.

options.text: permanently resolved the national dispute over slavery, leaving no room for further political action by either section
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: Only Excerpt A hopes the question is closed; Wendover insists the decision 'settles nothing' and calls for political action at the ballot box.

options.text: strengthened popular sovereignty by leaving the status of slavery in each territory to the decision of its own settlers
options.label: reversal
options.why: Both authors describe slavery as protected in every territory, which undercut popular sovereignty instead of strengthening it.

options.text: required free states such as Ohio to permit slaveholders to keep enslaved people within their borders
options.label: overstated
options.why: Wendover only fears a future ruling might reach Ohio; neither author says this ruling already applied to the free states.

facts: In Dred Scott v. Sandford (1857), the Supreme Court under Chief Justice Roger Taney held that Congress could not prohibit slavery in the territories, declaring the Missouri Compromise restriction unconstitutional.
Dred Scott had lived with his owner in Illinois and in the Wisconsin Territory before suing for freedom.

items.stem: Which of the following developments in the years 1857 to 1860 would most directly refute the prediction in Excerpt A about the ruling's effect?

options.text: The Republican Party grew in the North and won the presidency in 1860
options.label: key
options.why: Harrow predicts the ruling will 'close the question forever,' yet the Republican Party, committed to keeping slavery out of the territories, kept gaining Northern support and elected Lincoln in 1860, showing that agitation intensified.

options.text: Congress adopted the Compromise of 1850, admitting California as a free state and enacting a stronger fugitive slave law
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The Compromise of 1850 came seven years before the ruling and cannot show how the country responded to it.

options.text: The Ostend Manifesto urged the United States to acquire Cuba from Spain, by purchase or by force if necessary
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The Ostend Manifesto dates from 1854, before the decision, and concerns proslavery expansion abroad, not reaction to the ruling.

options.text: The Thirteenth Amendment abolished slavery throughout the nation, ending the dispute over its extension into the territories
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The Thirteenth Amendment was ratified in 1865, outside the years named in the stem, and it ended the dispute instead of showing that it continued after 1857.

facts: The Republican Party, founded in 1854 to oppose the expansion of slavery into the territories, won the presidency with Abraham Lincoln in 1860.
The Compromise of 1850 admitted California as a free state and included a stronger Fugitive Slave Act.

items.stem: The debate reflected in the two excerpts most directly arose in the context of

options.text: violent clashes between proslavery and antislavery settlers in Kansas Territory after 1854
options.label: key
options.why: Both authors focus on Kansas. The Kansas-Nebraska Act (1854) opened the territory to popular sovereignty, and the violence that followed ('Bleeding Kansas') made slavery in the territories the central national issue when the Court ruled in 1857.

options.text: the nullification crisis, in which South Carolina rejected federal tariff laws and threatened to leave the Union
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The nullification crisis took place in 1832-1833 and was about tariffs, not slavery in the territories in the 1850s.

options.text: the secession of Southern states following the election of a Republican president and the formation of the Confederacy
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: Secession began in late 1860, after both excerpts were written; it was a later result of the sectional crisis, not the setting for these 1857 responses.

options.text: the rise of the American (Know-Nothing) Party, which campaigned to restrict the political influence of Catholic immigrants
options.label: true_but_not_responsive
options.why: The Know-Nothings were active in the mid-1850s, but nativism is not the issue either author takes up; both focus on slavery and the territories.

facts: The Kansas-Nebraska Act of 1854 repealed the Missouri Compromise line and left slavery in Kansas and Nebraska to popular sovereignty.
Violence between proslavery and antislavery settlers in Kansas in the mid-1850s became known as Bleeding Kansas.

items.stem: The position on Black citizenship that the author of Excerpt B criticizes was most directly reversed by which later development?

options.text: The Fourteenth Amendment's guarantee of citizenship to all persons born in the United States
options.label: key
options.why: Wendover objects that the Court denied citizenship to free people of African descent born in the United States. The Fourteenth Amendment (ratified 1868) made all persons born or naturalized in the United States citizens, overturning that part of the ruling.

options.text: The Emancipation Proclamation, which declared enslaved people in Confederate-held areas free and granted them citizenship
options.label: misattributed
options.why: The Emancipation Proclamation (1863) declared enslaved people in rebelling areas free but did not grant citizenship.

options.text: The Fifteenth Amendment, which barred states from denying men the right to vote on account of race or previous servitude
options.label: true_but_not_responsive
options.why: The Fifteenth Amendment (1870) dealt with voting rights. Citizenship had already been established by the Fourteenth Amendment.

options.text: The Supreme Court's ruling in Plessy v. Ferguson, which upheld state laws requiring racial separation in public facilities
options.label: reversal
options.why: Plessy (1896) upheld segregation and weakened the rights of Black citizens; it did not reverse the denial of citizenship.

facts: The Dred Scott decision (1857) held that people of African descent, enslaved or free, were not citizens of the United States.
The Fourteenth Amendment, ratified in 1868, declared all persons born or naturalized in the United States to be citizens.

input.title: Two Interpretations of Nixon's Opening to China and Detente

sources.title: Excerpt A: The Opening as Strategic Design
sources.attribution: Dorothea Kilbride, fictional diplomatic historian, The Triangle Game: American Statecraft and the Communist Powers, 1969-1976, fictional book, 2009 (ALTON-composed, in the style of a diplomatic history monograph)
sources.body: The opening to Beijing is best understood as a calculated move on a three-sided board. By 1969 the two great Communist states were no longer allies but rivals, and the new president and his national security adviser saw that Washington could profit from their quarrel. Better relations with China gave the United States leverage in Moscow, where Soviet leaders feared being caught between a hostile West and a hostile East. The administration set aside two decades of refusing to deal with the People's Republic not because its view of communism had softened, but because ideology had become a poor guide to power. Detente, in this reading, was containment by other means: a way to restrain Soviet ambitions through negotiation as well as strength.

sources.title: Excerpt B: The Opening as Improvised Retreat
sources.attribution: Leonard Achterberg, fictional political historian, Exit Strategies: Vietnam, the Home Front, and the Making of Detente, fictional book, 2014 (ALTON-composed, in the style of a political history monograph)
sources.body: Accounts that celebrate the grand design of triangular diplomacy overlook how much the opening to China grew from weakness rather than mastery. The war in Southeast Asia had drained the treasury, divided the public, and helped persuade the previous president not to seek another term. The new administration needed a way out of Vietnam that would not look like defeat, and it hoped Beijing might nudge Hanoi toward a settlement. Just as important, a dramatic presidential journey promised headlines at home in an election year. The diplomacy was real, but it was improvised, and its gains proved thin. Within a few years critics in both parties charged that detente asked too little of the Soviets, and by the end of the decade it had few defenders left.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes a key difference between the interpretations in Excerpt A and Excerpt B?
facts: Richard Nixon visited the People's Republic of China in February 1972, a presidential election year.
Nixon pursued Vietnamization and a negotiated exit from the Vietnam War beginning in 1969.

options.text: Excerpt A treats the opening as a deliberate bid for leverage over the Soviet Union, while Excerpt B stresses pressures from the Vietnam War and domestic politics.
options.label: key
options.why: Kilbride frames the opening as triangular strategy to restrain Moscow; Achterberg says it grew from weakness, the need to exit Vietnam, and election-year politics.

options.text: Excerpt A emphasizes the need to end the Vietnam War and win an election, while Excerpt B stresses using the Sino-Soviet rivalry to pressure Moscow into concessions.
options.label: reversal
options.why: Swaps the two arguments: Vietnam and domestic politics are Achterberg's emphasis, while leverage over Moscow is Kilbride's.

options.text: Excerpt A argues that the opening reflected a genuine softening of American hostility toward communism, while Excerpt B argues that it reflected a hardening of anticommunist commitment.
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: Kilbride explicitly says the shift came not because the American view of communism had softened, and Achterberg says nothing about hardened anticommunism.

options.text: Excerpt A claims the opening ended Cold War rivalry with both Communist powers, while Excerpt B claims the diplomacy produced no agreements at all with China or the Soviet Union.
options.label: overstated
options.why: Kilbride calls detente containment by other means, not an end to rivalry, and Achterberg says the gains were thin, not nonexistent.

items.stem: Which of the following developments would best support the argument in Excerpt A about the purpose of the opening to China?
facts: Nixon and Soviet leader Leonid Brezhnev signed the SALT I agreements and the Anti-Ballistic Missile Treaty at a Moscow summit in May 1972, three months after Nixon's trip to China.

options.text: The signing of the SALT I agreements at a Moscow summit only months after Nixon's visit to Beijing
options.label: key
options.why: A major arms control deal with the Soviets soon after the China trip fits Kilbride's claim that ties with Beijing gave Washington leverage in Moscow.

options.text: The Paris Peace Accords of 1973, which arranged the withdrawal of remaining American combat troops from Vietnam
options.label: true_but_not_responsive
options.why: A real result of the period, but it bears on Achterberg's Vietnam-exit argument, not on Kilbride's claim about leverage over the Soviet Union.

options.text: The War Powers Resolution of 1973, which Congress passed over a presidential veto to limit the president's ability to commit troops abroad
options.label: unrelated_development
options.why: A congressional check on executive war-making that says nothing about using China to gain leverage over Moscow.

options.text: The Truman administration's refusal in 1949 to recognize the new People's Republic of China after the Communist victory
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: Earlier nonrecognition is background to the policy that was later reversed, not evidence for why Nixon reversed it.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes the international context in which the opening to China discussed in both excerpts took place?
facts: Chinese and Soviet forces fought armed clashes along their border, including at the Ussuri River, in 1969.
The Sino-Soviet split had developed through the late 1950s and 1960s.

options.text: Growing hostility between China and the Soviet Union, including armed clashes along their border in 1969
options.label: key
options.why: The Sino-Soviet split, which turned violent in 1969, is the rivalry Kilbride describes and the opening Nixon exploited.

options.text: The Korean War armistice, which had brought Chinese and American forces into a negotiated truce along the thirty-eighth parallel
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The armistice came in 1953, nearly two decades earlier, and was followed by continued hostility, not a diplomatic opening.

options.text: Soviet efforts to pull China into a renewed military alliance aimed at forcing the United States out of Southeast Asia
options.label: reversal
options.why: By the late 1960s China and the Soviet Union were rivals, not partners renewing an alliance.

options.text: The collapse of Communist governments across Eastern Europe, which left the People's Republic of China searching for new partners
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: Eastern European communism collapsed in 1989, long after the 1972 opening.

items.stem: The detente described in the excerpts was most seriously undermined by which of the following later developments in the 1970s?
facts: The Soviet Union invaded Afghanistan in December 1979.
In response, President Jimmy Carter withdrew the SALT II treaty from Senate consideration, imposed a grain embargo, and announced a boycott of the 1980 Moscow Olympics.

options.text: The Soviet invasion of Afghanistan in 1979 and the American response to it
options.label: key
options.why: The invasion led Carter to shelve SALT II, impose sanctions, and boycott the 1980 Olympics, effectively ending detente, as Achterberg's note about its fading support suggests.

options.text: The Iran hostage crisis of 1979 to 1981, in which revolutionaries held American diplomats captive in Tehran for over a year
options.label: unrelated_development
options.why: The crisis hurt Carter politically, but it did not involve the Soviet Union and was not what ended superpower detente.

options.text: The fall of the Berlin Wall in 1989 and the reunification of Germany that followed within a year
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: These events came a decade later and marked the end of the Cold War, not the breakdown of 1970s detente.

options.text: The Camp David Accords of 1978, in which Carter brokered a peace agreement between the leaders of Egypt and Israel
options.label: unrelated_development
options.why: A Middle East peace agreement that did not cause the collapse of U.S.-Soviet detente.

input.title: Friars, Encomenderos, and the New Laws in New Spain

sources.title: Letter of a Dominican friar to the Council of the Indies
sources.attribution: Fray Anselmo de Zárate, a fictional Dominican friar, writing from Antequera in the valley of Oaxaca to the Council of the Indies, 1549 (ALTON-composed, in the style of mid-sixteenth-century missionary letters)
sources.body: Most powerful lords, I have walked these valleys for eleven years, and I tell you the people here are not beasts, as some in Mexico claim. They keep markets more orderly than those of Seville, they choose officers to govern their towns, and their children learn the catechism faster than our own. Yet the holders of encomiendas drive them to the mines at Taxco and the sugar mills of the coast, and whole villages are left with only widows. How can a people love the Gospel when it comes to them with the overseer's whip? Faith must enter by persuasion and good example, never by force. I beg Your Lordships to enforce the new ordinances His Majesty has given, and to let no Spaniard hold Indians as his own.

sources.title: Petition of a town council in New Spain to the Crown
sources.attribution: Petition signed by Hernando Villagómez, a fictional alderman, on behalf of the town council of a Spanish settlement in New Spain, addressed to the king, 1544 (ALTON-composed, in the style of colonial petitions against the New Laws)
sources.body: We who won this land at our own cost, with our own horses and arms, now learn that the new ordinances would take our encomiendas from our widows and sons. If this is done, the Spaniards will leave, and the Indians, left to themselves, will return to their idols and their idleness. It is the encomendero who builds the church in each town, pays the priest, and teaches the natives to work as Christians do. Without our labor and theirs, the mines will stand empty and Your Majesty's royal fifth will vanish. We ask only that the ordinances be suspended, so that this realm may remain both Christian and profitable.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes a similarity between the arguments in Excerpt A and Excerpt B?

options.text: Both treat the Christian conversion of Native peoples as a legitimate aim of Spanish rule in the Americas.
options.label: key
options.why: The friar wants the Gospel to reach Native peoples by persuasion, and the council claims encomenderos keep Native towns Christian. They disagree about forced labor, but both accept conversion as a proper goal, which matched Spanish policy in the period.

options.text: Both argue that the Crown should hand control of Native towns to Spanish settlers instead of royal officials and friars.
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: Only Excerpt B defends settler control. Excerpt A asks that no Spaniard hold Native people as his own.

options.text: Excerpt A defends compulsory Native labor in the mines, while Excerpt B warns that such labor is destroying Native communities.
options.label: reversal
options.why: This swaps the positions. The friar condemns the mine labor and the council defends it.

options.text: Both propose that enslaved Africans replace Native laborers so that the encomienda system can be brought to an end.
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: Neither excerpt mentions African labor, and Excerpt B wants to keep the encomienda.

facts: Spanish colonization of the Americas was justified in part as a mission to convert Native peoples to Christianity, a goal pursued throughout the 1500s.
The encomienda granted Spanish colonists the labor or tribute of Native communities in return for a duty to Christianize them.

items.stem: Which of the following, if true, would most directly support the argument about Native labor in Excerpt A?

options.text: Native populations on Hispaniola fell sharply within a few decades after encomienda labor began there.
options.label: key
options.why: The friar claims encomienda labor empties villages. The steep population decline on Hispaniola in the early 1500s under forced labor (along with disease) backs his warning.

options.text: Large amounts of silver from the mines at Potosí and Zacatecas flowed to Spain and greatly enriched the royal treasury.
options.label: true_but_not_responsive
options.why: Silver wealth is real, but it fits Excerpt B's point about royal revenue better than the friar's claim that forced labor harms Native people.

options.text: Pueblo peoples in New Mexico rose up against Spanish missionaries and settlers in 1680 and drove them out for over a decade.
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The Pueblo Revolt happened more than a century after this debate, in another region, so it is not evidence for conditions in 1549 Oaxaca.

options.text: Spanish settlers who held encomiendas founded towns, built churches, and set up cattle ranches across much of New Spain.
options.label: true_but_not_responsive
options.why: This fits Excerpt B's claim that encomenderos built churches. It does not back the friar's argument that the system was destroying Native communities.

facts: The Taíno population of Hispaniola declined drastically in the decades after 1492 due to epidemic disease and forced labor.
The Pueblo Revolt took place in 1680.

items.stem: The debate shown in the two excerpts took place most directly in the context of

options.text: royal efforts to limit the power of conquistadors and encomenderos after Spain's conquest of the Aztec Empire
options.label: key
options.why: The Spanish Crown issued the New Laws in 1542 to restrict the encomienda and ban Native enslavement, partly to keep conquerors from becoming a hereditary nobility. The 'new ordinances' in both excerpts are these laws.

options.text: competition with English colonists who had set up profitable tobacco plantations around Jamestown in the Chesapeake
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: Jamestown was founded in 1607 and tobacco became its staple only later, decades after these excerpts were written.

options.text: Spanish and French rivalry over the fur trade and Native alliances in the Great Lakes and the St. Lawrence region
options.label: unrelated_development
options.why: French fur-trading rivalries in the north had nothing to do with labor policy in New Spain in the 1540s.

options.text: the spread of Enlightenment ideas about natural rights that challenged the divine authority of European monarchs
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The Enlightenment was an eighteenth-century movement. Both excerpts appeal to the king's authority and do not challenge it.

facts: The Spanish Crown issued the New Laws in 1542, restricting the encomienda and prohibiting the enslavement of Native peoples.
Hernán Cortés and his Native allies conquered the Aztec capital of Tenochtitlan in 1521.

items.stem: Spanish restrictions on Native enslavement, like those debated in the excerpts, most directly contributed to which development later in the sixteenth century?

options.text: Spanish colonists relied more and more on enslaved Africans as limits on Native enslavement grew
options.label: key
options.why: As the Crown restricted Native enslavement and Native populations declined, Spanish colonists imported more enslaved Africans. This helped the transatlantic slave trade grow.

options.text: The Spanish Crown ended all forced Native labor and required colonists to pay Native workers market wages in every colony
options.label: overstated
options.why: Forced Native labor went on through the repartimiento and the mita in Peru. The Crown regulated coerced labor but did not abolish it.

options.text: English colonizers adopted the encomienda system to organize tobacco labor in early Virginia and Maryland
options.label: misattributed
options.why: The encomienda was a Spanish institution. Chesapeake planters used indentured servants and later enslaved Africans.

options.text: Spanish authorities abandoned missionary work and allowed Native peoples to keep their own religious practices
options.label: reversal
options.why: Missionary efforts grew after the mid-1500s, and Spanish authorities kept suppressing Native religious practices.

facts: Spanish colonists increasingly imported enslaved Africans in the sixteenth century as Native populations declined and the Crown restricted Native enslavement.
Coerced Native labor continued in Spanish America through the repartimiento and the mita after the New Laws of 1542.

input.title: A London Merchant Defends the Roanoke Venture, 1587

sources.title: Letter urging renewed investment in a colony on the Roanoke coast
sources.attribution: Letter from Edmund Rawcliffe, a fictional London cloth merchant who had invested in the 1585 voyage to Roanoke, to fellow merchants, early 1587 (ALTON-composed, in the style of Elizabethan promotional writing)
sources.body: Good sirs, I hear that some of the men lately come home from the island of Roanoke speak ill of that country, saying they found neither gold nor plenty and went hungry. I answer that they went hungry because they would rather dig for mines than plant corn, and because they quarreled with the very natives who first fed them. The soil there bears maize twice in a season, the woods yield cedar and sassafras, and the waters are thick with fish. Let us send families this time, and not soldiers only, so that they may till the ground and stay. Consider also that the King of Spain grows fat on the silver of the Indies and turns it against us and against the true religion. A settlement on that coast would furnish goods we now buy dear from strangers, set our idle poor to honest labor, and give our ships a harbor near his treasure fleets. I pray you, venture your purses once more.

items.stem: Rawcliffe's purpose in writing the letter was most likely to
facts: Ralph Lane's Roanoke colonists, sent in 1585, abandoned the settlement and returned to England in 1586.
A new group including families sailed to Roanoke under John White in 1587.

options.text: persuade investors to fund another colony despite reports of failure
options.label: key
options.why: Rawcliffe answers returned men who 'speak ill of that country' and closes by asking merchants to 'venture your purses once more,' matching the effort to fund a new Roanoke venture after Lane's colonists returned in 1586.

options.text: petition the queen for a charter permitting dissenting Protestants to worship freely abroad
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: Seeking religious refuge drove later Separatist and Puritan settlement in the 1620s; the letter is addressed to merchants and is about profit and rivalry, not a petition for dissenters.

options.text: announce to London merchants the discovery of gold and silver mines near the Roanoke settlement
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: The letter admits the colonists found no gold and criticizes them for hunting mines instead of planting.

options.text: urge the crown to send soldiers to defend the settlers against attacks led by Powhatan's confederacy
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The Powhatan confederacy's conflicts were with Jamestown after 1607, and Rawcliffe actually asks for families rather than only soldiers.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes Rawcliffe's explanation for the hardships suffered by the earlier Roanoke colonists?
facts: The 1585-1586 Roanoke colonists depended heavily on food from the local Algonquian peoples, and relations broke down into violence.

options.text: The settlers' own choices, such as seeking mines over farming, caused their hunger
options.label: key
options.why: Rawcliffe says the men went hungry because they 'would rather dig for mines than plant corn' and quarreled with the natives who fed them, which blames the colonists' conduct.

options.text: The coast's poor soil and harsh climate made growing food impossible for any settlers
options.label: reversal
options.why: Rawcliffe praises the soil as bearing maize twice in a season, the opposite of this claim.

options.text: Spanish raids from Florida destroyed the colony's crops and supply ships before harvest
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: The letter mentions Spain only as a rival growing rich on silver, not as the cause of the colonists' hunger.

options.text: Native peoples refused all contact with the English from the moment the colonists first landed there
options.label: reversal
options.why: The letter says the natives 'first fed' the colonists before the English quarreled with them.

items.stem: Rawcliffe's references to the King of Spain best reflect which broader context of the late 1500s?
facts: Spain drew enormous silver wealth from American mines such as Potosí in the 1500s.
Protestant England and Catholic Spain were rivals, leading to open war and the Spanish Armada's defeat in 1588.

options.text: Anglo-Spanish rivalry fueled by religious conflict and Spain's American silver
options.label: key
options.why: The letter links Spain's 'silver of the Indies' to hostility toward England and 'the true religion,' reflecting Protestant England's rivalry with Catholic Spain that led to war in 1585-1588.

options.text: English acceptance of the Treaty of Tordesillas, which had granted England rights to North America's coast
options.label: misattributed
options.why: The 1494 Treaty of Tordesillas divided newly claimed lands between Spain and Portugal and gave England nothing. England ignored it rather than accepting it.

options.text: Competition among European powers to control the Atlantic slave trade under the Navigation Acts
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: England's Navigation Acts began in 1651, well after this letter, and the letter does not discuss the slave trade.

options.text: Spain's alliance with England against France for control of the fur trade along the Saint Lawrence River
options.label: unrelated_development
options.why: Spain and England were enemies in the 1580s, and the Saint Lawrence fur trade involved the French, not an Anglo-Spanish alliance.

items.stem: The colonizing venture Rawcliffe promotes was most similar to the English settlement at Jamestown, founded in 1607, in that both
facts: Jamestown was founded in 1607 by the Virginia Company of London, a joint-stock company chartered in 1606.
Jamestown suffered severe food shortages in its early years, including the 'starving time' of 1609-1610.

options.text: relied on private investors and struggled at first to feed their settlers
options.label: key
options.why: Roanoke depended on private investors, as Rawcliffe's appeal to merchants shows, and its colonists went hungry. Jamestown was funded by the joint-stock Virginia Company and nearly collapsed from food shortages.

options.text: were organized mainly to provide a refuge for Puritans seeking to purify the Church of England
options.label: misattributed
options.why: Religious refuge for Puritans describes Massachusetts Bay (1630), not Roanoke or Jamestown, which aimed at profit and rivalry with Spain.

options.text: quickly achieved prosperity by exporting tobacco grown by enslaved Africans on large plantations
options.label: overstated
options.why: Roanoke never prospered. Jamestown's tobacco boom came after 1612 and relied mostly on indentured servants at first, so 'quickly' and 'enslaved Africans' are wrong for its early years.

options.text: depended on Native laborers forced to work under the encomienda system established by the English crown
options.label: misattributed
options.why: The encomienda was a Spanish colonial labor system, not an English one.

input.title: The War of 1812 and the Remaking of Party Politics

sources.title: A Peace Without Victory, A Victory for Nationalism
sources.attribution: Historian Lucinda Ferrante-Holt, The Quiet Revolution of 1815: Parties and Power After the Second War with Britain, a fictional monograph published in 2009 (ALTON-composed, in the style of a historian's interpretive monograph)
sources.body: The War of 1812 settled almost nothing at the negotiating table. The Treaty of Ghent, signed in December 1814, restored prewar boundaries and said not a word about impressment. Yet the war transformed American politics. New England Federalists who gathered at Hartford that winter to demand constitutional amendments limiting embargoes and declarations of war had the misfortune of seeing their grievances reach Washington along with news of Jackson's triumph at New Orleans and of the peace. Their protest now looked like disloyalty, and the party never recovered as a national force. Meanwhile, Republicans who had once fought Hamilton's program learned from wartime chaos that the nation needed stronger central institutions. Unpaid troops, collapsing state banknotes, and roads too poor to move supplies taught that lesson. By 1816 they had chartered a new national bank and passed a protective tariff, borrowing their rivals' ideas even as they buried their rivals' organization.

items.stem: Which of the following does the author use as evidence for the claim that the Federalist Party lost its standing as a national force?
facts: The Hartford Convention of New England Federalists met from December 1814 to January 1815.
The Battle of New Orleans was fought in January 1815, and news of it and of the Treaty of Ghent reached Washington about the same time as the Hartford delegates.

options.text: Federalist demands from Hartford arrived just as news of peace and of New Orleans did
options.label: key
options.why: The author argues the Hartford protest looked disloyal because it reached Washington along with news of the victory at New Orleans and the Treaty of Ghent, and the party never recovered.

options.text: Federalist resistance to the Louisiana Purchase as an unconstitutional expansion of federal power
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: Federalists did criticize the 1803 purchase, but the excerpt never mentions it as evidence for the party's decline.

options.text: Popular anger at the Alien and Sedition Acts, which had punished Republican editors for criticizing the government
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The 1798 acts hurt Federalists in the election of 1800, which is an earlier stage of decline the excerpt does not discuss.

options.text: Federalist gains in New England after the Embargo Act of 1807 crippled the region's shipping trade
options.label: reversal
options.why: The embargo briefly revived Federalist strength. That is the opposite of decline, and the excerpt does not cite it.

items.stem: Which of the following developments would most directly modify the author's argument that Republicans embraced stronger central institutions after the War of 1812?
facts: In 1817 President James Madison vetoed the Bonus Bill, which would have funded internal improvements with federal money, arguing the Constitution did not authorize it.
Congress chartered the Second Bank of the United States in 1816.

options.text: Madison's 1817 veto of a bill to fund roads and canals with federal money
options.label: key
options.why: Madison rejected the Bonus Bill on strict-construction grounds. This shows that Republican nationalism had constitutional limits, which qualifies the author's claim about a turn toward central institutions.

options.text: Congress's decision in 1816 to charter the Second Bank of the United States for twenty years
options.label: reversal
options.why: The bank charter supports the author's argument instead of modifying it, and the excerpt already cites it.

options.text: James Monroe's easy victory in 1816 as the Federalist opposition collapsed in nearly every state
options.label: true_but_not_responsive
options.why: Monroe's win reinforces the claim that the Federalists collapsed. It says nothing that qualifies the Republicans' turn to central institutions.

options.text: Andrew Jackson's 1832 veto of the bill to recharter the Second Bank of the United States
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: Jackson's veto came about fifteen years later from a different party coalition. It does not show how Republicans acted in the years right after the war.

items.stem: The war described in the excerpt was fought in the context of which of the following?
facts: During the Napoleonic Wars, Britain and France both restricted neutral American trade, and Britain impressed sailors from American ships.
British forts in the Northwest were evacuated in 1796 under Jay's Treaty, and the Oregon and Maine boundary disputes were settled in the 1840s.

options.text: Conflict between Britain and France that led both to restrict neutral American shipping
options.label: key
options.why: The Napoleonic Wars led to British orders in council, French decrees, and impressment. These were the main grievances behind the 1812 declaration of war, and the excerpt mentions impressment.

options.text: Continued British occupation of forts in the Northwest despite the terms of the 1783 Treaty of Paris
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: Britain gave up those forts in 1796 under Jay's Treaty, well before 1812.

options.text: Spanish efforts to close the port of New Orleans and the Mississippi River to American farmers' goods
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: This issue was settled by Pinckney's Treaty and then by the Louisiana Purchase of 1803, so it was no longer the context for the war.

options.text: Anglo-American disputes over the Maine boundary and joint occupation of the Oregon Country
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: These disputes came mostly after the war, and they were settled by treaties in 1842 and 1846.

items.stem: The protective tariff policy described at the end of the excerpt most directly contributed to which of the following later developments?
facts: In 1832 South Carolina adopted an Ordinance of Nullification declaring the federal tariffs of 1828 and 1832 void within the state.
The Whiskey Rebellion took place in 1794.

options.text: South Carolina's attempt to nullify federal tariff laws in 1832
options.label: key
options.why: Protective tariffs that began in 1816 grew into the 1828 Tariff of Abominations and led to the Nullification Crisis. That crisis set Southern opposition to tariffs against federal authority.

options.text: The Missouri Compromise, which balanced free and slave states and set a line for slavery's expansion
options.label: unrelated_development
options.why: The 1820 compromise came from disputes over slavery in new states, not from tariff policy.

options.text: The Panic of 1819, which followed a collapse in cotton prices and tighter credit from the national bank
options.label: misattributed
options.why: The panic is usually blamed on speculation, falling prices, and Second Bank credit policy, not on the protective tariff.

options.text: The Whiskey Rebellion, in which western farmers resisted a federal excise tax on distilled spirits
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The rebellion happened in 1794, before the war, and it was a protest against an excise tax, not a tariff.

input.title: A Town Meeting Responds to the Fugitive Slave Act, 1850

sources.title: Address of a Citizens' Meeting at Harmon's Falls, Ohio
sources.attribution: Address adopted at a public meeting in Harmon's Falls, Ohio, presented by the meeting's chairman, schoolmaster Josiah W. Pratt, October 1850 (ALTON-composed, in the style of Northern antislavery town-meeting resolutions of 1850)
sources.body: Fellow citizens: Congress calls its late measures a settlement, and bids us rest content. But the bill for the recovery of fugitives makes every man in Ohio a slave catcher at the call of a federal commissioner. That commissioner is paid ten dollars when he hands the accused to the claimant, and only five when he sets him free. Is this not a premium paid upon bondage? The accused may not speak in his own defense, nor ask for a jury of his neighbors, while the affidavit of a stranger from across the river is taken as proof. We are told that California, admitted free, is our reward. We will not buy a free state on the Pacific with the liberty of our neighbors on the Ohio. Resolved, that no citizen of this town will aid any officer in seizing a fugitive, whatever the fine; and resolved, that we petition Congress for the speedy repeal of this law.

items.stem: The purpose of the address in the excerpt was most likely to
facts: The Fugitive Slave Act was passed in 1850 as part of the Compromise of 1850.
The act penalized those who obstructed the capture of fugitives or refused to assist officers, with fines of up to 1,000 dollars and imprisonment.

options.text: organize local refusal to assist in enforcing a new federal law and to seek its repeal
options.label: key
options.why: The resolutions pledge that no citizen will aid officers in seizing fugitives and call for petitioning Congress for repeal of the 1850 Fugitive Slave Act.

options.text: urge Congress to repeal the Missouri Compromise line and let territorial settlers decide on slavery by popular sovereignty
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: Repeal of the Missouri Compromise line came with the Kansas-Nebraska Act of 1854, and the address does not concern territorial organization.

options.text: persuade slaveholders in neighboring Kentucky to accept a plan of gradual, compensated emancipation
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: The address speaks to fellow Ohio citizens and Congress, not to slaveholders, and proposes no emancipation plan.

options.text: praise the measures of 1850 as a final settlement that would preserve the Union and calm agitation
options.label: reversal
options.why: The meeting rejects the claim that the measures are a settlement and condemns the fugitive law.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes a claim the author makes about the law discussed in the excerpt?
facts: Under the Fugitive Slave Act of 1850, commissioners received 10 dollars if they ruled for the claimant and 5 dollars if they freed the accused.
The 1850 act denied accused fugitives a jury trial and barred them from testifying on their own behalf.

options.text: The law's procedures and fees were structured to favor claimants over accused persons
options.label: key
options.why: The author points to the unequal commissioner fees, the denial of testimony and jury, and the acceptance of a claimant's affidavit as proof.

options.text: Congress had no authority to prohibit slavery in federal territories acquired from Mexico in the recent war
options.label: misattributed
options.why: This was a proslavery Southern argument, later adopted in Dred Scott, and the author makes no such claim.

options.text: The law was unnecessary because very few enslaved people had escaped across the Ohio River to free states
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: The excerpt objects to the law's injustice, not to its necessity, and gives no figures on escapes.

options.text: Northern acceptance of the law depended on admitting California as a slave state to balance the Senate
options.label: reversal
options.why: California was admitted as a free state, and the author refuses to trade the liberty of neighbors for that admission.

items.stem: The law criticized in the excerpt was adopted most directly in the context of
facts: The United States acquired the Mexican Cession through the Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo in 1848.
The Compromise of 1850 admitted California as a free state and strengthened the fugitive slave law as part of resolving disputes over slavery in the Mexican Cession.

options.text: disputes over whether slavery would expand into territory acquired from Mexico
options.label: key
options.why: The Compromise of 1850, including the Fugitive Slave Act and California's admission, resolved the crisis over slavery in lands taken in the Mexican-American War.

options.text: the crisis over South Carolina's attempt to nullify federal tariffs on imported manufactured goods
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The nullification crisis took place in 1832-1833, nearly two decades earlier, and concerned tariffs, not fugitives.

options.text: the Supreme Court's ruling in Dred Scott v. Sandford that Congress could not bar slavery from territories
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: Dred Scott was decided in 1857, after the 1850 law.

options.text: the rapid rise of the nativist Know-Nothing movement opposed to Irish and German Catholic immigration
options.label: unrelated_development
options.why: Nativism grew in the 1850s but did not produce the compromise over slavery and fugitives.

items.stem: Northern responses to the law like the one expressed in the excerpt contributed most directly to which of the following developments in the 1850s?
facts: Northern resistance to the Fugitive Slave Act, including rescues of captured fugitives in the early 1850s, angered many white Southerners.
The Fugitive Slave Act was not repealed until 1864.
In Ableman v. Booth (1859), the Supreme Court held that state courts could not override federal law on fugitive slaves.

options.text: Growing Southern conviction that the North would not honor the terms of the compromise
options.label: key
options.why: Northern defiance and rescues of fugitives convinced many Southerners that the North would not keep its side of the 1850 bargain, deepening sectional distrust.

options.text: Congressional repeal of the Fugitive Slave Act in 1852 in response to mass petitions from free-state voters
options.label: overstated
options.why: Petitions did not achieve repeal; the law stayed in force until 1864, during the Civil War.

options.text: A revival of the Whig Party, which united behind an antislavery platform and won the presidential election of 1852
options.label: reversal
options.why: The Whigs split over slavery and lost badly in 1852 to Democrat Franklin Pierce, then collapsed.

options.text: A Supreme Court decision affirming that state courts could override federal laws on the return of fugitives
options.label: reversal
options.why: In Ableman v. Booth (1859) the Court ruled the opposite, upholding federal supremacy over state courts.

input.title: Backing Into Slavery: Labor Change in the Tobacco Chesapeake

sources.title: Tobacco Planters and the Turn to Slave Labor
sources.attribution: Miriam Halloway, historian, Leaf and Bond: Labor on the James and York Rivers, 1640-1720, 2009 (ALTON-composed, in the style of a social history of the colonial Chesapeake)
sources.body: In the Chesapeake, slavery did not arrive as a finished system. Planters backed into it. For most of the seventeenth century, tobacco growers on the James and York Rivers preferred English servants bound for four to seven years, whose passage earned masters headrights to fifty acres of land. That preference eroded after 1660. Slower population growth and rising wages in England reduced the number of young men willing to sign indentures. Servants who outlived their terms crowded onto poor land and complained about taxes and frontier defense, grievances that exploded into armed revolt in 1676. When the Royal African Company lost its monopoly in 1698, independent traders brought far more captives into the Bay. Lawmakers, meanwhile, wrote the new order into statute, declaring in 1662 that a child's status followed that of its mother. By 1710, enslaved Africans had become the core of the field labor force. That outcome grew out of shifts in supply and price more than out of any single decision.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes the author's main argument in the excerpt?
facts: Chesapeake planters relied mainly on English indentured servants for much of the 1600s before shifting to enslaved African labor around 1700.
Bacon's Rebellion in Virginia took place in 1676.

options.text: Chesapeake planters adopted slavery gradually as the supply and cost of English servant labor changed.
options.label: key
options.why: The author says planters 'backed into' slavery and credits 'shifts in supply and price more than any single decision,' pointing to fewer English servants after 1660 and more African captives after 1698.

options.text: Chesapeake planters rejected indentured servants from the start because Africans were cheaper to buy and to feed.
options.label: reversal
options.why: The excerpt states that planters preferred English servants for most of the seventeenth century, so this reverses the timeline the author describes.

options.text: Virginia's elite deliberately planned a racial labor system in the 1620s to divide poor whites from enslaved Africans.
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: The author explicitly rejects the idea of a single planned decision and dates the shift to after 1660, not the 1620s.

options.text: The Royal African Company's monopoly was the main source of enslaved people for the Chesapeake through the 1700s.
options.label: reversal
options.why: The author argues that imports grew after the company lost its monopoly in 1698, when independent traders took over much of the trade.

items.stem: Which of the following, if true, would most directly challenge the author's argument about the causes of the Chesapeake shift to slave labor?
facts: Surviving Virginia court records from the 1640s show some Africans being held as servants for life, decades before slavery became the main labor system.
The Royal African Company lost its monopoly on the English slave trade in 1698.

options.text: Virginia courts had treated some Africans as servants for life well before English servants grew scarce.
options.label: key
options.why: If Africans were already held in lifelong bondage before the servant supply dropped, racial distinctions came before the economic changes the author stresses. That would weaken the claim that supply and price, not deliberate choices, drove the shift.

options.text: Rising wages in late seventeenth-century England made long colonial indentures less attractive to young English men.
options.label: true_but_not_responsive
options.why: This is true, but it supports the author's argument about a shrinking servant supply instead of challenging it.

options.text: After the Royal African Company lost its monopoly, private traders sharply increased slave imports into the Chesapeake Bay.
options.label: true_but_not_responsive
options.why: This is true and repeats the author's own evidence about a growing supply of captives, so it supports the argument and does not challenge it.

options.text: Puritan New England relied mainly on family farm labor rather than on large numbers of bound workers.
options.label: unrelated_development
options.why: Labor in New England is a real regional contrast, but it says nothing about why Chesapeake planters turned to slavery.

items.stem: The labor transition described in the excerpt is best understood in the context of which broader development of the period 1607-1754?
facts: In the 1600s and 1700s an Atlantic trade system linked colonial staple crops such as tobacco to European markets and to the African slave trade.
The Seven Years' War began in North America in 1754, at the very end of Period 2.

options.text: The expansion of an Atlantic trade system linking colonial staple crops, European markets, and African captives
options.label: key
options.why: Chesapeake tobacco was grown for English and European markets, and the growing supply of enslaved Africans came through the Atlantic slave trade. The excerpt's account of planters and slave traders fits inside this commercial system.

options.text: The spread of evangelical revivals that challenged established churches and encouraged colonists to question authority
options.label: unrelated_development
options.why: The Great Awakening was a real development of the 1730s and 1740s, but it was a religious movement and did not cause the labor shift the excerpt traces from 1660 to 1710.

options.text: The imperial rivalry with France over the Ohio River valley that led to the outbreak of the Seven Years' War in 1754
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The contest over the Ohio valley came decades after the shift to slave labor the excerpt describes, and it was about territory, not plantation labor.

options.text: The Spanish encomienda system, which granted colonists the labor of native peoples in return for their Christian instruction
options.label: misattributed
options.why: The encomienda belonged to Spanish colonies and to Native labor. It was not the framework for English planters in the Chesapeake.

items.stem: Compared with the Chesapeake labor transition described in the excerpt, the development of labor in the Carolina lowcountry after 1670 differed most in that
facts: Carolina was settled from 1670 largely by migrants from Barbados, who brought a plantation system based on enslaved African labor.
Georgia's trustees banned slavery in 1735, and the ban was repealed in 1751.

options.text: settlers from Barbados brought a reliance on enslaved Africans nearly from the colony's founding
options.label: key
options.why: The Chesapeake moved from servants to slaves over several decades. Carolina's Barbadian founders brought a West Indian model of slave labor with them, and enslaved Africans quickly became central to rice cultivation there.

options.text: planters there relied mainly on German and Scots-Irish indentured servants to grow rice and indigo into the 1750s
options.label: reversal
options.why: Lowcountry rice and indigo were grown mainly by enslaved Africans. German and Scots-Irish migrants settled mostly in the backcountry and other colonies.

options.text: the colony banned slavery in its early years, until trustees repealed the prohibition under pressure from settlers in 1751
options.label: misattributed
options.why: This describes Georgia, whose trustees banned slavery in 1735 and repealed the ban in 1751. It does not describe Carolina.

options.text: planters there used enslaved American Indians as their only bound labor, because Indian slave raiding supplied all field hands
options.label: overstated
options.why: Carolina did run a large trade in enslaved Indians, but enslaved Africans soon became the main plantation workforce. Calling Indians the 'only' bound labor overstates it.

input.title: A Georgia Town Prepares During the Cuban Missile Crisis

sources.title: Civil Defense Bulletin to the Households of Calder Springs
sources.attribution: Bulletin issued by Walter Brandt, civil defense director of Calder Springs, a fictional town in southern Georgia, October 24, 1962 (ALTON-composed, in the style of a local civil defense bulletin)
sources.body: To the Households of Calder Springs: On Monday evening the President told the nation that Soviet offensive missiles are being installed in Cuba, scarcely ninety miles from our coast, and that our Navy will stop any ship carrying such weapons to the island. Our town lies well within the reach of these missiles. I do not write to frighten you but to ask you to act. Every family should store two weeks of canned food and water in a cellar or in the inner room farthest from windows. The basement of the First Methodist Church and the county courthouse have been stocked as public fallout shelters, and the yellow and black signs are now posted. Schoolchildren will continue the drills they have practiced since spring. The President has chosen firmness over surrender, and the strength of the nation rests on calm, prepared citizens at home as much as on ships at sea. Keep your radio tuned to the civil defense frequencies marked on the dial, and do not crowd the telephone lines.

items.stem: Brandt's purpose in issuing the bulletin was most likely to
facts: On October 22, 1962, President Kennedy announced in a televised address that Soviet missiles were in Cuba and that the United States would impose a naval quarantine.
During the early 1960s federal and local civil defense programs urged Americans to prepare fallout shelters and emergency supplies.

options.text: prepare local residents for a possible nuclear attack while building support for the President's response
options.label: key
options.why: The bulletin gives practical shelter and supply instructions and praises the President for choosing firmness, reflecting civil defense efforts during the crisis after Kennedy's October 22 address.

options.text: urge residents to petition Congress for a declaration of war and an immediate invasion of Cuba by American troops
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: Brandt backs the President's quarantine, not a war declaration or invasion; nothing in the bulletin calls for congressional action.

options.text: persuade residents that the naval quarantine of Cuba was a reckless provocation likely to drag the nation into nuclear war
options.label: reversal
options.why: Brandt endorses the quarantine as firmness over surrender; he does not criticize it.

options.text: recruit local volunteers for the force of Cuban exiles being trained by the CIA to land at the Bay of Pigs
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The Bay of Pigs invasion failed in April 1961, more than a year before this bulletin, and the bulletin recruits no one.

items.stem: Which of the following would best support Brandt's claim that Soviet offensive missiles were being installed in Cuba in October 1962?
facts: In October 1962, photographs taken by American U-2 reconnaissance planes revealed Soviet missile sites under construction in Cuba.
The Soviet Union launched Sputnik in 1957, and the Berlin Blockade took place in 1948-1949.

options.text: Aerial photographs from U-2 reconnaissance flights showing missile sites under construction in Cuba
options.label: key
options.why: U-2 photographs taken in mid-October 1962 gave the direct evidence of Soviet missile sites that led to Kennedy's announcement, which Brandt repeats.

options.text: Reports that the Soviet Union had launched Sputnik, the first artificial satellite, into orbit around the earth in 1957
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: Sputnik showed Soviet rocket ability five years earlier but gives no evidence about missiles in Cuba in 1962.

options.text: Evidence that the Soviet Union had blockaded the land routes into West Berlin to force the Western powers out of the city
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The Berlin Blockade of 1948-1949 was an earlier Cold War crisis and says nothing about missiles in Cuba.

options.text: Records showing that the Castro government had nationalized American-owned sugar mills, oil refineries, and other property
options.label: true_but_not_responsive
options.why: Cuba did seize American property in 1960, which helped cause U.S.-Cuban hostility, but this does not prove that missiles were being installed.

items.stem: The civil defense measures described in the bulletin are best understood in the context of which broader development?
facts: After the Soviet Union tested an atomic bomb in 1949, the United States and the Soviet Union competed in a nuclear arms race, including the development of hydrogen bombs and ballistic missiles in the 1950s.
Detente and the SALT I agreement came under President Nixon in 1972, and large-scale American combat deployment to Vietnam began in 1965.

options.text: A nuclear arms race in which both superpowers expanded their arsenals and their means of delivering them
options.label: key
options.why: Fallout shelters and emergency supplies were responses to the growing nuclear and missile arsenals of the arms race, which the missiles in Cuba made feel immediate.

options.text: The pursuit of detente, in which the United States and the Soviet Union negotiated limits on strategic weapons
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: Detente and the SALT I agreement came in the early 1970s, after this bulletin, and eased tensions rather than causing shelter preparations.

options.text: A Red Scare in which congressional committees and loyalty boards investigated alleged communist influence in government
options.label: unrelated_development
options.why: The Red Scare dealt with fears of communists inside the country, not with preparing for nuclear attack from abroad.

options.text: The domino theory, which American leaders used to justify sending large numbers of combat troops to South Vietnam in 1965
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The large troop buildup in Vietnam came after 1962, and the domino theory concerned Southeast Asia, not civil defense at home.

items.stem: Which of the following best explains how the crisis described in the bulletin was resolved later in 1962?
facts: In late October 1962, the Soviet Union agreed to remove its missiles from Cuba in exchange for a United States pledge not to invade Cuba.
The United States also privately agreed to remove its Jupiter missiles from Turkey, but it did not withdraw from NATO or from Western Europe.

options.text: The Soviet Union removed its missiles from Cuba after the United States pledged not to invade the island
options.label: key
options.why: Khrushchev agreed to remove the missiles in exchange for a U.S. promise not to invade Cuba, which ended the crisis without war.

options.text: American forces invaded Cuba, destroyed the missile sites, and removed Fidel Castro's government from power
options.label: reversal
options.why: The United States never invaded Cuba during the crisis, and Castro stayed in power for decades.

options.text: A United Nations force occupied Cuba and supervised the dismantling of the missile sites and a new national election
options.label: unrelated_development
options.why: The UN was a forum for debate during the crisis, but no UN force occupied Cuba and no election was held.

options.text: The United States agreed to withdraw all of its troops and nuclear weapons from its NATO allies in Western Europe
options.label: overstated
options.why: The United States only privately agreed to remove its Jupiter missiles from Turkey; American forces stayed in Western Europe.
